nodes.title: Guide to Constrained Maximization
GUIDE TO PERFORM CONSUMER MAXIMIZATION
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{APPLICATION: Consumer Problem vs CE --- same KKT recipe, different feasibility check.}}


\begin{tabular}{p{4.5cm}|p{18cm}|p{18cm}}
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step}} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Consumer Problem (1 agent)}} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Competitive Equilibrium ($H$ agents)}} \\
\hline
\textbf{(0)} \emph{Setup: objective, choice variables, constraints.} \textcolor{orange}{Consumer: $p,w$ EXOGENOUS. CE: $p$ ENDOGENOUS, wealth $=p\cdot\omega^h$, plus market clearing.} &
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Objective (utility).}} $\max\; U(x)$, with $x=(x_1,\dots,x_N)\in\mathbb{R}^N_+$.

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Choice variables:}} the bundle $x=(x_1,\dots,x_N)$ --- \textbf{$N$ variables}.

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Constraints:}}
$\bullet$ Budget: $p\cdot x \le w$ \quad($p,w$ \emph{given / exogenous}).
$\bullet$ Non-negativity: $x_i \ge 0\;\forall i$.
$$ \boxed{\;\max_{x\ge 0}\; U(x)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad p\cdot x \le w.\;} $$
&
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Objective (utility).}} Each agent $h=1$: $\max\; U^h(x^h)$, $x^h\in\mathbb{R}^N_+$

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Choice variables:}} the bundles $\{x^h\}_{h=1}^{H}$, each $x^h=(x_1^h,\dots,x_N^h)$, \textbf{$N\cdot H$ variables};

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Constraints:}}
$\bullet$ Each agent's budget: $p\cdot x^h \le p\cdot\omega^h$ \quad(\textcolor{orange}{wealth $w^h=p\cdot\omega^h$ endogenous}).
$\bullet$ Non-negativity: $x_i^h \ge 0\;\forall i,h$.
\\
\hline
\textbf{(1)} \emph{Write FOCs --- one per choice variable, for each agent.} \textcolor{orange}{Consumer P: $N$ FOCs total (1 agent). CE: $N \cdot H$ FOCs total ($H$ agents).} &
\textcolor{blue}{One agent, $N$ choice variables} $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{$N$ FOCs}.

$\mathcal{L} = U(x) + \lambda\bigl[w - p \cdot x\bigr]$.
$$ \boxed{\;\tfrac{\partial U(x^*)}{\partial x_i} = \underbrace{\lambda}_{\text{from the BC}}, p_i \;\;\forall i = 1,\ldots,N.\;} $$
\emph{$N$ equations, each pinning down one $x_i^*$.}

{{img:2|w=680}} 

Notice what $\lambda$ is! $\lambda$ is the marginal value of relaxing the BC!! extremely interesting the lhs is equated to this. "Why one λ": one budget constraint ⇒ one shadow price. An agent has a single pot of wealth, so there's a single scarcity price on it, and every good must earn that same return per dollar at the margin (COMMON, not "EXOGENOUS"). This also explains the cross-agent side of Plot 3 perfectly: each agent has their own budget constraint. There is a within agent unification in bang for buck! 
If $\frac{MU_a}{p_a} > \frac{MU_b}{p_b}$, moving one dollar of spending from $B$ to $A$ raises utility (for the same dollar spent). So at an optimum no such move can be profitable ⇒ bang-for-buck must be equal across all goods.

&
\textcolor{blue}{$H$ agents, each with $N$ choice variables} $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{$N \cdot H$ FOCs}.

Each agent $h = 1, \ldots, H$ solves \emph{their own} consumer problem with their own multiplier $\lambda^h$:
$$ \boxed{\;\tfrac{\partial U^h(x^{h*})}{\partial x_i^h} = \lambda^h\, p_i \;\;\forall i = 1, \ldots, N,\;\; \forall h = 1, \ldots, H.\;} $$
\emph{$N \cdot H$ equations: $N$ per agent, $H$ agents.}

{{img:1|w=680}}
This plot is the counterpart of the FOC optimality conditions: 1) the focs are a within agent condition; and 2) it is obvious the MU cannot easily be the same across agents. Note here we have agents with heterogeneous utility functions!

\\
\hline
\textbf{(2)} \emph{Merge FOCs (take ratios) $\to$ optimality condition.} &
The famous optimality condition: Taking ratios of FOC$_i$ / FOC$_j$ eliminates $\lambda$:
$\underbrace{\dfrac{\partial U/\partial x_i}{\partial U/\partial x_j}}_{\substack{\text{MRS}_{i,j} = \text{internal exchange rate}\\ = -\,\text{slope indiff.\ curve}\;(\dagger,\ddagger)}} = \underbrace{\dfrac{p_i}{p_j}}_{-\,\text{slope budget}}.$

{{img:0|w=380}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{$N$-dimensional MRS.}} With $N$ goods, MRS is \emph{not} a single number --- it's a \textcolor{orange}{family of pairwise ratios}:
$$ \text{MRS}_{i,j} := \dfrac{\partial U/\partial x_i}{\partial U/\partial x_j}, \quad \text{total of } \binom{N}{2} = \tfrac{N(N-1)}{2} \text{ pairs.} $$
Optimality: \emph{every} pair satisfies $\text{MRS}_{i,j} = p_i/p_j$. Equivalently, \textcolor{orange}{all $N$ ratios $MU_i / p_i$ are equal}, with common value $\lambda$ (the multiplier). Note how when within agent liens touch thism eans ther eis no longer and incentive to trade x for y because the dollar MB is unified!
&
Same condition for each agent. Since the RHS is \emph{common} across agents (everyone faces the same prices):
$$ \boxed{\;\text{MRS}^1 = \text{MRS}^2 = \cdots = \text{MRS}^H = \tfrac{p_i}{p_j}.\;} $$
\textcolor{orange}{MRS equalization across all agents at CE.}
This, again, means they optimized against the same ratio of prices. Plus, it also means no profitable exchange is left.


\\
\hline
\textbf{(3)} \emph{Apply CS to identify binding constraints, THEN substitute (FOCS in budget).} &
\textbf{Which constraints bind?} Apply complementary slackness $\lambda g_0 = 0$ and $\mu_i g_i = 0$:
$\bullet$ \emph{Non-negativity}: $x_i^* > 0\;\forall i$, so $g_i > 0$, hence $\mu_i = 0$ by CS. 
$\bullet$ \emph{Budget $g_0$ binds} (i.e.\ $p \cdot x^* = w$): under strict monotonicity (more is strictly better), $\lambda > 0$, so by CS $g_0 = 0$ $\rightarrow$ \textbf{Always use budget as an EQUALITY.}


\underline{Substitute} the FOC ratios into the binding BC equation and get:
$$ \boxed{\;x_i^* = x_i^*(p, w)\;} \quad \text{(\textcolor{orange}{Marshallian demand}).} $$

&
Same, done for each agent separately. 
\\
\hline
\textbf{(4)} \emph{Market clearing} &
\textcolor{orange}{Embedded:} budget binds, nonneg auto from FOC. \emph{Nothing extra to check.}
&
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{CE viewpoint (decentralized).}} Aggregate market clearing is \emph{not} a constraint in any agent's problem --- it must be \textcolor{orange}{closed separately}:
$$ \sum_h x_i^{h*}(\hat p,\, \hat p \cdot \omega^h) = \sum_h \omega_i^h \;\;\forall i. $$
These $N$ equations determine the equilibrium price vector $\hat p$. SEE dedicated NOTE.

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Note on the Planner viewpoint (centralized).}} for the planner aggregate feasibility is \textcolor{orange}{embedded as a constraint from Step 1}, so it need not be checked separately.
\\
\end{tabular}



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Footnotes on MRS interpretation.}}

$(\dagger)$ \emph{Internal exchange rate.} At what rate is the consumer willing to exchange $x_2$ for $x_1$? If $\text{MRS} = 4/2 = 2$, then $MU_{x_1}$ is twice $MU_{x_2}$, so the consumer is willing to give up \textbf{2 units of $x_2$ for 1 unit of $x_1$} $=$ \textcolor{orange}{internal price ratio}.

$(\ddagger)$ \emph{Slope of indifference curve.} Along $\{U = \bar U\}$: $dU = 0 \Rightarrow MU_{x_1}\, dx_1 + MU_{x_2}\, dx_2 = 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{dx_2}{dx_1} = -\dfrac{MU_{x_1}}{MU_{x_2}} = -\text{MRS}.$



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Dynamics --- trade drives convergence (concrete numerical example).}}

\emph{Setup.} Consumer has $\text{MRS}_{b,a} = 2$: internally willing to give up \textcolor{blue}{$2$ units of $A$ for $1$ unit of $B$}. Market price: \textcolor{blue}{$1$ unit of $B$ costs $2.1$ units of $A$}, i.e.\ $p_b/p_a = 2.1$.

\textbf{Step 1 (compare).} $\;\text{MRS}_{b,a} = 2 \;<\; p_b/p_a = 2.1$. Market charges \textcolor{orange}{more for $B$} than consumer values it $\Rightarrow$ $B$ is \emph{overpriced} for this consumer.

\textbf{Step 2 (trade).} Consumer \textcolor{orange}{sells $B$, buys $A$}: pay $1$ unit of $B$, receive $2.1$ units of $A$ (better than internal rate of $2$).

\textbf{Step 3 (concavity of $U$ kicks in).}
$\bullet$ Less $B$ $\;\Rightarrow\; MU_B \uparrow$ (diminishing returns; see Plot 2).
$\bullet$ More $A$ $\;\Rightarrow\; MU_A \downarrow$.
$\bullet$ Hence $\text{MRS}_{b,a} = MU_B/MU_A$ \emph{rises} toward $p_b/p_a = 2.1$.

\textbf{Step 4 (stop at tangency).} When $\text{MRS}_{b,a} = 2.1$: now to give up $1$ unit of $B$ the consumer demands $2.1$ units of $A$ in compensation --- exactly what the market pays. \emph{No further profitable trade $\Rightarrow$ optimum reached.}

nodes.title: Application: Homothetic Preferences
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{HOMOTHETIC PREFERENCES --- demand scales linearly with wealth.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Definition (primitive: scaling property of preferences).}}
Preferences are \emph{homothetic} iff for any bundles $x, y$ and any $\alpha > 0$:
\[ \boxed{\;x \sim y \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\; \alpha x \sim \alpha y.\;} \]
\emph{Stated purely on the preference order $\sim$ --- the true definition.}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Characterization (corollary, functional form).}}
$U$ is homothetic iff
\[ U(x) = g\bigl(h(x)\bigr) \]
with \textcolor{blue}{$g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ strictly increasing} and \textcolor{blue}{$h: \mathbb{R}_+^N \to \mathbb{R}$ homogeneous of degree $1$}: $h(\alpha x) = \alpha\, h(x)\;\forall \alpha > 0$.

\emph{Example.} $U(x_1, x_2) = \ln x_1 + \ln x_2$: take $h(x_1, x_2) = \sqrt{x_1 x_2}$ (homogeneous degree 1) and $g(z) = 2 \ln z$. Then $g(h(x)) = 2 \ln\sqrt{x_1 x_2} = \ln(x_1 x_2) = \ln x_1 + \ln x_2 = U(x).\;✓$

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Property 1 --- MRS is constant along rays from the origin.}}

\emph{Concrete (1-good intuition).} If ``2 units of good $A$ $\sim$ 4 units of good $B$'' (exchange ratio $1{:}2$), then scaling by $\alpha = 4$: ``8 units of $A$ $\sim$ 16 units of $B$'' (still $1{:}2$). The willingness to substitute is preserved. The optimal point will have the same slope!

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Property 2 --- Indifference curves are radial scaled copies.}}

Pick a point $P = (x_1, x_2)$ on one indifference curve. Then for any $\alpha > 0$, the point $\alpha P = (\alpha x_1, \alpha x_2)$ lies on a \emph{different} indifference curve, but \emph{in the same direction} from the origin. Each indifference curve is the image of any other under a radial scaling.

{{img:0|w=720}}

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Property 3 --- Optimal consumption lies on a ray (income expansion path).}}

\emph{Claim.} If $x^*$ is optimal at prices $p$ and wealth $w$, then $\alpha x^*$ is optimal at the same prices with wealth $\alpha w$.

\emph{Proof.} Optimality: $\text{MRS}(x^*) = p_1/p_2$. By Property 1, $\text{MRS}(\alpha x^*) = \text{MRS}(x^*) = p_1/p_2$. So $\alpha x^*$ satisfies the same tangency condition. Budget: $p \cdot (\alpha x^*) = \alpha (p \cdot x^*) = \alpha w$. $\square$. The agent picks the \textcolor{orange}{same consumption ratio} (= direction in the bundle space) regardless of wealth. Wealth scales the bundle uniformly along that ray.

Corollary: $\;x_i^*(p, \alpha w) = \alpha\, x_i^*(p, w)$. Hence
\[ \boxed{\;\epsilon_{i, w} \;:=\; \dfrac{\partial \ln x_i^*}{\partial \ln w} \;=\; 1 \quad \forall i.\;} \]
\emph{Equivalently:} $x_i^*(p, w) = x_i^*(p) \cdot w$ and $v(p, w) = v(p) \cdot w$.

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why this matters: representative agent.}}
With homothetic preferences, \emph{aggregate demand depends only on total wealth, not on its distribution}:
\[ \sum_h x_i^*(p, w^h) \;=\; x_i^*(p) \cdot \sum_h w^h \;=\; x_i^*(p) \cdot W. \]
$\Rightarrow$ Replace many heterogeneous agents by a single \emph{representative agent} with total wealth $W$ --- a workhorse of macro.

\textbf{So think about the optimization:} there is a given aggregate $\omega_a/\omega_b$ ratio, and in the identical-homothetic case all agents pick the \emph{same} individual consumption ratio $x_a^h/x_b^h$ (because they share the same homothetic preferences, so ratios are wealth-independent and identical across agents). The aggregate consumption ratio --- being a sum of identical individual ratios --- equals that common individual ratio. Market clearing then forces it to equal $\omega_a/\omega_b$.

\bigskip\bigskip

nodes.title: Application: Quasilinear Preferences
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{QUASILINEAR PREFERENCES --- no wealth effect on non-numeraire goods.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Definition.}}
$$ \boxed{\;U(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_N) = \alpha\, x_1 + u(x_2, \ldots, x_N), \quad \alpha > 0.\;} $$
Good 1 is the \textcolor{orange}{numeraire}: utility \emph{linear} in $x_1$, so $MU_1 = \alpha$ is \textbf{constant} (no diminishing returns). $x_1$ unrestricted in sign (``money'', will see why).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 1 --- Two structurally different FOCs.}}

$\bullet$ \textbf{FOC for $x_1$:} $\;\alpha = \lambda p_1$. \emph{Does not pin down $x_1$!}, hence $\lambda^* = \alpha/p_1$ (constant), you see this is not pinning down an optimal quantity, once the BC will be used we will know ho wmuch each agent buys

$\bullet$ \textbf{FOC for $x_i$, $i \geq 2$:} optimal quantities pinned down by prices and alfa



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 2 --- Equimarginal principle (single agent).}}
Combining the FOCs: at interior solution ( $x_1^* > 0$ <- always check at the end) ...
Note how we are assumign each agent has the same alfa! Under such assumption, every good gives the same marginal-benefit-per-dollar (``bang for buck''):
$$ \frac{MU_1}{p_1} = \frac{\alpha}{p_1} = \frac{\partial u/\partial x_i}{p_i} = \frac{MB_i}{p_i} \quad \forall i. $$
The common level is fixed by the numeraire FOC at $\alpha/p_1$. \emph{This is the floor!} Note in the theory snippet you have the fact the MRS all have to be equal! Now if alfa is agent specific each agent will have a different floor. 

Once you buy enough of the other good and reach the floor, you stop buying it and buy only the numeraire good. 

Consequence:  $x_1^*(p, w) = w - \sum_{i\geq 2} p_i\, x_i^*(p)$, \emph{residual}: the numeraire absorbs all wealth, linear in $w$ with slope 1.


\textbf{Critical implication.} Same $MB/p$ across agents does \textbf{not} mean same $x_1$ (numeraire); 
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 3 --- Floor is the SAME across agents (CE with numeraire access).}}

\textbf{Critical implication.} Same $MB/p$ across agents does \textbf{not} mean same $x_1$ (numeraire); 
$$ \boxed{\;\frac{MB_i^h}{p_i} = \frac{\alpha}{p_1} \quad \forall h,\, \forall i.\;} $$

BUT, if agents have same preferences on the other goods: it means same they will consume the same $x_2^*$ (non-numeraire, since $\partial u/\partial x_2 = \alpha p_2$ pins a common $x_2^*$ when preferences are identical). All wealth differences go into $x_1$. 
So:  $x_i^*$ for $i \geq 2$ \textcolor{orange}{independent of $w$} $\Rightarrow$ wealth elasticity $\epsilon_{i,w} = 0$ for non-numeraire goods.



Interior $\Rightarrow$ $x_2^*$ independent of endowment $\Rightarrow$ same $x_2^*$ for all individuals $\Rightarrow$ Marshallian doesn't depend on wealth, personal demand is unchaned in endowments $\Rightarrow$ prices s.t. dpend on a marshallian indepenent of welath, so are indpeendent of endowment distribution, the idea is that no change in eprsonal demand is generatign no change in aggregate demand hence no change in prices. 

{{img:1|w=1100}}





\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 4 --- Geometric reading.}}
Indifference curves are \textcolor{orange}{horizontal translates} of one another (shifted along the $x_1$ axis), because you already consumed $x_2,..., x_3$ up to the bottom. Slope, that is the mrs. MRS depends \emph{only} on $(x_2, \ldots, x_N)$:
$$ \text{MRS}_{i,1} = \dfrac{\partial u/\partial x_i}{\alpha} \quad\text{(no $x_1$ in it).} $$

{{img:0|w=720}}


\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Worked example: same problem, two endowment configurations.}}

\emph{Setup.} $U^h(x_1, x_2) = \alpha\, x_1 + \ln(x_2)$ with $\alpha = 1$, $p_1 = 1$ (numeraire). Two configurations:
$\bullet$ \textbf{Case 1 (both interior):} $\omega = (10, 10),\; \omega^1 = (9, 9),\; \omega^2 = (1, 1)$.
$\bullet$ \textbf{Case 2 (Agent 2 at corner):} $\omega = (10, 10),\; \omega^1 = (9.5, 9),\; \omega^2 = (0.5, 1)$.

\begin{tabular}{p{10cm}|p{12cm}|p{12cm}}
\textbf{Operation} & \textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Case 1 (interior)}} & \textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Case 2 (corner)}} \\
\hline
\textbf{(1) Solve FOCs.}
For $x_2$: $u'(x_2) = \alpha p_2/p_1$ pins $x_2^*(p)$.
For $x_1$: $\alpha = \lambda p_1$ fixes the shadow price $\lambda$ but does \emph{not} pin $x_1$ (linearity). The level of $x_1$ comes from the budget. &$x_2$: $\dfrac{1}{x_2} = p_2 \;\Rightarrow\; x_2^*(p) = \dfrac{1}{p_2}$
$x_1$: $\lambda = 1$, $x_1$ unpinned (residual). &$x_2$: $\dfrac{1}{x_2} = p_2 \;\Rightarrow\; x_2^*(p) = \dfrac{1}{p_2}$
$x_1$: $\lambda = 1$, $x_1$ unpinned (residual). \\

\textbf{(2) Interior threshold} $\underline{w}(p) = p_2\, x_2^*(p)$. Wealth above this $\Rightarrow$ interior. This is about how much wealth you need to buy your optimal quantity (can you reach the optimum or not??) &$\underline{w} = p_2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{p_2} = 1$ &$\underline{w} = 1$ \\

Substitute into clearing (put focs into BC). 0.5 comes from: he has 0.5 units that have price 1!  &Not needed (both interior). &$x_2^{2*} = \dfrac{0.5 + p_2}{p_2} = \dfrac{0.5}{p_2} + 1$

\hline
\textbf{(7) Compute final allocations.} For each agent: $x_2^{h*}$ from FOC (interior) or $w^h/p_2$ (corner), then $x_1^{h*}$ from budget residual $x_1^{h*} = w^h - p_2 x_2^{h*}$. &$x_2^{1*} = 1/0.2 = 5$
$x_1^{1*} = 10.8 - 0.2(5) = 9.8$

$\Rightarrow$ buys 0.8 of $x_1$, sells 4 of $x_2$.

\begin{tabular}{p{4cm}|p{10cm}|p{10cm}}
 & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Col 2: IDENTICAL homothetic}} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Col 3: HETEROGENEOUS homothetic}} \\
\textit{Preferences} & both $U^h = x_a^{0.4} x_b^{0.6}$ & $U^1 = x_a^{0.2} x_b^{0.8}$, $\;U^2 = x_a^{0.8} x_b^{0.2}$ \\
\textit{Each agent homothetic?} & \textcolor{green}{✓} & \textcolor{green}{✓} \\
\textit{Same $r^*(p)$ across agents?} & \textcolor{green}{✓} & \textcolor{red}{✗} \\
\hline
\textbf{(1) Agent $h$'s problem.}
$\max U^h$ s.t.\ $p_a x_a + p_b x_b = w^h$, where $w^h = p_a \omega_a^h + p_b \omega_b^h$. &
\emph{Identical Marshallian structure in both columns;} &
\emph{the difference is only in $U^h$ (see row above).} \\
\hline
\textbf{(2) FOCs} (one per good) &
$0.4\, x_a^{-0.6} x_b^{0.6} = \lambda^h p_a$
$0.6\, x_a^{0.4} x_b^{-0.4} = \lambda^h p_b$
\emph{(same form for both agents)} &
Agent 1 ($\alpha = 0.2$): $0.2 \,x_a^{-0.8} x_b^{0.8} = \lambda^1 p_a$, $\,0.8\, x_a^{0.2} x_b^{-0.2} = \lambda^1 p_b$.
Agent 2 ($\alpha = 0.8$): $0.8\, x_a^{-0.2} x_b^{0.2} = \lambda^2 p_a$, $\,0.2\, x_a^{0.8} x_b^{-0.8} = \lambda^2 p_b$. \\
\hline
\textbf{(3) Ratio of FOCs} (kill $\lambda^h$) $\to$ $r^*(p)$ &
$\dfrac{x_a^h}{x_b^h} = \dfrac{0.4}{0.6}\,\dfrac{p_b}{p_a} = \dfrac{2}{3}\dfrac{p_b}{p_a} \equiv r^*(p).$
\textcolor{orange}{Same function for both agents.} &
Agent 1: $\dfrac{x_a^1}{x_b^1} = \dfrac{0.2}{0.8}\,\dfrac{p_b}{p_a} = \dfrac{1}{4}\dfrac{p_b}{p_a} \equiv r_1^*(p).$
Agent 2: $\dfrac{x_a^2}{x_b^2} = \dfrac{0.8}{0.2}\,\dfrac{p_b}{p_a} = 4\dfrac{p_b}{p_a} \equiv r_2^*(p).$
\textcolor{red}{Different functions: $r_1^* \neq r_2^*$.} \\
\hline
\textbf{(4) FOC ratio $+$ budget} $\to$ \emph{Marshallian demand}.
Take budget $p_a x_a^h + p_b x_b^h = w^h$ (with $w^h = p_a \omega_a^h + p_b \omega_b^h$ known), and plug in $p_b/p_a$ from the FOC ratio (Step 3) to eliminate one variable. &
$r^*(p) = \tfrac{2}{3}\tfrac{p_b}{p_a}$.
$p_a r^* + p_b = \tfrac{2}{3} p_b + p_b = \tfrac{5}{3} p_b.$
$x_b^h \cdot \tfrac{5}{3} p_b = w^h \;\Rightarrow\; x_b^h = \tfrac{3}{5}\dfrac{w^h}{p_b} = \dfrac{0.6\, w^h}{p_b}.$
$x_a^h = r^*(p)\, x_b^h = \tfrac{2}{3}\tfrac{p_b}{p_a} \cdot \tfrac{3}{5}\tfrac{w^h}{p_b} = \dfrac{0.4\, w^h}{p_a}.$
\textcolor{orange}{Same coefficient $0.4$ on $w^h$ for both agents.} &
\emph{Agent 1} ($r_1^* = \tfrac{1}{4}\tfrac{p_b}{p_a}$): $p_a r_1^* + p_b = \tfrac{1}{4} p_b + p_b = \tfrac{5}{4} p_b.$
$x_b^1 = \tfrac{4}{5}\dfrac{w^1}{p_b} = \dfrac{0.8\, w^1}{p_b}.\;\;x_a^1 = r_1^* x_b^1 = \dfrac{0.2\, w^1}{p_a}.$
\emph{Agent 2} ($r_2^* = 4\tfrac{p_b}{p_a}$): $p_a r_2^* + p_b = 4 p_b + p_b = 5 p_b.$
$x_b^2 = \tfrac{1}{5}\dfrac{w^2}{p_b} = \dfrac{0.2\, w^2}{p_b}.\;\;x_a^2 = r_2^* x_b^2 = \dfrac{0.8\, w^2}{p_a}.$
\textcolor{red}{Different coefficients on $w^h$ across agents.} \\
\hline
\textbf{(5) Market clearing for $A$} \emph{(the pivot step)} &
$\sum_h x_a^h = \dfrac{0.4 (w^1 + w^2)}{p_a} = \omega_a$
$\Rightarrow 0.4\,(p_a \omega_a + p_b \omega_b) = p_a \omega_a$
$\Rightarrow 0.4(6 p_a + 5 p_b) = 6 p_a$
$\Rightarrow 2 p_b = 3.6 p_a.$
\textcolor{orange}{Truly depends on aggregate $\omega$!} &
$\sum_h x_a^h = \dfrac{0.2\, w^1 + 0.8\, w^2}{p_a} = \omega_a$
$\Rightarrow 0.2(5 p_a + p_b) + 0.8(p_a + 4 p_b) = 6 p_a$
$\Rightarrow 1.8 p_a + 3.4 p_b = 6 p_a$
$\Rightarrow 3.4 p_b = 4.2 p_a.$
\textcolor{red}{Individual $\omega^h$ enter \emph{separately}.} \\
\hline
\textbf{(6) Equilibrium prices} &
$\hat p_b/\hat p_a = 3.6/2 = 1.8.$
\emph{Normalize:} $\hat p_a = 1$, $\hat p_b = 1.8.$ &
$\hat p_b/\hat p_a = 4.2/3.4 \approx 1.235.$
\emph{Normalize:} $\hat p_a = 1$, $\hat p_b \approx 1.235.$ \\
\hline
\textbf{(7) Wealths at CE} &
$w^1 = 5 + 1.8 = 6.8$, $w^2 = 1 + 7.2 = 8.2$. &
$w^1 = 5 + 1.235 = 6.235$, $w^2 = 1 + 4.94 = 5.94$. \\
\hline
\textbf{(8) Individual demands and ratios} &
$x^1 = (0.4 \cdot 6.8,\, 0.6 \cdot 6.8 / 1.8) = (2.72,\, 2.267)$.
$x^2 = (3.28,\, 2.733)$.
\emph{Ratios:} $2.72/2.267 = 1.2$;\; $3.28/2.733 = 1.2$.
\textcolor{orange}{Both $= \omega_a/\omega_b = 1.2$.} &
$x^1 \approx (0.2 \cdot 6.235,\; 0.8 \cdot 6.235 / 1.235) \approx (1.247,\, 4.039)$.
$x^2 \approx (4.752,\, 0.962)$.
\emph{Ratios:} $1.247/4.039 \approx 0.31$;\; $4.752/0.962 \approx 4.94$.
\textcolor{red}{Wildly different; neither $= 1.2$.} \\
\hline
\textbf{(*) Swap test} \;($\omega^1 \leftrightarrow \omega^2$, same aggregate) &
Identical agents $\Rightarrow$ swapping is a relabel: clearing equation \emph{unchanged}.
$\hat p_b/\hat p_a = 1.8$ (\textcolor{green}{unchanged}).
\textcolor{orange}{Distribution irrelevant.} &
After swap: $0.2(p_a + 4 p_b) + 0.8(5 p_a + p_b) = 6 p_a \Rightarrow 4.2 p_a + 1.6 p_b = 6 p_a \Rightarrow \hat p_b/\hat p_a = 1.125$.
\textcolor{red}{Prices change from $1.235$ to $1.125$.}
Distribution \textcolor{red}{matters}. \\
\end{tabular}

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{orange}{In the specific context of this question: why is the aggregate endowment ratio equal to the optimal individual consumption ratio?}}

\emph{The point:} agents are identical and homothetic, so each one wants a fixed consumption ratio $x_a^h/x_b^h$ (wealth-independent, and the \emph{same} across agents). The only feasible value of that common ratio --- i.e., **the only one for which prices exist** that clear the market --- is the one matching the aggregate endowment ratio $\omega_a/\omega_b$. Note how prices reflect scarcity!

Elasticities on the Marshallian demands
Application: Labor Supply Elasticities (General, Frisch, Applied)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{LABOR SUPPLY ELASTICITIES --- general, Frisch, applied:}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Setup.}}
\[ \max_{c, h} \;U(c) - v(h) \quad\text{s.t.}\quad c = w h + I, \;\; c, h > 0. \]
$U$ concave in $c$, $v$ convex in $h$. Lagrangian (multiplier $\lambda$ on the budget):
\[ \mathcal{L} = U(c) - v(h) - \lambda\,(c - w h - I). \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Question.}} How does the optimal hours $h^*$ respond to a wage change?
\[ \boxed{\;\epsilon_{h, w} \;:=\; \dfrac{\partial h^*}{\partial w} \cdot \dfrac{w}{h^*}.\;} \]



\textbf{\textcolor{orange}{Reminder: every FOC step starts by setting the relevant partial of $\mathcal{L}$ to $0$.}}

\textbf{Notation:} the multiplier $\lambda^*$ depends on the \emph{exogenous} parameters of the Lagrangian $(w, I)$ --- never on the endogenous choice variables $c, h$ (they get absorbed into $c^*(w, I), h^*(w, I)$ after solving).

\begin{tabular}{p{7cm}|p{13cm}|p{10cm}|p{10cm}}
\textbf{Step} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{GENERAL}} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{FRISCH ($\bar\lambda$ fixed)}} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{APPLIED}  $v(h) = h^{1+1/\epsilon}/(1+1/\epsilon)$, $U(c) = c$} \\
\hline
\textbf{(1) Retrieve $h^*$} from FOC w.r.t.\ $h$. &
\textbf{FOC$_h$:} $-v'(h^*) + \lambda^*(w, I)\, w = 0$
$\Rightarrow v'(h^*(w, I)) = w \lambda^*(w, I)$

A wage change has two channels:

$\bullet$ \textcolor{blue}{Direct ($+\Delta w$):} higher wage $\to$ more work.
$\bullet$ \textcolor{blue}{Indirect / income ($-\Delta w$):} $\lambda^* \downarrow$ (richer $\to$ less marginal value of $c$) $\to$ work less. &
\textbf{FOC$_h$:} $-v'(h^*) + \bar\lambda\, w = 0$
$\Rightarrow v'(h^*) = w \bar\lambda$

\emph{(no income effect: $\bar\lambda$ fixed by assumption $\Rightarrow$ only the direct channel survives)} &
\textbf{FOC$_h$:} $-h^{*\,1/\epsilon} + \bar\lambda\, w = 0$
$\Rightarrow h^*(w, \lambda) = (w \lambda)^{\epsilon}$ \\
\hline
\textbf{(2) Find $\lambda^*$} from FOC w.r.t.\ $c$. &
\textbf{FOC$_c$:} $U'(c^*) - \lambda^* = 0$
$\Rightarrow \lambda^*(w, I) = U'(c^*(w, I))$
\emph{(depends on $w, I$ through $c^*$)} &
\emph{No need;} $\bar\lambda$ fixed by assumption. &
\textbf{FOC$_c$:} $1 - \lambda^* = 0$
\emph{(since $U(c) = c \Rightarrow U'(c) = 1$)}
$\Rightarrow \lambda^* = \bar\lambda = 1$ \\
\hline
\textbf{(3) Compute $\partial h^*/\partial w$.} Differentiate FOC$_h$ (and FOC$_c$, FOC$_{BC}$ where needed) w.r.t.\ $w$. &
From FOC$_h$ (product rule): $v''(h^*)\, \dfrac{\partial h^*}{\partial w} = \lambda^*(w, I) + w\, \boxed{\dfrac{\partial \lambda^*}{\partial w}}$

\emph{Need} $\boxed{\partial \lambda^*/\partial w}$. From FOC$_c$ (chain rule): $\boxed{\dfrac{\partial \lambda^*}{\partial w}} = U''(c^*)\, \boxed{\dfrac{\partial c^*}{\partial w}}$

\emph{Need} $\boxed{\partial c^*/\partial w}$. From FOC$_{BC}$ (product rule): $\boxed{\dfrac{\partial c^*}{\partial w}} = h^* + w\, \dfrac{\partial h^*}{\partial w}$
 &
From FOC$_h$ (with $\partial \bar\lambda/\partial w = 0$):
$v''(h^*)\, \dfrac{\partial h^*}{\partial w} = \bar\lambda$ &
Direct from $h^*(w, \bar\lambda) = (w\bar\lambda)^{\epsilon}$:
$\dfrac{\partial h^*}{\partial w} = \epsilon\, \bar\lambda^{\epsilon}\, w^{\epsilon - 1}$ \\
\hline
\textbf{(4) Convert to elasticity:} multiply by $w/h^*$. &
Substitute (FOC$_c$, FOC$_{BC}$) into the differentiated FOC$_h$ and solve:
$\boxed{\;\epsilon_{h, w} = -\dfrac{U'(c^*) + h^* w\, U''(c^*)}{w^2 U''(c^*) - v''(h^*)} \cdot \dfrac{w}{h^*}\;}$ &
$\epsilon^{F}_{h, w} = \dfrac{\underbrace{\bar\lambda\, w}_{v'(h^*)}}{v''(h^*)\, h^*}$
 &
$\epsilon^{*}_{h, w} = \epsilon\, \bar\lambda^{\epsilon} w^{\epsilon - 1} \cdot \dfrac{w}{(w \bar\lambda)^{\epsilon}}$
$\Rightarrow \boxed{\;\epsilon^{*}_{h, w} = \epsilon\;}$ \\
\end{tabular}


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{LABOR SUPPLY ELASTICITIES WITH TAXES --- general, Frisch, applied:}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Setup with labor income tax.}}
\[
\max_{c,h} \; U(c)-v(h)
\quad \text{s.t.} \quad
c=(1-\tau)wh+I, \qquad c,h>0.
\]

Here \(\tau\) is the proportional labor income tax and \(1-\tau\) is the net-of-tax rate. The gross wage is \(w\), while the private net wage is \((1-\tau)w\).

The Lagrangian is
\[
\mathcal{L}
=
U(c)-v(h)-\lambda\big(c-(1-\tau)wh-I\big).
\]

now optimal h* will depend on $\tau$ as well!

nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXCHANGE ECONOMY --- the standard setting for PO and CE.}}


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Ingredients.}}
$\bullet$ \textbf{$I$ consumers / agents}, indexed by $i = 1, 2, \ldots, I$.
$\bullet$ \textbf{$N$ goods}, indexed by $n = 1, 2, \ldots, N$.
$\bullet$ \textbf{Initial endowments} $\omega^i = (\omega_1^i, \ldots, \omega_N^i) \in \mathbb{R}^N_+$: agent $i$'s initial stock of each good \emph{before} any trade.
$\bullet$ \textbf{Utility functions} $U^i : \mathbb{R}^N_+ \to \mathbb{R}$, one per agent.
$\bullet$ **GE setting**: 
- Anonymous agents interacitng, they are small, they take prices as given
- General equilibrium: all prices are free to adjust vs Partial Equilirbium, some prices are fixed
$\bullet$ **No production **--- the only way goods change hands is by exchange between consumers.



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Feasible set.}}
$$ \mathcal{F} \;=\; \bigl\{\, x = (x^1, \ldots, x^I) \;:\; x_n^i \geq 0 \;\forall i, n, \;\; \textstyle\sum_i x_n^i = \omega_n \;\forall n \,\bigr\}. $$

Remark: **price takers** agents mean they do not know they cannot affect prices. But then note that at CE we look for prices such that AS = AD, and this clearly is composed of individual agents demand decisions!

In the standard exchange-economy setup, the feasible set $\mathcal{F} = {x : \sum_i x^i = \omega,; x^i \geq 0}$ is automatically compact (closed, bounded by $\omega$). Then for any        $\lambda \in (0,1)$, the continuous linear functional $\lambda U^1 + (1-\lambda)U^2$ attains its max on $\mathcal{F}$ by Weierstrass. The argmax is in PS (forward direction of [A], proven  without convexity). Hence PS $\neq \emptyset$.

Compact set + continuous function!

nodes.title: Conditions for existence of CE
PO and CE: FWT and SWT
nodes.content:
If CE exists (given this omega), is it PO? 

YES \textbf{\textcolor{red}{FIRST WELFARE THEOREM --- every CE is Pareto Optimal.}}


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Statement.}} If $(\hat p, \hat x)$ is a Competitive Equilibrium \emph{and} each $U^i$ is strictly increasing in every good, then $\hat x$ is Pareto Optimal.
$$ \boxed{\;\text{CE} \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \text{PO}\quad \text{(under strict monotonicity)}.\;} $$
Moreover $U^i(\hat x_i) \ge U^i(\omega^i)$
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Proof sketch.}}
\textbf{(i)} Suppose for contradiction $\hat x$ is not PO. Then $\exists y \in \mathcal{F}$ with $U^i(y^i) \geq U^i(\hat x^i)$ $\forall i$ (ahemts) and strict for some $j$.
\textbf{(ii)} Strict monotonicity $+$ consumer optimization at prices $\hat p$:
$\bullet$ For agent $j$ (strictly better off): $\hat p \cdot y^j > \hat p \cdot \hat x^j$ (otherwise $y^j$ would have been chosen). The point is that he is already at the boudnary and this $y^j$ is not feasible
$\bullet$ For other agents: $\hat p \cdot y^i \geq \hat p \cdot \hat x^i$.
\textbf{(iii)} Sum: $\hat p \cdot \sum_i y^i \;>\; \hat p \cdot \sum_i \hat x^i = \omega$. Not feasible!

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Key takeaway.}} CE allocations are always on the \emph{*Pareto Set*} (and in fact on the \emph{Contract Curve}, since they're individually rational by construction). The market efficiently rules out wasteful allocations \emph{without a planner}.

\textbf{\textcolor{orange}{What FWT does NOT say.}}
$\bullet$ CE allocations need not be \emph{fair}. The endowment distribution determines who gets what at the CE.



If a point is PO, can some $\omega$ exists where $\hat x$ is the CE ? failure is not CE non existence for one omega, but for all omega.

 \textbf{\textcolor{red}{SECOND WELFARE THEOREM --- any PO can be supported as a CE with lump-sum transfers.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Statement (ALL CASES EXCEPT THE ONES UNDER "CE FAILURE").}} Under \emph{convexity of preferences} (concave $U^i$), \emph{strict monotonicity}, and continuity: \emph{any} Pareto-optimal allocation $\bar x$ can be supported as a CE relative to some prices $\hat p \in \mathbb{R}^N_+$ \emph{after} lump-sum transfers $T = (T^1, \ldots, T^I)$ with $\sum_i T^i = 0$.

$$ \boxed{\;\text{Any PO} \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \text{CE} \;\;\text{with transfers (under convexity)}.\;} $$



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Reading the picture (Edgeworth box).}} At any PO interior point, the two agents' ICs are tangent. The \emph{slope of the common tangent} = $-\hat p_a / \hat p_b$ = supporting prices. Transfers shift the budget line (omega changes eq p, recall the big picture) so it passes through the desired PO bundle instead of through the original endowment.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why this matters.}}
$\bullet$ \textcolor{orange}{Equity-efficiency separation.} The planner can pick the most equitable PO and \emph{implement it via the price mechanism} just by redistributing endowments. Market efficiency and distributional choice are separable.
$\bullet$ \textcolor{orange}{Decentralization.} A planner doesn't need to choose individual allocations --- they just set transfers and let markets clear.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Super-concise intuition (why SWT works).}}

Recall PO:
$$ \frac{\partial U^i/\partial x^i_n}{\partial U^i/\partial x^i_m} \;=\; \frac{\mu_n}{\mu_m} \qquad \text{for both } i=1, 2. $$
\emph{Each agent's MRS equals the planner's relative shadow prices.} That is, the marginal value of consuming one extra unit of good l and the marginal value of consuming the extra unit of good h. What is this?? exacly the same role of prices in the CE

Recall CE:
$$ \frac{\partial U^i/\partial x^i_n}{\partial U^i/\partial x^i_m} \;=\; \frac{p_n}{p_m}. $$
\emph{Same equations, with $p$ replacing $\mu$.}

\emph{The link.} Set $\;\boxed{\;p_n \,=\, \mu_n\;}\;$ (up to a positive normalization). Then the planner's allocation \emph{is} a consumer-optimal bundle at those prices --- the FOCs match. 


How do you change prices? 
Lump-sum transfers $T^i$ are picked so each agent's budget at $p$ exactly affords the planner's bundle: $p \cdot \bar x^i = p \cdot \omega^i + T^i$, with $\sum_i T^i = 0$.

\textbf{Slogan:} \emph{decentralization is just renaming Lagrange multipliers as prices}. The planner's shadow prices on market clearing $=$ the CE market prices.

\textbf{1)} Whenever you solve $P(u_1) = \max\ldots$ sub $\ldots u_2 \ge \bar u$ you are not agnostic on $y_1^*, y_2^*, x_1^*, x_2^*$ $\to$ system will pin down these quantities.

nodes.title: Characetrizations of PS
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{(6) Two characterizations of Pareto Set (PS).}}

\emph{Why a planner?} Both characterizations are written from the viewpoint of a benevolent social planner who chooses an allocation
$$
(x_h^1,x_l^1,x_h^2,x_l^2)\in\mathcal F
$$
to maximize a welfare objective. The superscript identifies the agent, whereas the subscript identifies the good. The planner therefore chooses an allocation on the Pareto set, whose utility representation lies on the utility-possibility frontier.

\textbf{\textcolor{green}{(6a) Linear scalarization --- weighted SWF.}}

$$
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
[\mathrm A]:\qquad
x^*(\lambda)\in
\arg\max_{\substack{x_h^1,x_l^1\geq0 \\ x_h^2,x_l^2\geq0}}
&\ \lambda U^1(x_h^1,x_l^1)
+(1-\lambda)U^2(x_h^2,x_l^2) \\
\text{s.t.}\qquad
&x_h^1+x_h^2=\omega_h, \\
&x_l^1+x_l^2=\omega_l, \\
&\lambda\in(0,1).
\end{aligned}}
$$

\textbf{FOCs and result for $[\mathrm A]$:}

Writing the Lagrangian with an explicit shadow price $\mu_h$ for the resource constraint of good $h$ and an explicit shadow price $\mu_l$ for the resource constraint of good $l$ gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal L_{\mathrm A}
={}&
\lambda U^1(x_h^1,x_l^1)
+(1-\lambda)U^2(x_h^2,x_l^2) \\
&+\mu_h\left(\omega_h-x_h^1-x_h^2\right)
+\mu_l\left(\omega_l-x_l^1-x_l^2\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

The planner chooses the four consumption variables
$$
x_h^1,\qquad x_l^1,\qquad x_h^2,\qquad x_l^2.
$$

For an interior solution, the first-order conditions for Agent 1 are
$$
\lambda\frac{\partial U^1}{\partial x_h^1}=\mu_h,
\qquad
\lambda\frac{\partial U^1}{\partial x_l^1}=\mu_l,
$$
while the first-order conditions for Agent 2 are
$$
(1-\lambda)\frac{\partial U^2}{\partial x_h^2}=\mu_h,
\qquad
(1-\lambda)\frac{\partial U^2}{\partial x_l^2}=\mu_l.
$$
Note how beautiful the math is: the common rhs allows you to unify the utility you give to agent 1 to the utility you give to agent 2. This means that $\mu_h$ is gonna be the unified value of consuming good h and $\mu_l$ the unified value of consuming good l





Therefore,
$$\underbrace{\frac{\partial U^1/\partial x_h^1}
{\partial U^1/\partial x_l^1}}_{\mathrm{MRS}_{h,l}^1}
=
\frac{\mu_h}{\mu_l}
=
\underbrace{\frac{\partial U^2/\partial x_h^2}
{\partial U^2/\partial x_l^2}}_{\mathrm{MRS}_{h,l}^1},
$$


Hence, at an interior Pareto-efficient allocation, the two agents have the same marginal rate of substitution between goods $h$ and $l$.

\textbf{The theory:}

\begin{enumerate}
\item There is an underlying feasible allocation set $\mathcal F$. Through the agents' utility functions, this feasible allocation set generates a utility-possibility set.

\item The planner chooses a feasible allocation that maximizes social welfare.

\item Under linear scalarization, the planner uses the weighted social-welfare function
$$
W=\lambda U^1+(1-\lambda)U^2,
$$
where $\lambda$ is the welfare weight assigned to Agent 1 and $1-\lambda$ is the welfare weight assigned to Agent 2.

More general nonlinear social-welfare functions can also be considered, but their properties and geometric interpretation may differ from those of the linear weighted sum.

\item In utility space, an isowelfare line satisfies
$$
W=\lambda U^1+(1-\lambda)U^2.
$$
Solving for $U^2$ gives $U^2 = -\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda}U^1 + \underbrace{\frac{W}{1-\lambda}}_{K}.$ Thus, the isowelfare line has slope $-\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda},$ and its vertical intercept is $ K=\frac{W}{1-\lambda}.$

For a fixed value of $\lambda$, maximizing welfare means moving the isowelfare line outward, parallel to itself, until it reaches the utility-possibility set. The highest attainable isowelfare line determines the planner's optimum.

If the utility-possibility set is compact and the weighted welfare function is continuous, the Weierstrass theorem guarantees that a maximum exists. This means that, for every fixed $\lambda$, the weighted social-welfare problem has at least one solution.

\item \textbf{Key point:} if $\lambda\in(0,1)$ strictly, every maximizer of the weighted social-welfare function is Pareto optimal.

To see why, suppose that a maximizer were Pareto dominated by another feasible allocation. The dominating allocation would give at least as much utility to both agents and strictly more utility to at least one agent. Because both welfare weights are strictly positive, it would produce strictly greater social welfare, contradicting optimality.

If instead $\lambda=0$ or $\lambda=1$, the planner assigns zero welfare weight to one of the agents. In that case, a chosen maximizer may be Pareto dominated by another maximizer that gives the same utility to the positively weighted agent and greater utility to the agent receiving zero weight.

\item There are two important cases.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Convex utility-possibility set.}

If the utility-possibility set is convex, the supporting-hyperplane theorem implies that every point on the utility-possibility frontier can be supported by an isowelfare line for some welfare weight $\lambda$.

Therefore, every Pareto-efficient utility allocation can be recovered as a solution to the weighted social-welfare problem for some $\lambda\in[0,1]$.

Note: A given value of $\lambda$ does not necessarily select a unique point (you need monotonicity). Uniqueness requires additional assumptions, such as strict convexity of the utility-possibility set or strict concavity of the planner's objective over the feasible allocation set.

\item \textbf{Nonconvex utility-possibility set.}

If the utility-possibility set is not convex, some points on the utility-possibility frontier may not admit a supporting isowelfare line.

Consequently,
$$
\boxed{\text{some points on the UPF cannot be reached by any value of }\lambda.}
$$

The weighted-sum method retrieves only the supported Pareto-efficient points.
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{The practice:}



Their ratio,
$$\frac{\mu_h}{\mu_l},
$$
equals the common marginal rate of substitution between the two goods at an interior Pareto-efficient allocation.

\textbf{From PS to UPF.}

Once $x^*(\lambda)$ is obtained, the corresponding point on the utility-possibility frontier is
$$
\left(
U^1(x_h^{1*},x_l^{1*}),
U^2(x_h^{2*},x_l^{2*})
\right).
$$

Varying $\lambda$ traces the supported points of the utility-possibility frontier.

\textbf{\textcolor{green}{(6b) Constrained maximization --- UPF as an explicit function.}}

$$
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
[\mathrm B]:\qquad
P(\bar u^1)=
\max_{\substack{x_h^1,x_l^1\geq0 \\ x_h^2,x_l^2\geq0}}
&\ U^2(x_h^2,x_l^2) \\
\text{s.t.}\qquad
&U^1(x_h^1,x_l^1)\geq\bar u^1, \\
&x_h^1+x_h^2=\omega_h, \\
&x_l^1+x_l^2=\omega_l.
\end{aligned}}
$$

\textbf{FOCs and result for $[\mathrm B]$:}

Let $\gamma\geq0$ be the multiplier on Agent 1's utility constraint. Let $\tilde\mu_h$ and $\tilde\mu_l$ be the shadow prices associated with the resource constraints for goods $h$ and $l$. The Lagrangian is
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal L_{\mathrm B}
={}&
U^2(x_h^2,x_l^2)
+\gamma\left[U^1(x_h^1,x_l^1)-\bar u^1\right] \\
&+\tilde\mu_h\left(\omega_h-x_h^1-x_h^2\right)
+\tilde\mu_l\left(\omega_l-x_l^1-x_l^2\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

For an interior solution, differentiating with respect to Agent 1's consumption choices gives
$$
\gamma\frac{\partial U^1}{\partial x_h^1}
=
\tilde\mu_h,
\qquad
\gamma\frac{\partial U^1}{\partial x_l^1}
=
\tilde\mu_l.
$$

Differentiating with respect to Agent 2's consumption choices gives
$$
\frac{\partial U^2}{\partial x_h^2}
=
\tilde\mu_h,
\qquad
\frac{\partial U^2}{\partial x_l^2}
=
\tilde\mu_l.
$$

Taking the ratio of the FOCs for Agent 1 gives
$$
\frac{\partial U^1/\partial x_h^1}
{\partial U^1/\partial x_l^1}
=
\frac{\tilde\mu_h}{\tilde\mu_l}.
$$

Taking the ratio of the FOCs for Agent 2 gives
$$
\frac{\partial U^2/\partial x_h^2}
{\partial U^2/\partial x_l^2}
=
\frac{\tilde\mu_h}{\tilde\mu_l}.
$$

Therefore,
$$
\frac{\partial U^1/\partial x_h^1}
{\partial U^1/\partial x_l^1}
=
\frac{\tilde\mu_h}{\tilde\mu_l}
=
\frac{\partial U^2/\partial x_h^2}
{\partial U^2/\partial x_l^2},
$$
which implies
$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{MRS}_{h,l}^1
=
\mathrm{MRS}_{h,l}^2
=
\frac{\tilde\mu_h}{\tilde\mu_l}.
}
$$

Thus, the constrained-maximization approach gives the same Pareto-efficiency condition as the weighted social-welfare approach.

The planner fixes Agent 1 at a utility floor $\bar u^1$ and maximizes Agent 2's utility. By varying $\bar u^1$ over its feasible range,
$$
\bar u^1\in[u_{\min}^1,u_{\max}^1],
$$
the planner traces the utility-possibility frontier as an explicit decreasing function
$$
U^2=P(U^1).
$$

Under local nonsatiation, Agent 1's utility constraint binds at a frontier allocation:
$$
U^1(x_h^1,x_l^1)=\bar u^1.
$$

If the constraint did not bind, the planner could transfer some resources away from Agent 1 while keeping Agent 1 above the required utility floor and use those resources to increase Agent 2's utility.

\textbf{Solve:}

Apply the usual KKT conditions:

\begin{enumerate}
\item stationarity;
\item primal feasibility;
\item dual feasibility;
\item complementary slackness.
\end{enumerate}

In particular, complementary slackness for Agent 1's utility constraint requires
$$
\gamma\left[U^1(x_h^1,x_l^1)-\bar u^1\right]=0.
$$

\textbf{\textcolor{orange}{Example --- one-good economy.}}

Suppose there is only one good, with total endowment $\omega$, and that $U^i$ is strictly increasing for each agent. Since there is only one good, denote the amount consumed by Agent $i$ simply by $x^i$. The constrained-maximization problem becomes
$$
P(\bar u^1)
=
\max_{x^1,x^2\geq0}
U^2(x^2)
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad
U^1(x^1)\geq\bar u^1,
\qquad
x^1+x^2=\omega.
$$

Strict monotonicity implies that Agent 1's utility constraint binds:
$$
U^1(x^1)=\bar u^1.
$$

Therefore,
$$
x^1=(U^1)^{-1}(\bar u^1).
$$

Resource feasibility then implies
$$
x^2
=
\omega-x^1
=
\omega-(U^1)^{-1}(\bar u^1).
$$

Hence,
$$
\boxed{
P(\bar u^1)
=
U^2\left(
\omega-(U^1)^{-1}(\bar u^1)
\right).
}
$$

\textbf{Prices and trade in a one-good exchange economy.}

In the two-good economy, the general budget constraint of Agent $i$ is
$$
p_hx_h^i+p_lx_l^i
=
p_h\omega_h^i+p_l\omega_l^i.
$$

Prices $p_h$ and $p_l$ do not carry an agent index because competitive-equilibrium prices are common to all agents.

In a one-good economy, the budget constraint becomes
$$
px^i=p\omega^i.
$$

For any strictly positive price $p>0$,
$$
x^i=\omega^i.
$$

Thus, each agent can afford only their initial endowment. There is no relative price because there is only one good, and setting
$$
p=1
$$
is merely a numéraire normalization.

The relevant statement is not that the budget line has slope one: with only one good, the budget set is a point on a one-dimensional consumption space rather than a line in a two-dimensional diagram. In a pure one-good exchange economy, there is no mutually beneficial exchange through which both agents can alter their consumption while satisfying their individual budget constraints.

nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{GUIDING EXAMPLE --- worker + planner, two parametrisations.}}

\emph{Population: a $\%$ of skills $w_i$ with frequencies $\pi_i$. Planner balances $\sum_i \pi_i T(y_i) = G = 0$.}

\begin{tabular}{p{7cm}|p{15.5cm}|p{15.5cm}}
\textbf{Step} & \textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{Example 1 --- linear tax, quasi-linear $U$}} & \textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{Example 2 --- HSV schedule, log $U$}} \\
\hline
\textbf{0. Setting.} \emph{Utility and tax schedule.} & $U(c, h) = c - \dfrac{h^{1+\gamma}}{1+\gamma}$, $\gamma > 0$.

$T(y) = -B + \tau y$,\;\; $y = w h$,\;\; $c = B + (1-\tau)\, w\, h$.

\emph{Linear flat tax.} & $U(c, h) = \ln c - \dfrac{h^{1+\gamma}}{1+\gamma}$.

$T(y) = y - B y^{1-\tau}$,\;\; $c = B\, y^{1-\tau}$.

\emph{Sub} $y = w h$:\;\; $c = B\,(w h)^{1-\tau}$.

\emph{Multiplicative HSV.} \\
\hline
\textbf{Govt budget.} $G = 0 \Rightarrow \sum_i \pi_i T(y_i) = 0$ & $\sum_i \pi_i \tau y_i = B$

$\Rightarrow\; B = \tau\, Y(\tau)$,\;\; $Y(\tau) = \sum_i \pi_i\, w_i\, h^*(\tau, w_i)$. & $\sum_i \pi_i B y_i^{1-\tau} = \sum_i \pi_i y_i = Y(\tau)$,\;\; with $Y(\tau) = \sum_i \pi_i\, w_i\, h^*(\tau, w_i)$.

$\Rightarrow\; B(\tau) = \dfrac{Y(\tau)}{\sum_i \pi_i\, y_i^{1-\tau}} = \dfrac{\sum_i \pi_i\, w_i\, h^*(\tau, w_i)}{\sum_i \pi_i\, \bigl(w_i\, h^*(\tau, w_i)\bigr)^{1-\tau}}$. \\
\hline
\textbf{① Worker picks $h^*$} \emph{($B$ taken as given!)} & $\displaystyle h^* = \arg\max_{h \geq 0}\; \bigl[\, c - \tfrac{h^{1+\gamma}}{1+\gamma} \,\bigr]\;\;\text{sub.}\;\; c = y - T(y)$.

\emph{Expand $T(y)$:} $c = y - (-B + \tau y) = B + (1-\tau)\, y$.

\emph{Expand $y = w h$:} $c = B + (1-\tau)\, w\, h$.

$\Rightarrow\; \max_{h \geq 0}\; \bigl[ B + (1-\tau)\, w\, h - \tfrac{h^{1+\gamma}}{1+\gamma} \bigr]$.

\textbf{FOC:} $(1-\tau)\, w = h^\gamma$.

$\boxed{\; h^*(\tau, w) = (1-\tau)^{1/\gamma}\, w^{1/\gamma},\;\; \varepsilon = 1/\gamma. \;}$ & $\displaystyle h^* = \arg\max_{h \geq 0}\; \bigl[\, \ln c - \tfrac{h^{1+\gamma}}{1+\gamma} \,\bigr]\;\;\text{sub.}\;\; c = y - T(y)$.

\emph{Expand $T(y)$:} $c = y - (y - B y^{1-\tau}) = B\, y^{1-\tau}$.

\emph{Expand $y = w h$:} $c = B\,(w h)^{1-\tau}\;\Rightarrow\; \ln c = \ln B + (1-\tau)(\ln w + \ln h)$.

$\Rightarrow\; \max_{h \geq 0}\; \bigl[ \ln B + (1-\tau)(\ln w + \ln h) - \tfrac{h^{1+\gamma}}{1+\gamma} \bigr]$.

\textbf{FOC:} $(1-\tau)/h = h^\gamma$.

$\boxed{\; h^*(\tau) = (1-\tau)^{1/(1+\gamma)}. \;}$

\textcolor{purple}{\emph{Doesn't depend on $w$ $\to$ no effect on his workload!}} \\
\hline
\textbf{② Planner picks $\tau$ --- 2A) Utilitarian.}\emph{Knowing worker's $h^*(\tau,w)$ response.}& \textbf{1.} Write $W^U = \sum_i \pi_i \bigl[ c_i - \tfrac{h_i^{1+\gamma}}{1+\gamma} \bigr]$.

\textbf{2.} Sub $c_i = B + (1-\tau)\, w_i\, h_i$:

$W^U = B + \sum_i \pi_i \bigl[ (1-\tau)\, w_i\, h_i - \tfrac{h_i^{1+\gamma}}{1+\gamma} \bigr]$.

\textbf{3.} Sub $h_i^* = (1-\tau)^{1/\gamma} w_i^{1/\gamma}$. Both terms become $(1-\tau)^{1+1/\gamma}\, w_i^{1+1/\gamma}$:

$W^U = B + (1-\tau)^{1+1/\gamma}\!\sum_i \pi_i w_i^{1+1/\gamma} - \tfrac{(1-\tau)^{1+1/\gamma}}{1+\gamma}\!\sum_i \pi_i w_i^{1+1/\gamma}$.

\textbf{4.} Call $M := \sum_i \pi_i\, w_i^{1+1/\gamma}$:

$W^U = B + (1-\tau)^{1+1/\gamma} M - \tfrac{(1-\tau)^{1+1/\gamma}}{1+\gamma}\, M$.

\textbf{5.} Sub $B = \tau\, Y_t$. With $y_i = w_i h_i^* = (1-\tau)^{1/\gamma} w_i^{1+1/\gamma}$, $Y_t = (1-\tau)^{1/\gamma} M$:

$B = \tau\,(1-\tau)^{1/\gamma}\, M\;\;\Rightarrow\;\;$
$W^U(\tau) = \tau\,(1-\tau)^{1/\gamma} M + (1-\tau)^{1+1/\gamma} M - \tfrac{(1-\tau)^{1+1/\gamma}}{1+\gamma}\, M$.

\textbf{6.} Expand the central term: $(1-\tau)^{1+1/\gamma} = (1-\tau)\cdot(1-\tau)^{1/\gamma}$:

$W^U(\tau) = (1-\tau)^{1/\gamma} M \bigl[\, \tau + (1-\tau) - \tfrac{1-\tau}{1+\gamma} \,\bigr]$.

\textbf{7.} Factor: $\tau + (1-\tau) = 1$, so

$\boxed{\;\; W^U(\tau) = (1-\tau)^{1/\gamma}\, M\, \Bigl[\, 1 - \dfrac{1-\tau}{1+\gamma} \,\Bigr]\,. \;\;}$ & \textbf{1.} Write $W^U = \sum_i \pi_i\bigl[ \ln c_i - \tfrac{h_i^{1+\gamma}}{1+\gamma}\bigr]$.

\textbf{2.} Sub $c_i = B\, y_i^{1-\tau}$:

$W^U = \ln B + (1-\tau)\sum_i \pi_i \ln y_i - \sum_i \pi_i \tfrac{h_i^{1+\gamma}}{1+\gamma}$.

\textbf{3.} Sub $h_i^* = (1-\tau)^{1/(1+\gamma)}$, $y_i = w_i\,(1-\tau)^{1/(1+\gamma)}$, so $h_i^{1+\gamma} = 1-\tau$:

$W^U = \ln B + (1-\tau)\sum_i \pi_i \ln w_i + \tfrac{1-\tau}{1+\gamma}\ln(1-\tau) - \tfrac{1-\tau}{1+\gamma}$.

\textbf{4.} \emph{(No $M$ aggregator needed --- the labor terms are not $w$-weighted because $h^*$ is independent of $w$.)}

\textbf{5.} Sub $B(\tau) = (1-\tau)^{\tau/(1+\gamma)} \cdot \dfrac{\sum_i \pi_i w_i}{\sum_i \pi_i w_i^{1-\tau}}$:

$\ln B(\tau) = \tfrac{\tau}{1+\gamma}\ln(1-\tau) + \ln\!\bigl(\sum_i \pi_i w_i\bigr) - \ln\!\bigl(\sum_i \pi_i w_i^{1-\tau}\bigr)$.

\textbf{6--7.} Combine ($\tau + (1-\tau) = 1$ collapses the $\ln(1-\tau)$ terms):

$\boxed{\;\; W^U(\tau) = \dfrac{1}{1+\gamma}\bigl[\ln(1-\tau) - (1-\tau)\bigr] + (1-\tau)\sum_i \pi_i \ln w_i + \ln\!\Bigl(\sum_i \pi_i w_i\Bigr) - \ln\!\Bigl(\sum_i \pi_i w_i^{1-\tau}\Bigr). \;\;}$

\emph{Closed form --- but only the FOC blows up.} \\
\hline
\textbf{FOC} $\partial W^U / \partial \tau = 0$. & \emph{Trick: let $T := 1-\tau$, so $dT/d\tau = -1$. The FOC in $\tau$ becomes the FOC in $T$, just sign-flipped.}

Rewrite $W^U = T^{1/\gamma}\, M\,\dfrac{1+\gamma - T}{1+\gamma}$ (since $1 - T/(1+\gamma) = (1+\gamma - T)/(1+\gamma)$).

$\dfrac{\partial W^U}{\partial T} = \dfrac{M}{1+\gamma}\Bigl[\tfrac{1}{\gamma}T^{1/\gamma - 1}(1+\gamma - T) - T^{1/\gamma}\Bigr] = \dfrac{M\, T^{1/\gamma - 1}}{\gamma}\,(1 - T) = 0$.

$\Rightarrow\; T = 1\;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\;\; \tau^{*\,U} = 0. \;\;}$

\textcolor{orange}{\emph{QL utility $\Rightarrow$ planner has \textbf{no taste for redistribution} (linear in $c$); only efficiency matters --- optimum is laissez-faire.}} & Differentiate the boxed $W^U(\tau)$ above. The term $-\ln\bigl(\sum_i \pi_i w_i^{1-\tau}\bigr)$ has derivative

$\dfrac{\sum_i \pi_i w_i^{1-\tau} \ln w_i}{\sum_i \pi_i w_i^{1-\tau}} \;=\; \mathbb{E}_{1-\tau}[\ln w]$

--- a $\tau$-dependent weighted log-moment of the skill distribution.

FOC: $-\dfrac{1}{(1+\gamma)(1-\tau)} - \dfrac{1}{1+\gamma} - \sum_i \pi_i \ln w_i + \mathbb{E}_{1-\tau}[\ln w] = 0$.

\textcolor{red}{\emph{Transcendental in $\tau$ --- closed-form $W^U$ exists but FOC needs a numerical $\tau^{*\,U}$.}} \\
\hline
\textbf{2B) Rawlsian.} \emph{Max utility of the worst-off agent.} & Assume $w_1 = 0 \Rightarrow h_1^* = 0$, $y_1 = 0$, $c_1 = B$ \emph{(lives off the transfer)}.

$W^R(\tau) = U(c_1, 0) = c_1 = B = \tau\, Y(\tau) = \tau\,(1-\tau)^{1/\gamma}\, M$.

\emph{Trick: $T := 1-\tau$, so $\tau = 1 - T$ and $W^R = (1 - T)\, T^{1/\gamma}\, M$.}

\textbf{FOC:} $\dfrac{\partial W^R}{\partial T} = M\, T^{1/\gamma - 1}\,\dfrac{1 - T(1+\gamma)}{\gamma} = 0$.

$\Rightarrow\; T = \dfrac{1}{1+\gamma}\;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\;\; \tau^{*\,R} = \dfrac{\gamma}{1+\gamma}. \;\;}$

\textcolor{orange}{\emph{Coincides with the Laffer peak --- Rawlsian taxes all the way to revenue max.}} & Same logic: worst-off has $w_1 = 0$, $c_1 = B(\tau)$, $W^R(\tau) = \ln B(\tau)$.

$\ln B(\tau) = \tfrac{\tau}{1+\gamma}\ln(1-\tau) + \ln\!\bigl(\sum_i \pi_i w_i\bigr) - \ln\!\bigl(\sum_i \pi_i w_i^{1-\tau}\bigr)$.

FOC also mixes $\ln(1-\tau)$ and a $\tau$-dependent weighted average $\Rightarrow$ \textcolor{red}{\emph{numerical $\tau^{*\,R}$.}} \\
\end{tabular}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Efficiency vs equity --- why the FB shape matters.}}

{{img:0|w=900}}

\textbf{Left} (Example 1, $U(c) = c$ $\Rightarrow$ linear FB). Isowelfare lines $\lambda u_1 + (1-\lambda) u_2 = $ const are \emph{parallel} to the FB. So every point on the FB sits on the \emph{same} isowelfare line $\Rightarrow$ the planner is indifferent among FB allocations $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{no welfare gain from redistribution} $\Rightarrow$ $\tau^{*\,U} = 0$.

\textbf{Right} (Example 2, $U(c) = \ln c$ $\Rightarrow$ concave FB). The FB curve is \emph{steeper than the isowelfare lines} at the rich end and \emph{flatter} at the poor end. A lump-sum transfer from rich (point $A$, the CE projection) to the symmetric point $B$ on the FB lands on a \emph{higher} isowelfare line $\Rightarrow$ $W(B) > W(A)$ $\Rightarrow$ \emph{equity offsets efficiency} $\Rightarrow$ positive $\tau^{*\,U}$.

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Cross-refs:}} setup (1st vs 2nd best UPF), HSV framework (Example 2 tax schedule), Rawlsian + Laffer (deeper dive).

**$\mu_y = 0$ in the cross externality case **

\emph{Setup: concave utility $u(y) = a \ln y \Rightarrow MB(y) = a/y$ (decreasing); convex damage $D(y) = (b/2) y^2 \Rightarrow |MC|(y) = b\, y$ (increasing). Two agents, endowment $\omega_y$, planner FOC $MB - |MC| = \mu_y$ at interior.}

\textbf{The whole question:} does the planner want \emph{less} $y$ than CE, or more? Check the sign of $MB - |MC|$ at the CE allocation $y_{CE} = \omega_y/2$:

$\bullet$ \textbf{Negative} (externality dominates scarcity) $\Rightarrow$ planner reduces $y$ $\Rightarrow$ constraint slacks $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{destruction}.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Positive} (scarcity dominates externality) $\Rightarrow$ planner would want \emph{more} $y$ but can't $\Rightarrow$ constraint binds $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{Pigou redundant} (no real change, only shadow-price wedge).

crucial point: this is totlaly different than what you have seen in the one side externality case, here in case B planner does not like the extenrality but still better to keep this consumption, he cannot move it from a tto be.
\begin{tabular}{p{19cm}|p{19cm}}
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Scenario A --- externality bites (canonical case)}} \;\;($a=10,\,b=60,\,\omega_y=1$) &
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Scenario B --- scarcity dominates (Pigou redundant)}} \;\;($a=10,\,b=20,\,\omega_y=1$) \\
\hline
\textbf{0. CE allocation (externality not internalized).} Each at $y_{CE} = 0.5$. $MB = a/y_{CE} = 20$, $|MC| = b\, y_{CE} = 30$. \newline
\textbf{Net social MB} $= 20 - 30 = -10 < 0$. \newline \emph{At CE, an extra unit of $y$ causes more damage than benefit. Over-provision.}
&
\textbf{0. CE allocation (externality not internalized).} Each at $y_{CE} = 0.5$. $MB = 20$, $|MC| = 10$. \newline
\textbf{Net social MB} $= 20 - 10 = +10 > 0$. \newline \emph{The externality EXISTS (damage is $10$) but is weak. At CE, an extra unit of $y$ would still raise welfare --- the planner would want more $y$ if it could.}
\\ \hline
\textbf{1. Planner internalizes.} Wants $MB - |MC| = \mu_y \ge 0$. At CE the gap is $-10$, infeasible $\Rightarrow$ planner reduces $y$.
&
\textbf{1. Planner internalizes.} Wants $MB - |MC| = \mu_y \ge 0$. At CE the gap is $+10 \ge 0$, already feasible. Planner doesn't want to reduce; if anything, would want more $y$ (but the constraint blocks).
\\ \hline
\textbf{2. Adjustment (causality).} The \emph{wedge $|MC|$ is added to the FOC first} $\Rightarrow$ agent's effective price of $y$ jumps up $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{agent reacts by cutting $y$}. As $y$ falls, two things follow: $MB \uparrow$ (concave $u$) and $|MC| \downarrow$ (convex damage). Both move \emph{toward each other}. Each agent reduces simultaneously and symmetrically; no idle agent absorbs the slack (both are polluter and victim at once).
&
\textbf{2. No adjustment.} Both stay at $y^i = 0.5$. Resource fully consumed ($\sum y^i = \omega_y$). The Pigou wedge $\mu_y = 10$ lives entirely as a shadow price; tax revenue raised but real allocation unchanged.
\\ \hline
\textbf{3. Equilibrium.} $y_{opt} = \sqrt{a/b} = \sqrt{1/6} \approx 0.408$ each. \newline $MB = MC \approx 24.49$. \newline \[\boxed{\;24.49 - 24.49 = 0 \;\; (=\mu_y)\;}\]
&
\textbf{3. Equilibrium.} $y^i = 0.5$ \emph{unchanged from CE}. \newline $MB = 20$, $|MC| = 10$. \newline \[\boxed{\;20 - 10 = 10 \;\; (=\mu_y)\;}\]
\\ \hline
\textbf{Destruction?} \textcolor{red}{\textbf{Yes.}} $2 y_{opt} \approx 0.816 < 1 = \omega_y$. About $18\%$ of the endowment sits idle.
&
\textbf{Destruction?} \textbf{No.} All of $\omega_y$ is consumed. \emph{But Pigou hasn't changed anything either.}
\\ \hline
\textcolor{purple}{\emph{Reading.}} CE was over-providing. The externality is severe enough that even with the constraint relaxed, social MB at $\omega_y/2$ is negative. Planner forces $y$ down until $MB = |MC|$. Since both reduce \emph{symmetrically} and no agent absorbs the slack, the leftover endowment is destroyed. \textbf{Destruction is how Pigou actually reduces consumption.}
&
\textcolor{purple}{\emph{Reading.}} Externality exists (damage is real) but is \emph{weak} relative to the resource scarcity. CE allocation already at the constraint, and planner would want \emph{more} $y$ if available. So Pigou tax is \textbf{redundant}: revenue is raised, $\mu_y = 10$ appears in shadow prices, but real consumption doesn't move. \emph{The externality is there in the math, but it doesn't bite.}
\\
\end{tabular}

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Takeaway.}}

$\bullet$ In symmetric cross externality, two regimes: \textbf{Pigou bites $\Leftrightarrow$ destruction occurs}. The two are the same event.

$\bullet$ Pigou is \textbf{redundant} when CE social MB at $\omega_y/2$ is non-negative --- i.e., when the resource is scarce enough that the planner would never push consumption below the constraint. In that case the externality exists but doesn't matter (tax is a pure transfer).

$\bullet$ The pivot: \textbf{sign of $MB(\omega_y/2) - |MC|(\omega_y/2)$ at CE}. Negative $\Rightarrow$ canonical case, destruction. Positive $\Rightarrow$ scarcity dominates, Pigou redundant.

$\bullet$ The asymmetric ``victim absorbs the slack'' story does NOT apply in either regime here: in symmetric cross, both reduce together (Scenario A) or neither reduces (Scenario B). No absorber.

in scenario B: applying a tax to everybody = applying a tax to nobody

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Three worked externality examples --- side-by-side.}}

\emph{Common setup.} Planner maximizes total utility with two resource constraints, $\sum x^i \le \omega_x$ (multiplier $\mu_x$) and $\sum y^i \le \omega_y$ (multiplier $\mu_y$). $y$ is the externality good. 
\begin{tabular}{p{5cm}|p{11cm}|p{11cm}|p{11cm}}
\textbf{Step} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{QL symmetric}} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{QL asymmetric}} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Cobb--Douglas symmetric}} \\
\hline
\textbf{0. Setup} &
$\sum_i \bigl(\ln y^i + x^i - y^{-i}\bigr)$. Each agent harmed by the other's $y$. &
$\bigl(\ln y^1 + x^1\bigr) + \bigl(\ln y^2 + x^2 - y^1\bigr)$. Only agent $1$ inflicts the spillover. &
$\sum_i \bigl(\sqrt{x^i y^i} - y^{-i}\bigr)$. Concave in both goods; both inflict spillover. \\
\hline
\textbf{1. FOC $x^i$} &
$1 - \mu_x = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\mu_x = 1}.$ Linear $x$ pins $\mu_x$. &
$1 - \mu_x = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\mu_x = 1}.$ &
$\tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{y^i/x^i} - \mu_x = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; x^i = \dfrac{y^i}{4\,\mu_x^{\,2}}.$ Endogenous $\mu_x$. \\
\hline
\textbf{2. FOC $y^i$} &
$\dfrac{1}{y^i} - 1 - \mu_y = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; y^i = \dfrac{1}{1+\mu_y}.$ Wedge of $1$ from the spillover, same for both. &
$y^1\!: \;\dfrac{1}{y^1} - 1 - \mu_y = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; y^1 = \dfrac{1}{1+\mu_y}.$ \;\;\; $y^2\!: \;\dfrac{1}{y^2} - \mu_y = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; y^2 = \dfrac{1}{\mu_y}.$ \textcolor{purple}{\emph{No wedge on $y^2$.}} &
$\tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{x^i/y^i} - 1 - \mu_y = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; y^i = \dfrac{x^i}{4\,(1+\mu_y)^{\,2}}.$ \\
\hline
\textbf{3. Plug into $\sum y^i = \omega_y$} &
$\dfrac{2}{1+\mu_y} = \omega_y.$ &
$\dfrac{1}{1+\mu_y} + \dfrac{1}{\mu_y} = \omega_y$ \;$\Rightarrow$\; $\omega_y\,\mu_y^{\,2} + (\omega_y - 2)\mu_y - 1 = 0.$ &
$\dfrac{\omega_x}{4(1+\mu_y)^{\,2}} = \omega_y$ (using $\sum x^i = \omega_x$). \\
\hline
\textbf{4. Solve $\mu_y$} &
$\boxed{\;\mu_y = \dfrac{2}{\omega_y} - 1\;}.$ &
$\boxed{\;\mu_y = \dfrac{(2-\omega_y) + \sqrt{\omega_y^{\,2}+4}}{2\,\omega_y}\;}$ \;\;(positive root). &
$\boxed{\;\mu_y = \tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{\omega_x/\omega_y} - 1\;}.$ \\
\hline
\textbf{5. When does $\mu_y$ bind?} &
$\mu_y > 0 \iff \omega_y < 2.$ \textit{Example:} $\omega_y = 1 \Rightarrow \mu_y = 1, y^i = 1/2.$ \;$\omega_y = 3 \Rightarrow \mu_y = 0, y^i = 1$, \textcolor{red}{$1$ unit destroyed.} &
$\mu_y > 0$ \textbf{for all $\omega_y$}: $y^2 = 1/\mu_y$ blows up at $\mu_y = 0$, infeasible. Constraint always binds; $\mu_y \to 0^+$ as $\omega_y \to \infty.$ &
$\mu_y > 0 \iff \omega_x/\omega_y > 4.$ \;Else $\mu_y = 0$, $\sum y^i = \omega_x/4 < \omega_y$, \textcolor{red}{$\omega_y - \omega_x/4$ destroyed.} \\
\hline
\textbf{6. Solution for $y^i$} &
$y^1 = y^2 = \omega_y/2$ (when $\mu_y > 0$); else $y^i = 1.$ &
$y^1 = \dfrac{1}{1+\mu_y}$ (small); $y^2 = \dfrac{1}{\mu_y}$ (large). \textcolor{red}{Heterogeneous allocation. THE PLANNER OBIVOULSY DOES NOT DESTROY AND GIVES TO THE NON POLLUTER!} &
$y^i$ determined by $\sum y^i = \omega_y$ + sym $\Rightarrow y^i = \omega_y/2.$ \\
\hline
\textbf{Reading} &
\textcolor{purple}{Even with abundant $y$, planner stops at $y^i = 1$: the social MB $1/y^i - 1$ goes negative beyond.} &
\textcolor{purple}{Planner squeezes the polluter ($y^1$ small) and lets the victim consume more ($y^2$ large). No symmetry $\Rightarrow$ heterogeneous wedges.} &
\textcolor{purple}{Interior split between $x$ and $y$ governed by $\omega_x/\omega_y$. When $y$ is too abundant relative to $x$, planner destroys some.} \\
\end{tabular}

nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{CE constraint problem \& solutions to the externality.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{CE constraint problem.}} Each agent solves
\[ \max_{y_i,\, x_i}\;\; U^i(y^1, y^2) + x^i\;\;\text{sub.}\;\; p_1 y^1 + p_2 y^2 + x^i = \omega_x^i + p_1 \omega_y^i\;\bigl(=: M_i\bigr). \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{FOCs (each agent, taking the other's $y$ as given).}} Lagrangian $\mathcal{L}^i = U^i(y^1, y^2) + x^i - \lambda^i\bigl(p_1 y^1 + p_2 y^2 + x^i - M_i\bigr)$. The QL form pins $\partial \mathcal{L}^i/\partial x^i: 1 - \lambda^i = 0 \Rightarrow \lambda^i = 1$. Then:

\[
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Agent 1:}}\;\; \dfrac{\partial U^1}{\partial y^1} = p_1, \qquad\quad
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Agent 2:}}\;\; \dfrac{\partial U^2}{\partial y^2} = p_2.
\]

\textcolor{purple}{\emph{Note: each agent equates own MU to own price. They DO NOT see $\partial U^j/\partial y^i$ --- the spillover on the other agent is ignored.}} This is the crucial step that creates the gap with the planner.


\textbf{The gap:} CE requires $\dfrac{\partial U^1}{\partial y^1} = p_1$ while the planner requires $\dfrac{\partial U^1}{\partial y^1} + \dfrac{\partial U^2}{\partial y^1} = \mu_y$. The planner's social MB \emph{includes the externality}; the CE doesn't.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Three classical solutions to restore Pareto-optimality.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{A. Quotas (Pigou-like).}} Impose the level of $c$ (consumption / output) directly at the planner's level. \emph{Blunt but works.} Two problems: 1) need to know the exact planner solution and 2) need to monitor (prhibitiionism problem)

\textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{B. Pigouvian tax.}} Tax agent 1's $y^1$ at the marginal external damage so he internalises the spillover via the price.

\emph{Asymmetric setting:}
\[
U^1 = U^1(y^1) + x^1, \qquad U^2 = U^2(y^2) - \varphi(y^1) + x^2,
\]
where $\varphi(\cdot)$ is the \textbf{damage function} ($\varphi' > 0$, typically convex). Agent 1 consumes only $y^1$, doesn't see $\varphi$. Agent 2 consumes $y^2$ \emph{and suffers} $-\varphi(y^1)$ from agent 1's choice.

\emph{Pigou tax with lump-sum revenue rebate.} The government taxes agent 1 at rate $t$ per unit of $y^1$, collects total revenue $T = t \cdot y^1$, and rebates lump-sum shares $T_1$ to agent 1 and $T_2$ to agent 2 with $T_1 + T_2 = T$ (balanced budget).
\[
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Agent 1:}}\;\; \max_{y^1,\, x^1}\;\; U^1(y^1) + x^1\;\;\text{sub.}\;\;(p_1 + t)\, y^1 + x^1 = \underbrace{\omega_x^1 + p_1\, \omega_y^1}_{M_1} + T_1,
\]
\[
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Agent 2:}}\;\; \max_{y^2,\, x^2}\;\; U^2(y^2) - \varphi(y^1) + x^2\;\;\text{sub.}\;\; p_2\, y^2 + x^2 = \underbrace{\omega_x^2 + p_1\, \omega_y^2}_{M_2} + T_2,
\]
\[ \boxed{\;\; T_1 + T_2 \;=\; T \;=\; t \cdot y^1 \;\;\;\text{(govt budget balance).}\;\;} \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{FOCs.}}
\[
\textbf{Agent 1:}\;\; \dfrac{\partial U^1}{\partial y^1} = p_1 + t, \qquad
\textbf{Agent 2:}\;\; \dfrac{\partial U^2}{\partial y^2} = p_2.
\]
\emph{The rebates $T_1, T_2$ are lump-sum --- they shift wealth but do NOT enter the FOCs.}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Planner condition} (from setup snippet):}
\[ \dfrac{\partial U^1}{\partial y^1} + \dfrac{\partial U^2}{\partial y^1} = \mu_y \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\; \dfrac{\partial U^1}{\partial y^1} = \mu_y + \varphi'(y^{1*}). \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Pigou choice.}} Set
\[ \boxed{\;\; t^* \;=\; \varphi'(y^{1*}) \;=\; -\,\dfrac{\partial U^2}{\partial y^1}, \qquad p_1 = \mu_y. \;\;} \]
Plug into agent 1's FOC: $\partial U^1/\partial y^1 = \mu_y + \varphi'(y^{1*})$ --- exactly the planner condition. \textbf{Output identical to the planner's.} The split $(T_1, T_2)$ only redistributes wealth (lump-sum), preserving Pareto optimality.

Remark: if pollution from cars is the negative extenrality you need to tax pollution, not cars. This is because peopel may buy say tractors that pollute even more if you just put a tax on cars. 

Interesting point: 
in the QL framework it is irrelevatn to whom you give the tax revenues. You can fully five the rebate to agent 1, fully expanding his BC, and result will not change:
1) he does not recognize his y consumption is funding is BC expansion. Note if he recognized he would understand there really is not tax. he is receivign every dollar he spends, and would buy the same quantity of y as before. 
2) with QL preferences, a expansion in budget = an expansion in endowments, does not affect consumption of y if the solution is interior. All the agents are consumign the same optimal y and the rest is going to the ql good. So we mean that rebate does not affect post tax expenditure. Obviously, still the guy is buying more than CE because he pays extra mc,  so the interior solution we are talkign about is with less quantity of y. 

\textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{C. Subsidy }} Pay agent 1 to consume \emph{less} $y^1$

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Subsidy (per unit \emph{not} consumed).}} Government pays agent 1 $s$ for each unit of $y^1$ \textbf{reduced from the pre-policy CE baseline} $\bar y^{1,CE}$:
\[ \text{subsidy payment} \;=\; s\,\bigl(\bar y^{1,CE} - y^1\bigr). \]

\emph{Why per unit \textbf{not} consumed (not per unit consumed):} a subsidy per unit consumed would lower the effective price to $p_1 - s$ and \textbf{incentivise more $y^1$} --- wrong direction. IS as taking the tax before and susbituting p1 + t with p1 - s- 
\emph{Agent 1's problem:}
\[
\max_{y^1,\, x^1}\;\; U^1(y^1) + x^1\;\;\text{sub.}\;\; p_1\, y^1 + x^1 = \underbrace{\omega_x^1 + p_1\, \omega_y^1}_{M_1} + s\,(\bar y^{1,CE} - y^1).
\]
Rearranging: $(p_1 + s)\, y^1 + x^1 = M_1 + s\, \bar y^{1,CE}$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{FOC:}}
\[ \dfrac{\partial U^1}{\partial y^1} = p_1 + s. \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Subsidy choice.}} Set
\[ \boxed{\;\; s^* \;=\; \varphi'(y^{1*}) \;=\; -\,\dfrac{\partial U^2}{\partial y^1}, \qquad p_1 = \mu_y. \;\;} \]
Plug into agent 1's FOC: $\partial U^1/\partial y^1 = \mu_y + \varphi'(y^{1*})$ --- exactly the planner condition. \textbf{Output identical to the planner's.}


Problem to approaches A, B C: 
You need to know $\varphi'(y^{1*})$ to solve the problem. 




\textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{D. Missing market (Coase).}} 
Missign market framework: if you assign the property right the problem will be solved as agents negotiate. Coase: which side gets the right doesn't change the allocation, only distribution.

\emph{Setting: right to agent 2 (e.g.\ the fisher owns the river).} Agent 2 holds the right to a clean environment; he can sell permits to agent 1 at price $r$. y is gasoline. Let $z$ be the tradeable right (one permit $\leftrightarrow$ one unit of $y^1$). $z^d$ = agent 1's demand, $z^s$ = agent 2's supply. \emph{Agent 2 controls how much $y^1$ agent 1 can consume by choosing how much $z^s$ to issue.}
\[
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Agent 1 (chooses $y^1, z^d, x^1$):}}\;\; \max\;\; U^1(y^1) + x^1\;\;\text{sub.}
\]
\[ p_1\, y^1 + r\, z^d + x^1 = \underbrace{\omega_x^1 + p_1\, \omega_y^1}_{M_1}, \qquad y^1 \le z^d. \]

\[
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Agent 2 (chooses $y^1, z^s, x^2$):}}\;\; \max\;\; U^2(y^2) - \varphi(y^1) + x^2\;\;\text{sub.}
\]
\[ p_2\, y^2 + x^2 = \underbrace{\omega_x^2 + p_1\, \omega_y^2}_{M_2} + r\, z^s \]


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Lagrangians.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Agent 1's FOCs.}}
in fixing y1, agent 1 has to anticipate how much r he will have to pay to agent 2 to buy y1 
\[
\partial \mathcal{L}^1/\partial x^1:\;\; 1 - \lambda_1 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\lambda_1 = 1},
\]
\[
\partial \mathcal{L}^1/\partial z^d:\;\; -\lambda_1 r + \xi_1 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\xi_1 = r},
\]
\[
\partial \mathcal{L}^1/\partial y^1:\;\; \dfrac{\partial U^1}{\partial y^1} - \lambda_1 p_1 - \xi_1 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\dfrac{\partial U^1}{\partial y^1} = p_1 + r}.
\]
the last equation is giving you the optimal $y^1$. 

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Agent 2's FOCs.}}
in fixing r, agent 2 has to anticipate how much y1 agent 1 will ask for. 
\[
\partial \mathcal{L}^2/\partial x^2:\;\; 1 - \lambda_2 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\lambda_2 = 1},
\]
\[
\partial \mathcal{L}^2/\partial y^2:\;\; \dfrac{\partial U^2}{\partial y^2} - \lambda_2 p_2 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\dfrac{\partial U^2}{\partial y^2} = p_2},
\]
\[
\partial \mathcal{L}^2/\partial z^s:\;\; \lambda_2 r - \xi_2 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\xi_2 = r},
\]
\[
\partial \mathcal{L}^2/\partial y^1:\;\; -\,\varphi'(y^1) + \xi_2 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{ r = \varphi'(y^1)}.
\]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Market-clearing.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why D beats A, B, C.}} The market \textbf{discovers $r^*$ endogenously} through agent 2's supply decision. \emph{The planner does NOT need to know $\varphi'(y^{1*})$ ex ante} --- agent 2 reveals it through his FOC for selling permits. Pigou (B), subsidy (C), and quota (A) all require the planner to compute $\varphi'$ in advance; D escapes this informational burden.

\textcolor{purple}{\emph{Coase caveats:}} (i) property rights must be well-defined and enforceable, (ii) transaction costs must be low, (iii) breaks with many parties / asymmetric info.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Public goods --- taxonomy, distinction from externalities, production model.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{1. Taxonomy: rivalry $\times$ excludability.}}

\begin{tabular}{p{6cm}|p{16cm}|p{16cm}}
& \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Rivalrous}} \;\;(my consumption blocks yours) & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Non-rivalrous}} \;\;(same unit enjoyed simultaneously) \\
\hline
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Excludable}} \;\;(can charge a price) & \textbf{Private}: panino. \emph{I eat the panino, you don't; price $6$\,\euro.} & \textbf{Club}: private beach. \emph{Both lie on the sand simultaneously; $30$\,\euro\ entry excludes outsiders.} \\
\hline
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Non-excludable}} \;\;(cannot prevent access) & \textbf{Common pool}: fish in the sea. \emph{I catch a fish, you don't have that one; but cannot prevent you from fishing.} & \textbf{Public}: defence / fireworks. \emph{Iron dome blocks a missile $\Rightarrow$ both houses saved; cannot let only some missiles pass.} \\
\end{tabular}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Pollution = public bad.}} Non-rivalrous (everyone breathes the same air), non-excludable. All consume the same amount.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{2. Public good vs externality.}}

$\bullet$ \emph{Externality}: agents choose private $y^1, y^2$; spillover is the side-effect on the other's utility.

$\bullet$ \emph{Public good}: a single $y$ is produced and consumed identically by all. \textbf{Both agents enjoy the SAME $y$} --- the structural difference.

\textcolor{purple}{\emph{Slogan: externality = private + spillover; public good = single quantity consumed by all.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{3. Production model.}} Devote $z$ units of the private good as input to produce $y$ units of public good:
\[ z \; \ge \; c(y), \qquad c(0) = 0, \quad c'(y) > 0. \]

about the first equation: we are saying that the cost of production cannot be greater of how much you invest/input = z.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Cost curvature.}}

$\bullet$ \emph{Convex} ($c'' > 0$): \textbf{the second unit is more expensive than the first, the third more than the second, etc.} Diminishing marginal returns.

$\bullet$ \emph{Linear} ($c'' = 0$): every unit costs the same. Constant returns.

$\bullet$ \emph{Concave} ($c'' < 0$): the second cheaper than the first, the third cheaper than the second, etc. Increasing returns / economies of scale.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Rationales for public provision} --- two logically independent arguments.}

$\bullet$ (1) \textbf{Free-riding (behavioural)}: decentralised voluntary contributions under-provide; central provision via taxes solves. Holds for ANY cost shape.

$\bullet$ (2) \textbf{Economies of scale (technological)}: one big producer cheaper than many small. Only with concave $c$.

\textbf{Tension with convex costs:} by Jensen, $2c(y/2) < c(y)$ when $c''>0$, so splitting is cheaper --- convex tech \textbf{argues against} centralisation; public provision then rests only on rationale (1).
