\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Public goods --- competitive equilibrium (CE) with firms and profits, $p_x$ NOT normalised.}}

\emph{Same primitives as planner: $U^i(x^i, y)$, both agents consume the SAME $y$, production technology $z = c(y)$, $c' > 0$ convex. Prices: $p_x$ for private good, $p_y$ for public good. We do NOT normalise --- both prices kept general; only the ratio $p_y/p_x$ has economic content (Walras).}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Firm side --- production and profit.}} A firm produces the public good $y$ using $c(y)$ units of $x$ (cost in $x$-units). revenue is $p_y y$ and cost is $p_x c(y)$:
\[ \pi(y) \;=\; p_y\, y \;-\; \underbrace{p_x\, c(y)}_{\text{you need z inputs, of cost px}}. \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Firm's problem and FOC.}}
\[ \max_y\;\; p_y\, y - p_x\, c(y) \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \boxed{\;p_y \;=\; p_x\, c'(y) \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\; \dfrac{p_y}{p_x} = c'(y) = MRT\;}. \]
\emph{Relative price equals marginal rate of transformation.}

At the optimum the firm earns profit $\pi^* = p_y y^* - p_x c(y^*) > 0$ (producer surplus from convex cost). Profits distributed via ownership shares $\theta^i \ge 0$, $\sum_i \theta^i = 1$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Consumer side --- agent $i$'s problem.}} Each agent chooses private $x^i$ and his contribution $y^i$ (so total $y = y^1 + y^2$). Budget in dollar-terms:
\[
\max_{x^i,\, y^i}\;\; U^i(x^i, y^1 + y^2) \;\;\text{sub.}\;\; \underbrace{p_x\, x^i}_{\text{private spend}} + \underbrace{p_y\, y^i}_{\text{share of pub.\ good purchased}} \;=\; \underbrace{p_x\, \omega^i}_{\text{endowment value}} + \underbrace{\theta^i\, \pi^*}_{\text{firm profit share}}.
\]
\emph{Agent $i$ takes $p_x, p_y, \pi^*, y^{-i}$ as given.}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Consumer FOCs (with KKT for the corner $y^i = 0$).}}
\[ \mathcal{L}^i = U^i(x^i, y^1+y^2) - \lambda^i\bigl(p_x x^i + p_y y^i - p_x \omega^i - \theta^i \pi^*\bigr) + \xi^i\, y^i. \]
\[ \partial \mathcal{L}^i/\partial x^i:\;\; \dfrac{\partial U^i}{\partial x^i} = \lambda^i\, p_x \quad\Rightarrow\quad \boxed{\lambda^i = \dfrac{1}{p_x}\dfrac{\partial U^i}{\partial x^i}}, \]
\[ \partial \mathcal{L}^i/\partial y^i:\;\; \dfrac{\partial U^i}{\partial y} - \lambda^i\, p_y + \xi^i = 0 \quad\text{with}\quad \xi^i \ge 0,\; y^i \ge 0,\; \xi^i\, y^i = 0. \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The two regimes.}}

\emph{Let $\hat y^1, \hat y^2$ be \textbf{guessed} (candidate) contributions and $\hat y \equiv \hat y^1 + \hat y^2$ the candidate total provision. To find the equilibrium: \textbf{guess} who contributes (interior) vs who free-rides (corner), then verify KKT at $\hat y$. \textbf{$U^i$ and its derivatives are always evaluated at $\hat y$} (the common public-good level); the regimes differ only in what $\hat y$ ends up being.}

\begin{tabular}{p{8cm}|p{15cm}|p{15cm}}
& \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Interior $\hat y^i > 0$ (contributes)}} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Corner $\hat y^i = 0$ (free-rides)}} \\
\hline
KKT slack/binding & $\xi^i = 0$ & $\xi^i \ge 0$ \\
\hline
$y^i$-FOC & $\dfrac{\partial U^i}{\partial y}\Big|_{\hat y} = \lambda^i p_y$ & $\dfrac{\partial U^i}{\partial y}\Big|_{\hat y} \le \lambda^i p_y$ \\
\hline
In MRS form & $\boxed{MRS^i\Big|_{\hat y} = \dfrac{p_y}{p_x}}$ & $\boxed{MRS^i\Big|_{\hat y} \;\le\; \dfrac{p_y}{p_x}}$ \\
\hline
Equilibrium $\hat y$ & $\hat y = \hat y^1 + \hat y^2$ (both contribute) & $\hat y = \hat y^{-i}$ (only the other) \\
\end{tabular}


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why the corner happens to the LOWER-MU agent.}} Let agent $-i$ be the contributor: his interior FOC at $\hat y$ holds with equality, $\partial U^{-i}/\partial y|_{\hat y} = \lambda^{-i} p_y$. For agent $i$ at the SAME $\hat y$, if his marginal benefit is lower --- $\partial U^i/\partial y|_{\hat y} < \partial U^{-i}/\partial y|_{\hat y}$ --- then
\[ \dfrac{\partial U^i}{\partial y}\bigg|_{\hat y} \;<\; \lambda^i p_y \]
(in QL with $\lambda^i = 1/p_x$ the threshold is identical for both agents). So agent $i$'s FOC holds with strict inequality $\Rightarrow$ corner $\hat y^i = 0$. \textbf{The agent with weaker preference at the common $\hat y$ free-rides; the agent with stronger preference carries the full burden.} Three curical ingreidents: 1) shared y, 2) MU decreasing and 3) common $\lambda_i$ this  due to the fact they have a common quasilienar good. note the importance of the outside option, say the freeerider is rich, he is spesnign no money on y because he cares less, he spends a lot of money on x. But then his marginal utility from using from using x is going down a lot and he may end up buying some y as well (eg homothetic). actually quasilinear preferences make sense eh.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why corner exists in public goods (not in private goods).}}

\emph{Crucial:} agent $i$'s MB is $\partial U^i/\partial y$ evaluated at \textbf{total} $y = y^1 + y^2$, NOT at own $y^i$. This is the structural property of a public good --- both agents consume the same $y$.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Private good (counterfactual).} MB read at own $y^i$. At $y^i = 0$: MB $\to +\infty$ (Inada). So $MRS^i$ at zero exceeds any finite price $\Rightarrow$ \emph{always} interior. The idea is that for sure for some little quanityt you will buy even if prices are very low! 

$\bullet$ \textbf{Public good (our case).} MB read at total $y = y^1 + y^2$. At $y^i = 0$, total $y = y^{-i} > 0$ (other's contribution). Diminishing MU has already acted along $y^{-i}$. So MB at $y = y^{-i}$ \textbf{is below $p_y/p_x$ whenever agent $i$'s MU at $\hat y$ is strictly less than the contributor's} $\Rightarrow$ \emph{corner happens \textbf{generically}}. Usualy: I BUY UNTIL MB = MC HWERE WE ARLEADY START WITH MB < MCzf

\textcolor{purple}{\emph{Slogan: in private goods MB starts at $\infty$ (no corner, ever); in public goods MB starts at $\partial U^i/\partial y|_{y^{-i}}$ --- already discounted by the other's purchase. \textbf{Whenever the two agents have strictly different MU at $\hat y$, the lower-MU agent free-rides.} Interior + interior is a measure-zero knife-edge ($\alpha_1 = \alpha_2$ exactly). \textbf{Free-riding is the generic outcome}, not the exception.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Market-clearing CE condition (welfare loss!!).}} Combining firm FOC and contributor's FOC: each contributor has $MRS^i = c'(y) = MRT$. At CE,
\[ \boxed{\;\; MRS^i_{y,x} \;=\; \dfrac{p_y}{p_x} \;=\; c'(y) \;=\; MRT \;\; \text{for each contributing agent.}\;\;} \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The under-provision gap (vs Samuelson).}} Compare with planner:
\[ \text{CE (contributors):}\;\; MRS^i = MRT \quad\text{vs}\quad \text{Planner (Samuelson):}\;\; \sum_i MRS^i = MRT. \]
At CE each agent equates only his OWN MRS to the marginal cost --- he ignores that one more $y$ benefits all agents (non-rivalrous). $\sum_i MRS^i$ exceeds $MRT$ at the CE allocation:
\[ y^{CE} \;<\; y^{*\,\text{Planner}}. \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Asset pricing --- AD framework, Radner equilibrium.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{0. Prerequisites.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{i) Uncertainty.}} A finite set of \textbf{states of the world} $S = \{s_1, s_2, \dots, s_S\}$ captures all the ways the future may turn out. We then promise/receive \textbf{state-contingent commodities} $x_{s,i}$ = ``amount of good $i$ delivered if state $s$ realises.''

\emph{Example with $3$ states and $3$ goods:}

\begin{tabular}{p{6cm}|p{10cm}|p{10cm}|p{10cm}}
& \textbf{Good $x_1$} & \textbf{Good $x_2$} & \textbf{Good $x_3$} \\
\hline
\textbf{State $s_1$} & $x_{s_1, 1}$ & $x_{s_1, 2}$ & $x_{s_1, 3}$ \\
\hline
\textbf{State $s_2$} & $x_{s_2, 1}$ & $x_{s_2, 2}$ & $x_{s_2, 3}$ \\
\hline
\textbf{State $s_3$} & $x_{s_3, 1}$ & $x_{s_3, 2}$ & $x_{s_3, 3}$ \\
\end{tabular}

\textbf{Reading the table.}
$\bullet$ \emph{States of the world} let us describe \textbf{uncertainty} about a future value of $x_i$: the realisation of $s$ determines which column entry materialises.

$\bullet$ Each \textbf{row} is a \textbf{state-contingent commodity vector} $x_s = (x_{s,1}, x_{s,2}, x_{s,3})$ --- the bundle of goods you receive \emph{if state $s$ realises}.

$\bullet$ The \textbf{full matrix} $\bigl(x_{s,i}\bigr)_{s, i}$ is the entire state-contingent commodity allocation --- ``what I receive in every conceivable future.''

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{ii) Expected utility preferences.}} Aggregate utility from a state-contingent plan $x^i = (x_{s_1}^i, \dots, x_{s_S}^i)$ is the probability-weighted sum of state utilities:
$$ \boxed{\;\; U^i(x^i) \;=\; \sum_{s=1}^{S} \pi_s^i\, u^i(x_s^i) \;\;\quad (A)\;} $$
where $u^i$ is \textbf{strictly increasing} and \textbf{concave} (risk aversion). Equation (A) is the von Neumann--Morgenstern \emph{expected utility} representation.

\textcolor{purple}{\emph{Reading: agents collapse the entire random vector $(x_{s_1}^i, \dots, x_{s_S}^i)$ into a single number by taking the expectation of $u^i(x_s^i)$ over states.}}


Arrow securities span $\mathbb{R}^S$: any payoff vector $\zeta \in \mathbb{R}^S$ can be written as $\sum_s \zeta_s A^s$. Hence, \textbf{complete markets} $\Leftrightarrow$ assets span $\mathbb{R}^S$ $\Leftrightarrow$ the payoff matrix has rank $S$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{3. AD vs Radner --- complete comparison.}}

NOTE: JUST ONE CONSUMPTION GOOD (BEOFRE 2, NOW S)
\begin{tabular}{p{2cm}|p{16cm}|p{18cm}}
\textbf{Step} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{AD framework}} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Radner framework}} \\
\hline
\textbf{Setting} & $\bullet$ \textbf{At $t_0$}: state $s$ is unknown. Agents trade \emph{state-contingent commodities} (``pieces of paper'' promising delivery in each state). Budget constraint:
$$ \sum_{s \in S} \bigl(\omega_s^i - x_s^i\bigr) \;\ge\; 0. $$
\emph{The **sum** (!!!, not the single entry) of net trades across states must be non-negative (you can promise to deliver less in some state if you also promise to receive less in another).}

\emph{Example: $I = 2$, $S = 2$. Agent 1 endowed $(10, 0)$ across states; agent 2 endowed $(0, 10)$. They trade to smooth $\Rightarrow$ each ends up with $(5, 5)$. So $\omega_s^i - x_s^i$ is negative in one state (you receive more than you brought) but compensated by the other state and by the other agent.}

$\bullet$ \textbf{At $t_1$}: state $s$ is revealed; contracts are executed (each agent receives his promised $x_s^i$).

CRUCIAL: ~~THERE IS NO PRESENT VS FUTURE HERE. THESE TWO ARE BOTH FUTURE STATES~~ & Radner is just AD $+$ $C_0$ consumption $+$ \textcolor{darkgreen}{\textbf{extras}}.

$\bullet$ \textbf{At $t_0$:} agents are endowed with $\omega_0^i$, consume $x_0^i$, and trade \textcolor{darkgreen}{\textbf{assets}} \emph{(now instead of holding a contract for a contingent claim, you hold an asset).}

\emph{Asset definition:} a vector
$$ r^k \;=\; (r_1^k,\, \dots,\, r_s^k,\, \dots,\, r_S^k) $$
where $r_s^k$ is the amount to be received at time $1$ (if state $s \in S$ occurs) for each unit of $k$. The asset has quantity $\theta_k$ and price $q_k$.

\emph{Examples:}

$\bullet$ \textbf{Arrow}: pays $1$ only in $1$ state, $r^s = (0, \dots, 1, \dots, 0)$.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Risk-free bond}: $r^B = (1, 1, 1, \dots, 1)$ --- $1$ in each state.

$\bullet$ \textbf{At $t_1$:} state $s$ realises, contracts are enforced, assets delivered. \textcolor{darkgreen}{\textbf{The market reopens and the goods can be exchanged!}} This is an extra opportunity to trade at the spot market.
\\ \hline
\textbf{Maximisation problem} & $$ \max_{(x_s^i)_s}\;\; U^i(x^i) = \sum_{s \in S} \pi_s^i\, u^i(x_s^i) \;\;\text{sub.}\;\; \sum_{s} p_s\,(\omega_s^i - x_s^i) \ge 0. $$
\emph{MRS condition} (interior, two states $h, l$; \textbf{all agents face the same state prices} $p$). Write agent $1$'s condition, the common price ratio, and agent $2$'s condition as one chain:
$$ \boxed{\;\; \dfrac{\pi_l^1}{\pi_h^1} \cdot \underbrace{\dfrac{u^{1\prime}(\hat x_l^1)}{u^{1\prime}(\hat x_h^1)}}_{\textstyle A} \;=\; \dfrac{p_l}{p_h} \;=\; \dfrac{\pi_l^2}{\pi_h^2} \cdot \underbrace{\dfrac{u^{2\prime}(\hat x_l^2)}{u^{2\prime}(\hat x_h^2)}}_{\textstyle B} \;\;} $$
$A$ and $B$ are the pure \textbf{marginal-utility ratios}; multiplying each by its belief ratio $\pi_l^i/\pi_h^i$ gives that agent's probability-weighted $MRS$, and both are pinned to the same state-price ratio: $\dfrac{\pi_l^1}{\pi_h^1}A=\dfrac{\pi_l^2}{\pi_h^2}B$.

   & $$ \max_{\theta^i,\; x^i}\;\; u^i(x_0^i) + \beta^i\sum_{s=1}^{S} \pi_s^i\, u^i(x_s^i) \;\;\text{sub.} \underbrace{p_0\, x_0^i \;+\; \sum_{k=1}^{K} q_k\, \theta_k^i \;\le\; p_0\, \omega_0^i}_{\textbf{how much you can invest at $t_0$}\;\;},\underbrace{p_s\, x_s^i \;\le\; p_s\, \omega_s^i \;+\; \sum_{k=1}^{K} r_s^k\, \theta_k^i}_{\textbf{how much you can consume in each state $s$}\;\;(\omega_s \text{ + asset payoffs})} \quad\forall\, s = 1, \dots, S $$

$$ \underbrace{x_s^i \;\ge\; 0}_{\text{non-negativity, every $s$}} \quad\forall\, s = 0, 1, \dots, S $$

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Maximisation variables: $\theta^i$ and $x^i$.}}

$\bullet$ $x^i = (x_0^i, x_1^i, \dots, x_S^i)$ --- the usual state-by-state consumption plan ($t_0$ plus each future state). Notre this is not just where to place the investm if the future spot rate is needed. 

$\bullet$ $\theta^i = (\theta_1^i, \dots, \theta_K^i)$ --- how many units of each asset $k$ the agent buys at $t_0$.

\textcolor{purple}{\emph{The agent picks BOTH which assets to buy AND what consumption he wants in each (date, state). At $t_0$ he chooses his portfolio $\theta^i$ to use the asset structure as a vehicle for moving wealth across states; at each $t_1$ state he then consumes whatever his portfolio + endowment allows on the spot market.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Lagrangian and full FOCs.}}
$$ \mathcal{L}^i = u^i(x_0^i) + \beta^i \sum_s \pi_s^i\, u^i(x_s^i) - \lambda_0^i\Bigl[p_0 x_0^i + \sum_k q_k \theta_k^i - p_0 \omega_0^i\Bigr] - \sum_s \lambda_s^i\Bigl[p_s x_s^i - p_s \omega_s^i - \sum_k r_s^k \theta_k^i\Bigr]. $$
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{FOC 1} ($\partial \mathcal{L}^i/\partial x_0^i$, today's consumption):}
$$ u^{i\prime}(x_0^i) - \lambda_0^i\, p_0 = 0 \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \boxed{\;\lambda_0^i = \dfrac{u^{i\prime}(x_0^i)}{p_0}\;} $$
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{FOC 2} ($\partial \mathcal{L}^i/\partial x_s^i$, state-$s$ consumption, $s = 1, \dots, S$):}
$$ \beta^i \pi_s^i u^{i\prime}(x_s^i) - \lambda_s^i\, p_s = 0 \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \boxed{\;\lambda_s^i = \dfrac{\beta^i \pi_s^i u^{i\prime}(x_s^i)}{p_s}\;} $$
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{FOC 3} ($\partial \mathcal{L}^i/\partial \theta_k^i$, portfolio, $k = 1, \dots, K$):}
$$ -\lambda_0^i\, q_k + \sum_s \lambda_s^i\, r_s^k = 0 \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \boxed{\;q_k = \dfrac{1}{\lambda_0^i}\sum_s \lambda_s^i\, r_s^k\;} $$
\emph{Asset price = present value of payoffs weighted by marginal-utility-of-income per state.} Note how you take foc wrt CHOICE VARIABLES!



\textcolor{purple}{\emph{Note: ratios of FOC 2 give the state-price formula $p_s/p_0 = \pi_s^i \rho_s^i$, and ratios across two states give the cross-state MRS.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Combining FOC 1, 2, 3} (substitute $\lambda_0^i$ and $\lambda_s^i$):}
$$ q_k = \sum_{s=1}^{S} \pi_s^i\, \underbrace{\beta^i\, \dfrac{u^{i\prime}(x_s^i)}{u^{i\prime}(x_0^i)}}_{\equiv\; \rho_s^i\;=\; \textbf{SDF}}\, \dfrac{p_0}{p_s}\, r_s^k \;=\; \mathbb{E}^i[\rho^i \cdot r^k] $$
\emph{Price = expected discounted payoff via the SDF $\rho_s^i = \beta^i u'(x_s^i)/u'(x_0^i)$.}. Interpretation: discounted marginal utility of one unit of consumption in state s, relative to the marginal utility of one unit of consumption today. \textcolor{purple}{\emph{Note: $\mu_s$ is high in bad states (low $x_s$, high marginal utility); assets that pay there (insurance) are valued more; assets that pay only in good states (low $\mu_s$) are cheaper, hence the equity premium.}} 


\textcolor{red}{SDF}
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Key feature.}} If the asset pays \emph{nothing} in state $s$ ($r_s^k = 0$), that state contributes \textbf{zero} to the price --- no matter how high $\mu_s$ is. The SDF only ``charges'' for the payoff the asset actually delivers.

\vspace{0.3em}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{SDF $\times$ no-arbitrage: why $\mu > 0$ matters.}}

$\bullet$ \textbf{With arbitrage:} the agent can scale the arbitrage portfolio infinitely $\Rightarrow$ infinite consumption (either today or in some state). By concavity, $u'(\infty) \to 0$. So either the numerator $u'(x_s) \to 0$ (arb in state $s$) or the denominator $u'(x_0) \to 0$ (arb at $t_0$). The SDF $\mu_s = \beta\, u'(x_s)/u'(x_0)$ goes to inf. 

$\bullet$ \textbf{Proposition 1 (book):} if $(R, q)$ admits a strictly positive SDF $\mu > 0$ then $(R, q)$ is arbitrage-free.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Proposition 2 (book):} if $(R, q)$ is arbitrage-free, then $\exists$ at least one \textbf{non-negative} SDF $\mu \ge 0$ that prices every asset. \emph{Note: $\ge$, not $>$ --- under incomplete markets, some states $s$ can have $\mu_s = 0$ without contradicting NA. This happens when no asset pays in those states, so their state-price is not pinned down.}

$\bullet$ \textbf{Adding complete markets:} \emph{NA $+$ complete markets} $\Rightarrow$ $\mu > 0$ \textbf{strictly}.

\vspace{0.3em}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Uniqueness of the SDF.}}

    (S+1) + K
    $$
    first-order conditions: one for today's consumption $x_0$, one for each future-state consumption $x_s$ ($s=1,\dots,S$), and one for each asset holding $\theta_k$ ($k=1,\dots,K$).
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Approach B (worked example).}

\begin{itemize}
    \item First solve the budget constraints to express consumption as a function of the portfolio:
    $$
    x = x(\theta).
    $$
    \item Substitute these expressions directly into the utility function.
    \item The only remaining choice variable is $\theta$, so optimize only with respect to $\theta$.
\end{itemize}

\textit{Both approaches are mathematically equivalent and lead to exactly the same optimality condition.}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Worked example: 2 states, 1 incomplete asset (book).}}

\emph{Setup.} Two states $s_1,s_2$. There is \textbf{one} asset traded at $t_0$ with payoff
$$
r=(1,0),
$$
i.e. it pays one unit in state $s_1$ and nothing in state $s_2$. The asset price is $q$, and the agent chooses how many units $\theta$ to hold. Markets are \textbf{incomplete}: no asset pays in state $s_2$.

\medskip

\textbf{Step 1. Write the objective function.}

The agent maximises expected utility:
$$
U(x_0,x_1,x_2)
=
u(x_0)
+
\beta\left[
\pi_1u(x_1)
+
\pi_2u(x_2)
\right].
$$

\medskip

\textbf{Step 2. Write the budget constraints.}

Since there is only one asset,

$$
x_0=\omega_0-q\theta,
$$

$$
x_1=\omega_1+\theta,
$$

$$
\boxed{x_2=\omega_2.}
$$

Notice that there is \emph{no} decision affecting state $2$: the agent simply consumes their endowment there.

\medskip

\textbf{Step 3. Eliminate the consumption variables.}

Substitute the budget constraints directly into utility:

$$
U(\theta)
=
u(\omega_0-q\theta)
+
\beta\pi_1u(\omega_1+\theta)
+
\beta\pi_2u(\omega_2).
$$

Now the optimisation problem has only \textbf{one} choice variable:

$$
\boxed{\theta.}
$$

Once $\theta$ is chosen,

$$
x_0,\;x_1,\;x_2
$$

are automatically determined by the budget constraints.

\medskip

\textbf{Step 4. Differentiate with respect to the remaining choice variable.}

Using the chain rule,

$$
\frac{dU}{d\theta}
=
u'(x_0)
\underbrace{\frac{\partial x_0}{\partial\theta}}_{=-q}
+
\beta\pi_1u'(x_1)
\underbrace{\frac{\partial x_1}{\partial\theta}}_{=1}
+
\beta\pi_2u'(x_2)
\underbrace{\frac{\partial x_2}{\partial\theta}}_{=0}.
$$

Since

$$
x_2=\omega_2
$$

is fixed,

$$
\frac{\partial x_2}{\partial\theta}=0,
$$

so the third term disappears.

The FOC becomes

$$
-q\,u'(x_0)
+
\beta\pi_1u'(x_1)
=
0.
$$

Rearranging,

$$
\boxed{
q
=
\pi_1
\underbrace{
\beta
\frac{u'(x_1)}{u'(x_0)}
}_{\mu_1}.
}
$$

\medskip

\textbf{Step 5. Recover the pricing equation.}

The general pricing formula is

$$
q
=
\sum_{s=1}^2
\pi_s\mu_sr_s.
$$

Since

$$
r=(1,0),
$$

this becomes

$$
q
=
\pi_1\mu_1(1)
+
\pi_2\mu_2(0)
=
\boxed{\pi_1\mu_1.}
$$

Only the state in which the asset pays contributes to its price.

\medskip

\textbf{Step 6. Interpret the SDF.}

The implied SDF vector is

$$
\mu
=
(\mu_1,\mu_2)
=
\left(
\underbrace{\frac{q}{\pi_1}}_{\text{identified from prices}},
\;
\underbrace{?}_{\text{not identified}}
\right).
$$

Because no asset ever pays in state $2$, the market provides no information about $\mu_2$. Any non-negative value of $\mu_2$ is consistent with the observed asset price.
\\

\hline
\textbf{Expansion 1: heterogeneous beliefs} \;\;($\pi_l^1 \ne \pi_l^2$) & 
{{img:1|w=460}}

\emph{Setup:} relax $\pi^1 = \pi^2$. Each agent's MRS becomes
$$ \dfrac{p_l}{p_h} = \dfrac{\pi_l^i}{\pi_h^i} \cdot \dfrac{u^{i\prime}(x_l^i)}{u^{i\prime}(x_h^i)}. $$
PO: $(\pi_l^1/\pi_h^1) A = (\pi_l^2/\pi_h^2) B$.

\emph{Result:} contract curve \textbf{bends away from the $45^\circ$ line}, toward the optimistic agent's preferred state.

\emph{Proof.} Assume $\pi_l^1 > \pi_l^2$, so $\pi_l^1/\pi_h^1 > \pi_l^2/\pi_h^2$. For PO,
$$ \dfrac{\pi_l^1}{\pi_h^1} A \;=\; \dfrac{\pi_l^2}{\pi_h^2} B \quad\Longrightarrow\quad A \;<\; B. $$
This is obious as the Mu of agent 1 is going to be lower as he buys more!
\textbf{Claim:} $x_l^1 > x_h^1$. \emph{(per contra)} Suppose $x_l^1 < x_h^1$. Then by concavity, $A = u'(x_l^1)/u'(x_h^1) > 1$. By no aggregate risk, $x_l^2 = \omega - x_l^1 > \omega - x_h^1 = x_h^2$, so $B = u'(x_l^2)/u'(x_h^2) < 1$. Hence $A > 1 > B$, contradicting $A < B$. $\square$

\emph{Conclusion: agent 1 takes more in $l$ (his preferred state); agent 2 takes more in $h$. Agents consume disproportionately in their respective preferred states.} & 

\\ \hline
\textbf{Expansion 2: aggregate risk} \;\;($\omega_h \ne \omega_l$) & 
{{img:2|w=400}}

\emph{Setup:} $\sum_i \omega_s^i$ varies across states. Box becomes \textbf{rectangular} $\omega_l \times \omega_h$.

\emph{Result:} contract curve = \textbf{diagonal of the rectangle} (slope $\omega_h/\omega_l \ne 1$). Both agents consume in proportion to aggregate; both have $x_h^i > x_l^i$ (everyone exposed to aggregate risk).

\emph{Proof.}

\textbf{Claim:} $x_h^i > x_l^i$ for each agent $i$.

\emph{(per contra)} Suppose $x_h^1 < x_l^1$. By aggregate constraint, $x_h^2 = \omega_h - x_h^1$ and $x_l^2 = \omega_l - x_l^1$:
$$ x_h^2 - x_l^2 \;=\; (\omega_h - \omega_l) - (x_h^1 - x_l^1) \;>\; 0 $$
(both summands non-negative under our assumption $\omega_h > \omega_l$ and $x_h^1 < x_l^1$). So $x_h^2 > x_l^2$.

Hence by concavity:
$$ A = \dfrac{u'(x_l^1)}{u'(x_h^1)} \;<\; 1 \;<\; \dfrac{u'(x_l^2)}{u'(x_h^2)} = B \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; A < B, $$
contradicting PO (with same beliefs requires $A = B$). $\square$

\emph{Conclusion:} $x_h^i > x_l^i$ for BOTH agents. This is a silly proof by contraddiction but Note this is necessary due to a way deeper understanding: if they have the same prefernces, and the same beliefs (pi) then the condition MRS1 = MRS2 = p1/p2 means that the MRS will pin down the sme quantities. so the onlly price that works (recall we already made this discussionis a price such that the aggregate edowments and the individual quantities are in the same ratio. 
and note that the price of the scarce good has to be higher to ensure feasibilty, otherwise both agents demand more of the scarce good and the aggregate quantity is higher of the feasible one. 


\emph{\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Price intuition.}}} Both agents consume more of the more abundant good ($x_h^i > x_l^i$ when $\omega_h > \omega_l$). At CE, the agent's FOC gives the state-price ratio:
$$ \dfrac{\hat p_l}{\hat p_h} \;=\; \dfrac{\pi_l}{\pi_h} \cdot \dfrac{u'(x_l)}{u'(x_h)}. $$
With $x_l < x_h$ (less consumed in $l$), concavity gives $u'(x_l) > u'(x_h)$, so the second factor $> 1$. Hence
$$ \boxed{\;\;\dfrac{\hat p_l}{\hat p_h} \;>\; \dfrac{\pi_l}{\pi_h} \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\; \dfrac{\hat p_l}{\pi_l} \;>\; \dfrac{\hat p_h}{\pi_h}\;\;} $$

\textcolor{purple}{\emph{Reading: in the less abundant state, the price per unit of probability is higher --- there is less of the good around, so each unit is worth more. The scarce state earns a premium beyond what raw probability would suggest.}} & 

\\ \hline
\textbf{Expansion 3: $+$ $t_0$ consumption + silly excursus} & 
\emph{Setup:} now add $t_0$ consumption $x_0^i$. Choice variables: $x_0^i, x_1^i, x_2^i, \dots, x_S^i$ --- one consumption number per (date, state).
$$ \max_{\underbrace{\,x_0^i,\, x_1^i,\, x_2^i,\, \dots,\, x_S^i\,}_{\substack{\text{state-contingent contracts:} \\ \text{how much to consume in each state}}}}\;\; u^i(x_0^i) + \beta^i \sum_{s = 1}^{S} \pi_s^i\, u^i(x_s^i) $$
$$ \text{sub.}\;\; p_0(\omega_0^i - x_0^i) + \sum_{s = 1}^{S} p_s(\omega_s^i - x_s^i) \;\ge\; 0. $$
\emph{Market clearing:} $\sum_i x_s^i = \sum_i \omega_s^i$ for each $s \ge 0$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Silly excursus} ($S = 1$, no future uncertainty).}
$$ \max_{\;x_0^i,\; x_1^i\;}\;\; u(x_0^i) + \beta^i\, u(x_1^i)\;\;\text{sub.}\;\; p_0(\omega_0^i - x_0^i) + p_1(\omega_1^i - x_1^i) \ge 0. $$
FOC: $\boxed{\;p_1/p_0 = \beta^i\, u'(x_1^i)/u'(x_0^i)\;}$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Q.STN 1.}} \emph{$\beta^A = \beta^B = \beta$ and no aggregate risk ($\omega_0^{\text{agg}} = \omega_1^{\text{agg}}$). Show $x_0^i = x_1^i$ (constant cons.) and $p_1/p_0 = \beta$.}

\emph{At PO:} $MRS^1 = MRS^2$, i.e.\ $\beta\, A = \beta\, B \Rightarrow A = B$. With same utility, if quantities are not equal across dates then $A \ne B$ --- contradiction. The only allocation that satisfies PO \emph{and} feasibility (no agg.\ risk) is $\boxed{x_0^i = x_1^i}$ for each agent.

\emph{At CE:} the agent's FOC gives
$$ \dfrac{\hat p_1}{\hat p_0} \;=\; MRS \;=\; \beta\, \dfrac{u'(\hat x_1)}{u'(\hat x_0)} \;=\; \beta \cdot 1 \;=\; \boxed{\beta}. $$

\textcolor{purple}{\emph{Interpretation: with $\beta \le 1$, future consumption is priced lower than present (pure impatience).}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Q.STN 2.}} \emph{$\beta^A > \beta^B$ (agent $A$ more patient).}

PO with same beliefs: $\beta^A A = \beta^B B$. Since $\beta^A > \beta^B$,
$$ A < B \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \dfrac{u'(x_1^A)}{u'(x_0^A)} < \dfrac{u'(x_1^B)}{u'(x_0^B)}. $$
By concavity, this is restored only with $\boxed{x_0^A < x_1^A}$ \textbf{and} $\boxed{x_0^B > x_1^B}$.

\textcolor{purple}{\emph{Interpretation: agent $A$ (more patient) consumes less today, more tomorrow $\Rightarrow$ he \textbf{saves}. Agent $B$ (less patient) consumes more today, less tomorrow $\Rightarrow$ he \textbf{borrows}.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Q.STN 3.}} \emph{$\omega_0^1 + \omega_0^2 > \omega_1^1 + \omega_1^2$ (aggregate scarce in future).}

By the same per-contra logic as Expansion 2 (just one period later instead of one state), $x_0^i > x_1^i$ for both agents.

\emph{At CE:}
$$ \dfrac{\hat p_1}{\hat p_0} \;=\; \beta\, \dfrac{u'(x_1)}{u'(x_0)}. $$
With $x_1 < x_0$, concavity gives $u'(x_1) > u'(x_0) > 0 \Rightarrow$ the ratio $> 1$. Hence
$$ \boxed{\;\;\dfrac{\hat p_1}{\hat p_0} \;>\; \beta\;\;} $$

\textcolor{purple}{\emph{Interpretation: future is scarce, so future consumption commands a price ABOVE the pure discount factor $\beta$.}}
&

\\
\end{tabular}


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Footnote: how Arrow securities collapse the two Radner BCs into the single AD BC.}}

Recall: an Arrow security for state $s$ pays $r_{s'}^{A^s} = 1$ if $s' = s$, $0$ otherwise. Take $K = S$ Arrow securities, one per state, and call the agent's holding of Arrow $s$ simply $\theta^s$.

\emph{Step 1 --- simplify the state-$s$ BC.} The asset payoff sum collapses: $\sum_k r_s^k \theta_k^i = \theta^s$. So
$$ \underbrace{p_s\, x_s^i \;\le\; p_s\, \omega_s^i + \theta^s}_{\text{Radner BC}_s\;\text{with Arrows}} \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \theta^s = p_s\,(x_s^i - \omega_s^i). $$
\emph{Holding $\theta^s$ Arrow units in state $s$ funds exactly the state-$s$ net spending $p_s(x_s^i - \omega_s^i)$.}

\emph{Step 2 --- substitute into the $t_0$ BC.} The portfolio cost simplifies because each Arrow $s$ has its own price $q_s$:
$$ \underbrace{p_0\, x_0^i + \sum_s q_s\, \theta^s \le p_0\, \omega_0^i}_{\text{Radner BC}_0\;\text{with Arrows}} $$
Plug in $\theta^s = p_s(x_s^i - \omega_s^i)$ from Step 1:
$$ p_0\, x_0^i + \sum_s q_s\, p_s\,(x_s^i - \omega_s^i) \;\le\; p_0\, \omega_0^i. $$

\emph{Step 3 --- rearrange to the AD intertemporal form.} Bring $\omega$ terms to the right:
$$ \boxed{\;\; p_0\, x_0^i + \sum_s \underbrace{q_s\, p_s}_{\tilde p_s} \, x_s^i \;\le\; p_0\, \omega_0^i + \sum_s \underbrace{q_s\, p_s}_{\tilde p_s}\, \omega_s^i \;\;} $$
\textbf{This is exactly the AD intertemporal BC} with AD state-prices $\tilde p_s = q_s\, p_s$ (price today of one unit of state-$s$ consumption $=$ Arrow price $\times$ state-$s$ spot price).

\textcolor{purple}{\emph{Conclusion: Arrow securities (1 per state, $K = S$) span $\mathbb{R}^S$ and let the agent pre-fund each state's spot consumption at $t_0$. The two-stage Radner BC collapses into the single AD intertemporal BC --- this is the spanning/equivalence result, made constructive.}}

nodes.title: Asset pricing --- worked example (2 states, 3 assets): normalised vs $p_h = 100$
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Worked example: 2 states, 3 assets (2 Arrow + 1 risk-free bond) --- normalised vs $p_h = 100$.}}

\emph{$I = 2$ agents, $S = 2$ states $(h, l)$, single physical good per (date, state), assets $A^h, A^l, B$ with payoffs $r^{A^h} = (1, 0), r^{A^l} = (0, 1), r^B = (1, 1)$ in dollars. Prices $q^h, q^l, q^B$; quantities $\theta^h, \theta^l, \theta^B$. Preferences $u(x) = \ln x$, $\beta = 0.9$, $\pi_h = \pi_l = 0.5$.}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why $p_0 = p_h = p_l = 1$?}} 

**Intuition:** With a single physical good per (date, state), spot prices carry \emph{no economic content} (= no valuable information): you can normalise each to $1$ without losing anything. Walras's law guarantees only \emph{relative} prices matter. 
**mathematical proof:**
\emph{Notice:} if you had used $p_h = 100$ instead, the following \textbf{compensating rescalings} would all cancel out, leaving real allocations unchanged:

$\bullet$ \textbf{Consumption FOC:} $\lambda_h = \beta\pi_h u'(x_h)/p_h \;\Rightarrow\; \lambda_h$ scales by $1/p_h$ (\textcolor{red}{$\times 1/100$}).

$\bullet$ \textbf{Asset FOC:} $q^h = \lambda_h/\lambda_0 \;\Rightarrow\; q^h$ scales by $1/p_h$ (\textcolor{red}{$\times 1/100$}). When you merge focs you do not simplfy the 1/100

$\bullet$ \textbf{State-$h$ BC:} $p_h x_h \le p_h \omega_h + \theta^h \;\Rightarrow\; \theta^h$ scales by $p_h$ (\textcolor{red}{$\times 100$}) to deliver the same real position $\theta^h/p_h$.  here when you put the focs in the 1/100 simplified. 

$\bullet$ \textbf{$t_0$ BC:} the dollar cost $q^h \theta^h$ is \emph{invariant} --- the $1/p_h$ in $q^h$ cancels the $p_h$ in $\theta^h$.

=> \textbf{Real consumption $x_h$ invariant.} The SDF $\mu_s = \beta u'(x_s)/u'(x_0)$ depends only on real consumption, so it is invariant too.

\emph{Net: nominal numbers $(\lambda_h, q^h, \theta^h)$ rescale; the real economy is unchanged. This is exactly Walras's law in action.}

\begin{tabular}{p{4cm}|p{17cm}|p{17cm}}
\textbf{Step} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{One good (Walras: spot prices = normalisation)}} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Two goods (apple + banana, apple as numeraire)}} \\
\hline
\textbf{Endowments} & 
Two agents with mirror endowments: agent 1 owns the state-$h$ tree ($\omega_h^1 = \bar\omega_h, \;\omega_l^1 = 0$); agent 2 owns the state-$l$ tree ($\omega_h^2 = 0, \;\omega_l^2 = \bar\omega_l$). Same $\omega_0^i$ at $t_0$. Aggregate $\bar\omega_s$ constant across states $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{no aggregate risk}.
&
Each agent has $(\omega_s^a, \omega_s^b)$. Aggregate apples are scarce only in state $l$ ($\bar\omega_l^a < \bar\omega_0^a = \bar\omega_h^a$); aggregate bananas constant in every state $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{no banana risk, only apple risk in $l$}.
\\
\hline
\textbf{Budget constraints} & 
\emph{$t_0$:} $x_0^i + q^h \theta^h + q^l \theta^l + q^B \theta^B \le \omega_0^i$. \newline
\emph{State $h$:} $x_h^i \le \omega_h^i + \theta^h + \theta^B$. \newline
\emph{State $l$:} $x_l^i \le \omega_l^i + \theta^l + \theta^B$.
&
\emph{$t_0$:} $x_0^a + \textcolor{blue}{p_0^b} x_0^b + q^h \theta^h + q^l \theta^l \le \omega_0^a + \textcolor{blue}{p_0^b} \omega_0^b$. \newline
\emph{State $s$:} $x_s^a + \textcolor{blue}{p_s^b} x_s^b \le \omega_s^a + \textcolor{blue}{p_s^b} \omega_s^b + \theta^s$ for $s = h, l$. \newline
\emph{Asset payoff in numeraire $=$ apples.}
\\
\hline
\textbf{Max problem} & 
\[ \max\;\; u(x_0^i) + \beta\,\bigl[\pi_h u(x_h^i) + \pi_l u(x_l^i)\bigr] \;\;\text{sub.\ all 3 BCs.} \]
&
\[ \max\;\; u(x_0^a, x_0^b) + \beta \sum_s \pi_s\, u(x_s^a, x_s^b) \;\;\text{sub.\ 3 BCs.} \]
\\
\hline
\textbf{Lagrangian} & 
$\mathcal{L} \;=\; u(x_0) + \beta\bigl[\pi_h u(x_h) + \pi_l u(x_l)\bigr]$ \newline
$\;-\;\lambda_0 \bigl[\,p_0\, x_0 + q^h \theta^h + q^l \theta^l + q^B \theta^B - p_0\, \omega_0\,\bigr]$ \newline
$\;-\;\lambda_h \bigl[\,p_h\, x_h - p_h\, \omega_h - \theta^h - \theta^B\,\bigr]$ \newline
$\;-\;\lambda_l \bigl[\,p_l\, x_l - p_l\, \omega_l - \theta^l - \theta^B\,\bigr]$ \newline
\emph{We'll set $p_0 = p_h = p_l = 1$ at the end (normalisation).}
&
$\mathcal{L} \;=\; u(x_0^a, x_0^b) + \beta \sum_s \pi_s\, u(x_s^a, x_s^b)$ \newline
$\;-\;\lambda_0 \bigl[\,x_0^a + \textcolor{blue}{p_0^b}\, x_0^b + q^h \theta^h + q^l \theta^l - \omega_0^a - \textcolor{blue}{p_0^b}\, \omega_0^b\,\bigr]$ \newline
$\;-\;\sum_{s \in \{h,l\}} \lambda_s \bigl[\,x_s^a + \textcolor{blue}{p_s^b}\, x_s^b - \omega_s^a - \textcolor{blue}{p_s^b}\, \omega_s^b - \theta^s\,\bigr]$ \newline
\emph{Apple is numeraire ($p_s^a = 1$), so apple consumption enters with coefficient $1$; banana with coefficient $\textcolor{blue}{p_s^b}$.}
\\
\hline
\textbf{SDF definition} & 
\[ \boxed{\;\mu_s \;\equiv\; \beta\, \dfrac{u'(x_s)}{u'(x_0)}\;} \]
intertemporal MRS, agent's personal pricing kernel.
&
\[ \boxed{\;\mu_s^{(a)} \;\equiv\; \beta\, \dfrac{u_a(x_s)}{u_a(x_0)}\;} \;\text{(apple-numeraire).} \]
\textbf{Numeraire-dependent now:} switching to banana gives $\mu_s^{(b)} = \beta u_b(x_s)/u_b(x_0)$, generally different across states.
\\
\hline
\textbf{FOCs for consumption $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda$'s} & 
\emph{$\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial x_0$:} $\;u'(x_0) - \lambda_0\, p_0 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \lambda_0 = u'(x_0)/p_0$. \newline
\emph{$\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial x_h$:} $\;\beta\pi_h\, u'(x_h) - \lambda_h\, p_h = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \lambda_h = \beta\pi_h\, u'(x_h)/p_h$. \newline
\emph{$\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial x_l$:} $\;\beta\pi_l\, u'(x_l) - \lambda_l\, p_l = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \lambda_l = \beta\pi_l\, u'(x_l)/p_l$.

\emph{Combining the dated FOCs gives the \textbf{intertemporal MRS} (the SDF):}
\[ \dfrac{\lambda_s}{\lambda_0} \;=\; \beta\, \pi_s\, \dfrac{u'(x_s)}{u'(x_0)} \cdot \dfrac{p_0}{p_s} \;=\; \pi_s\, \mu_s \cdot \dfrac{p_0}{p_s}. \]
With $p_0 = p_s = 1$: $\;\lambda_s/\lambda_0 = \pi_s\, \mu_s$.
&
\emph{$\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial x_0^a$:} $\;u_a(x_0) - \lambda_0 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \lambda_0 = u_a(x_0)$. \newline
\emph{$\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial x_0^b$:} $\;u_b(x_0) - \lambda_0\, \textcolor{blue}{p_0^b} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \lambda_0 = u_b(x_0)/\textcolor{blue}{p_0^b}$. \newline
\emph{$\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial x_s^a$:} $\;\beta\pi_s\, u_a(x_s) - \lambda_s = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \lambda_s = \beta\pi_s\, u_a(x_s)$. \newline
\emph{$\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial x_s^b$:} $\;\beta\pi_s\, u_b(x_s) - \lambda_s\, \textcolor{blue}{p_s^b} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \lambda_s = \beta\pi_s\, u_b(x_s)/\textcolor{blue}{p_s^b}$. \newline\newline
\emph{Combining the two goods within each (date, state) gives the \textbf{intratemporal MRS}:}
\[ \textcolor{blue}{\dfrac{u_b(x_s)}{u_a(x_s)} \;=\; p_s^b} \;\;\;\text{(\textcolor{blue}{intratemporal MRS}: in every $s$ and at $t_0$).} \]
\emph{Combining apple FOCs across dates gives the \textbf{intertemporal MRS} (you can pick either apples or bananas, both work, this is intertemporal value of money):}
\[ \dfrac{\lambda_s}{\lambda_0} \;=\; \beta\, \pi_s\, \dfrac{u_a(x_s)}{u_a(x_0)} \;=\; \pi_s\, \mu_s^{(a)}. \]
\emph{At eq.\ $\lambda_l > \lambda_h$ when apples are scarce in $l$ (apple MU up).}
\\
\hline
\textbf{FOCs $\partial \mathcal{L}/\partial \theta_k = 0$ $\Rightarrow$ asset prices} 

\emph{Why $\theta$ ``disappears'':} $\theta_k$ enters $\mathcal{L}$ \emph{linearly} ($-\lambda_0 q^k \theta^k$ in $t_0$ BC, $+\lambda_s r_s^k \theta^k$ in state-$s$ BCs). Its derivative is just the coefficient --- $\theta$ vanishes; what remains pins down the PRICE.
& 
$\partial \mathcal{L}/\partial \theta^h$: $\;-\lambda_0 q^h + \lambda_h = 0$ $\Rightarrow$
\[ q^h = \dfrac{\lambda_h}{\lambda_0} = \beta\pi_h \dfrac{u'(x_h)}{u'(x_0)} = \pi_h \mu_h. \]
$\partial \mathcal{L}/\partial \theta^l$: $\;-\lambda_0 q^l + \lambda_l = 0$ $\Rightarrow$
\[ q^l = \dfrac{\lambda_l}{\lambda_0} = \pi_l \mu_l. \]
$\partial \mathcal{L}/\partial \theta^B$: $\;-\lambda_0 q^B + \lambda_h + \lambda_l = 0$ $\Rightarrow$
\[ q^B = \dfrac{\lambda_h + \lambda_l}{\lambda_0} = \pi_h \mu_h + \pi_l \mu_l = \sum_s \pi_s \mu_s = \mathbb{E}[\mu]. \]
\emph{Reading:} usually we expect FOCs to pin demand quantities --- here those quantities are inside $\mu$, but notation puts prices on the LHS. To get the actual $\theta$'s, combine with the BCs + market clearing.
& 
$\partial \mathcal{L}/\partial \theta^h$: $\;-\lambda_0 q^h + \lambda_h = 0$ $\Rightarrow$
\[ q^h = \dfrac{\lambda_h}{\lambda_0} = \beta\pi_h \dfrac{u_a(x_h)}{u_a(x_0)} = \pi_h \mu_h^{(a)}. \]
$\partial \mathcal{L}/\partial \theta^l$: $\;-\lambda_0 q^l + \lambda_l = 0$ $\Rightarrow$
\[ q^l = \dfrac{\lambda_l}{\lambda_0} = \beta\pi_l \dfrac{u_a(x_l)}{u_a(x_0)} = \pi_l \mu_l^{(a)}. \]
\emph{Implied bond:} $\;-\lambda_0 q^B + \lambda_h + \lambda_l = 0 \Rightarrow$
\[ q^B = \dfrac{\lambda_h + \lambda_l}{\lambda_0} = \pi_h \mu_h^{(a)} + \pi_l \mu_l^{(a)} = \sum_s \pi_s \mu_s^{(a)} = \mathbb{E}[\mu^{(a)}]. \]
\emph{Reading:} when apples scarce in $l$, $\mu_l^{(a)} > \mu_h^{(a)} \Rightarrow q^l > q^h$ (\textbf{state-$l$ Arrow expensive: insurance against apple scarcity}).
\\
\hline
\textbf{Sub FOCs into BCs $\to$ unique AD budget (complete markets)} & 
\emph{AD budget (under complete markets, with $p_s = 1$):}
\[ \boxed{\;x_0 + \sum_s q^s\, x_s \;=\; \omega_0 + \sum_s q^s\, \omega_s\;} \]
\emph{Now substitute the asset-FOC ratio $q^s = \pi_s\, \mu_s = \pi_s\, \beta\, u'(x_s)/u'(x_0)$:}
\[ x_0 + \sum_s \pi_s\, \beta\, \dfrac{u'(x_s)}{u'(x_0)}\, x_s \;=\; \omega_0 + \sum_s \pi_s\, \beta\, \dfrac{u'(x_s)}{u'(x_0)}\, \omega_s. \]
\emph{Multiply by $u'(x_0) = \lambda_0$ to land on the $\lambda$-weighted form:}
\[ \boxed{\;\lambda_0\, x_0 + \sum_s \lambda_s\, x_s \;=\; \lambda_0\, \omega_0 + \sum_s \lambda_s\, \omega_s\;} \]
\emph{i.e.\ marginal-utility-weighted consumption $=$ marginal-utility-weighted endowment.}
& 
\emph{AD budget (apple numeraire, complete markets):}
\[ \boxed{\;x_0^a + \textcolor{blue}{p_0^b}\, x_0^b + \sum_s q^s\, x_s^a + \sum_s q^s\, \textcolor{blue}{p_s^b}\, x_s^b \;=\; \text{(endowment side)}\;} \]
\emph{Substitute the FOC ratios:}
\emph{$\bullet$ asset FOC:} $q^s = \pi_s\, \mu_s^{(a)} = \pi_s\, \beta\, u_a(x_s)/u_a(x_0)$.
\emph{$\bullet$ \textcolor{blue}{intratemporal MRS}:} $\textcolor{blue}{p_s^b} = u_b(x_s)/u_a(x_s)$ (and $\textcolor{blue}{p_0^b} = u_b(x_0)/u_a(x_0)$).
\emph{Plug in. The mixed term $q^s\, \textcolor{blue}{p_s^b}$ collapses:}
\[ q^s\, \textcolor{blue}{p_s^b} \;=\; \pi_s\, \beta\, \dfrac{u_a(x_s)}{u_a(x_0)} \cdot \dfrac{u_b(x_s)}{u_a(x_s)} \;=\; \pi_s\, \beta\, \dfrac{u_b(x_s)}{u_a(x_0)}. \]
\emph{Multiply through by $u_a(x_0) = \lambda_0$:}
\[ \boxed{\;\lambda_0\, x_0^a + \underbrace{\lambda_0\, \textcolor{blue}{p_0^b}}_{u_b(x_0)}\, x_0^b + \sum_s \lambda_s\, x_s^a + \sum_s \underbrace{\lambda_s\, \textcolor{blue}{p_s^b}}_{\beta\pi_s\, u_b(x_s)}\, x_s^b \;=\; \text{(endowment side)}\;} \]
\emph{i.e.\ MU-weighted consumption (with apple-MU for apples, banana-MU for bananas) $=$ MU-weighted endowment.}
\\
\hline
\textbf{Equilibrium consumption (CE allocation)} & 
By symmetry + no agg.\ risk + identical $u$: $\boxed{x_0^i = x_h^i = x_l^i\;\;\forall i}$ (constant across states). $\Rightarrow \mu_h = \mu_l = \beta$.
&
\textbf{Eq. relative price (NEW):} from MRS + market clearing,
\[ \textcolor{blue}{p_s^b}/p_s^a \;=\; \bar\omega_s^a/\bar\omega_s^b \;\;\;(< 1 \text{ in state } l \text{ since apples scarce}). \]
\textbf{Allocation:} half-aggregate by symmetry, $x_s^g = \bar\omega_s^g/2$. $\Rightarrow$ $\mu_l^{(a)} > \mu_h^{(a)}$.
\\
\hline
\textbf{General pricing formula} \;\;(any asset $k$ with payoffs $r^k$) & 
Any asset is a basket of Arrow claims with payoff weights $r_s^k$:
\[ q_k \;=\; \sum_s q_s\, r_s^k \;=\; \sum_s \pi_s\, \mu_s\, r_s^k \;=\; \mathbb{E}[\mu\, r^k]. \]
\emph{Linear combination of Arrow prices weighted by state payoffs.} Checks: $q^h = \mathbb{E}[\mu \cdot (1,0)] = \pi_h \mu_h$; $q^B = \mathbb{E}[\mu \cdot (1,1)] = \pi_h \mu_h + \pi_l \mu_l$. \checkmark
&
\[ q_k \;=\; \sum_s \pi_s\, \mu_s^{(a)}\, r_s^k \;=\; \mathbb{E}[\mu^{(a)} r^k] \]
\emph{Same form, but $\mu$ now depends on numeraire choice.} Banana-numeraire: $\mu_s^{(b)} = \beta u_b(x_s)/u_b(x_0)$; if banana consumption is constant across $s$, this collapses to $\beta$. Different numerical SDFs price the same real claims consistently.
\\
\hline
\textbf{No-arbitrage check} \;\;($r^B = r^{A^h} + r^{A^l}$) & 
$q^h + q^l = q^B$. \checkmark
&
$q^h + q^l = q^B$ \checkmark\;(if bond traded). Holds in \emph{any} numeraire --- both sides rescale identically with the chosen $p^g$.
\\
\hline
\textbf{Agent 1's portfolio} \;(set $\theta^B = 0$) & 
$\theta^h < 0$ (shorts $A^h$: he already holds the state-$h$ endowment), $\theta^l > 0$ (longs $A^l$: transfers wealth to state $l$), $\theta^B = 0$. Verifications via the 3 BCs hold by construction.
&
$\theta^h = 0, \;\theta^l = 0$ \textbf{(autarky)}. By symmetric endowments, each agent's endowment value at eq prices = half-aggregate $\Rightarrow$ no Arrow trade. Agents trade \emph{goods} on spot markets within each state (here, none, since endowments per agent are already symmetric).
\\
\hline
\textbf{Real consumption and real trade} & 
$x_0^i = x_h^i = x_l^i$: equal across $(t_0, h, l)$ for each agent (no agg.\ risk + identical $u$). Agent 1 swaps her state-$h$ endowment for a state-$l$ claim via Arrow trade; agent 2 the mirror.
&
$x_s^g = \bar\omega_s^g/2$ for each agent. No Arrow trade, no spot trade in this symmetric example. The economy still has aggregate uncertainty: apple consumption drops in state $l$.
\\
\hline
\textbf{Spot-price (ir)relevance} & 
Arrow $h$ pays \$$1$ which equals $1/p_h$ units of consumption. With $p_h$ normalised to $1$, the dollar payoff equals the real payoff. Spot prices only rescale nominal numbers ($\lambda_h, q^h, \theta^h$).
&
\textbf{Why relative prices matter here:} $\textcolor{blue}{p_s^b}/p_s^a$ is \emph{endogenous} --- pinned by MRS at the eq.\ allocation, reflecting \emph{real} scarcity within each state. \textbf{Cannot be normalised away.} Walras only kills the \emph{level}, not the \emph{ratio}, of spot prices when there are $\ge 2$ goods.
\\
\hline
\textbf{Real risk-free rate} & 
$1/(1 + r_f) = q^B = \mathbb{E}[\mu]$. With no agg.\ risk + log utility, $\mathbb{E}[\mu] = \beta$ $\Rightarrow$ $r_f = (1 - \beta)/\beta$.
&
$1/(1 + r_f) = q^B = \mathbb{E}[\mu^{(a)}]$. With $\mathbb{E}[\mu^{(a)}] > 1$ (strong insurance demand against state-$l$ apple scarcity), $r_f$ can be \textbf{negative}.
\\
\hline
\textbf{Completeness} & 
Rank $R = S \Rightarrow$ complete; bond redundant.
&
Rank $R = S \Rightarrow$ complete in numeraire (apple) payoffs. To span a banana claim: $1$ banana in state $s$ = $\textcolor{blue}{p_s^b}$ apples; convert via spot price. With $\ge 2$ goods and only $S$ Arrow assets, all real claims are spanned via the spot markets.
\\
\hline
\textbf{Bottom line} & 
SDF $\mu$, real consumption, real trades, NA law, $r_f$, completeness --- all are properties of \emph{primitives}.
&
\textbf{Relative spot prices BITE.} They are endogenous (= eq.\ MRS), reflect state-contingent scarcity, and \emph{cannot} be normalised away. The SDF is \textbf{numeraire-dependent}: $\mu^{(a)}$ varies with apple scarcity; $\mu^{(b)} = \beta$ flat if banana abundance constant. The \emph{same real claim} priced via different numeraire SDFs gives consistent answers --- only the nominal numbers differ.
\\
\end{tabular}

nodes.title: Lucas Tree Model (book, ch.\ 5)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The Lucas Tree Model.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why we need it: the circularity / fixed-point problem in the general AD/Radner setup.}} In the general setup, both $x_s$ and $q_s$ are \emph{jointly determined} in equilibrium:

$\bullet$ Asset prices: $q_s = \pi_s\, \mu_s$, with the SDF $\mu_s = \beta\, u'(x_s)/u'(x_0)$.

$\bullet$ But $x_s$ itself is determined by prices, via BCs and market clearing.

$\bullet$ So $q_s$ is a function of $x_s$, which is a function of $q_s$: a \textbf{fixed-point problem}.

\emph{This is \textbf{not a logical defect}} --- equilibrium exists and is well-defined. The issue is purely \textbf{computational}: there is \textbf{no closed-form} $q_s = f(\text{primitives})$. To get numerical asset prices you must (i) guess prices, (ii) compute demand, (iii) check market clearing, (iv) iterate until convergence.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Setup.}} Two consumers, two states, \textbf{one single physical good}. The agents are \emph{identical} in every dimension:

$\bullet$ Same period-zero endowment: $\omega_0^1 = \omega_0^2$.

$\bullet$ Same period-1 endowment in each state: $\omega_s^1 = \omega_s^2 = \omega_s$ for all $s > 0$.

$\bullet$ Same vN-M utility: $u^A = u^B = u$.

$\bullet$ Same beliefs: $\pi_s^A = \pi_s^B = \pi_s$.

\emph{Variation of $\omega_s$ across $s$ constitutes \textbf{aggregate uncertainty}.}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Equilibrium = autarky.}} Since preferences and endowments are identical, there are \emph{no gains from trade} --- each agent consumes their own endowment.
\[ \boxed{\;\hat x_s^i \;=\; \omega_s^i \;\;\;\forall\, i,\, s.\;} \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Edgeworth-box intuition.}} In the (3-dimensional) Edgeworth box the endowment sits exactly at the \emph{centre} (along the symmetry diagonal). Indifference curves are identical and tangent at the endowment point: budget line passes through $\omega$, and the autarky allocation IS the CE. Prices are the \emph{endogenous} objects that support $\omega$ as equilibrium, while $\hat x_s^i = \omega_s^i$ is \emph{exogenous}.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{SDF (collapses to primitives).}} Substituting $x_s = \omega_s$ into the agent's intertemporal FOC:
\[ \boxed{\;\;\mu_s \;=\; \dfrac{\beta\, u'(\omega_s)}{u'(\omega_0)}\;\;} \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Asset price.}} For asset $k$ with payoff vector $r^k = (r_1^k, \ldots, r_S^k)$:
\[ \boxed{\;\;q_k \;=\; \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} \pi_s\, \beta\, \dfrac{u'(\omega_s)}{u'(\omega_0)}\, r_s^k\;\;} \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why this is useful.}} We can now \emph{vary $\omega_s$ across states} and study how preferences (curvature of $u$) and the endowment distribution affect asset prices. So now qk depends direcly on a primitive and not on $\omega_s$

nodes.title: No-arbitrage --- definition + 3 worked examples (book, ch.\ 5)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{No-arbitrage condition (book, ch.\ 5).}}

Arbitrage = risk free return = return with full insurance tomorrow. 

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{1. Definition.}}
Take an arbitrary set of $K$ assets with return matrix $R$ and vector of prices $q = (q^1, \ldots, q^K)$. The system $(R, q)$ is \emph{arbitrage-free} if there does \textbf{not} exist any portfolio $\theta = (\theta^1, \ldots, \theta^K) \in \mathbb{R}^K$ such that:
\[ q\cdot\theta \le 0 \;\;\text{(non-positive cost today)} \]
\[ R\theta \ge 0 \;\;\text{(non-negative payoff in every state) and } R\theta \ne 0 \;\;\text{(strictly positive in at least one).} \]

\vspace{0.3em}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{2. The essence: full insurance against every future state.}}

The only condition that separates arbitrage from a ``good deal'' is $R\theta \ge 0$ \emph{in every state}. You must be \textbf{fully insured against the future}: no matter which state realises, you never owe anything.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Good deal / bet / loan:} positive expected payoff but at least one state where you owe. \emph{State risk remains.}

$\bullet$ \textbf{Arbitrage:} payoff $\ge 0$ in \textbf{every state} with one strictly positive. \emph{No state risk; pure free lunch.}

&
\textcolor{purple}{$\theta = (1, -2, 1)$ always gives $R\theta = (1, 0, 0)$ --- a synthetic Arrow-state-1 --- \emph{regardless of prices}. Whether it is arbitrage depends entirely on the cost $q\cdot\theta = q^A - 2q^B + q^C$, which equals the \emph{implied state-1 price} $\phi_1$:} \newline\newline

nodes.title: CAPM and risk-neutral probabilities (book \S 5.7.1)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{CAPM and Risk-Neutral Probabilities (book \S 5.7.1).}}

\emph{Throughout assume $\mu > 0$ (NA $+$ complete markets). Start from the SDF pricing equation $q_k = \mathbb{E}[\mu\, r^k]$.}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{1. From SDF to Risk-Return tradeoff.}}

\emph{Step 1 --- decompose via the covariance identity:}
\[ q_k \;=\; \mathbb{E}[\mu\, r^k] \;=\; \mathbb{E}[\mu]\, \mathbb{E}[r^k] \;+\; \text{cov}(\mu, r^k). \]

\emph{Step 2 --- bond.} For the risk-free bond ($r^b = (1, \ldots, 1)$): $\;q_b = \mathbb{E}[\mu]\cdot 1 = \mathbb{E}[\mu]$. Substitute:
\[ q_k \;=\; q_b\, \mathbb{E}[r^k] \;+\; \text{cov}(\mu, r^k). \]

\emph{Step 3 --- risk-free rate.} Define $R_f := 1/q_b$ (gross return on a 1-period bond). Solving for $\mathbb{E}[r^k]$:
\[ \mathbb{E}[r^k] \;=\; R_f\, q_k \;-\; R_f\, \text{cov}(\mu, r^k). \]

\emph{Step 4 --- normalise to returns.} Define the gross return $\tilde R_k := r^k / q_k$. Divide both sides by $q_k$ (uses $\text{cov}(\mu, r^k/q_k) = \text{cov}(\mu, r^k)/q_k$):
\[ \boxed{\;\;\mathbb{E}[\tilde R_k] \;=\; R_f \;-\; R_f\, \text{cov}(\mu, \tilde R_k)\;\;} \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Reading the tradeoff.}} $\mu$ is high in \textbf{bad states} (low aggregate endowment $\Rightarrow$ high marginal utility).

$\bullet$ \textbf{Insurance asset} (pays more in bad states): $\text{cov}(\mu, \tilde R_k) > 0$ $\Rightarrow$ $\mathbb{E}[\tilde R_k] < R_f$. \emph{Agents accept low expected return because the asset hedges bad states.}

$\bullet$ \textbf{Risky asset} (pays more in good states, e.g.\ stocks): $\text{cov}(\mu, \tilde R_k) < 0$ $\Rightarrow$ $\mathbb{E}[\tilde R_k] > R_f$. \emph{Risk premium required.}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{2. CAPM.}}

The tradeoff above can be re-expressed using the \textbf{market portfolio} $\tilde R_M$ as a proxy for $-\mu$ (since $\mu$ is decreasing in aggregate endowment, the market return $\tilde R_M$ is negatively correlated with $\mu$):
\[ \boxed{\;\;\mathbb{E}[\tilde R_k] \;-\; R_f \;=\; \beta_k\,\bigl(\mathbb{E}[\tilde R_M] - R_f\bigr),\;\;\;\;\;\beta_k \;=\; \dfrac{\text{cov}(\tilde R_k,\, \tilde R_M)}{\text{var}(\tilde R_M)}.\;\;} \]

\emph{Reading.} Expected excess returns are pinned by an asset's covariance with the market.

$\bullet$ \textbf{High $\beta_k$:} asset highly exposed to systematic risk $\Rightarrow$ high expected excess return.

$\bullet$ \textbf{$\beta_k = 0$:} no systematic risk $\Rightarrow$ expected return equals $R_f$.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Negative $\beta_k$:} hedges the market $\Rightarrow$ expected return below $R_f$ (negative premium).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{3. Risk-Neutral Probabilities.}}

\emph{Definition.} For each state $s$:
\[ \boxed{\;\;\hat\pi_s \;:=\; \dfrac{\pi_s\, \mu_s}{\mathbb{E}[\mu]} \;=\; \dfrac{\pi_s\, \mu_s}{q_b}\;\;} \]

\emph{Verify $\hat\pi$ is a probability measure.}

$\bullet$ \textbf{Positivity:} $\hat\pi_s > 0$ since $\pi_s > 0$ and $\mu_s > 0$.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Sums to 1:} $\sum_s \hat\pi_s = \dfrac{\sum_s \pi_s \mu_s}{\mathbb{E}[\mu]} = \dfrac{\mathbb{E}[\mu]}{\mathbb{E}[\mu]} = 1$. \checkmark

\emph{Pricing under $\hat\pi$.} Rewrite the pricing equation by pulling out $\mathbb{E}[\mu]$:
\[ q_k \;=\; \sum_s \pi_s\, \mu_s\, r_s^k \;=\; \mathbb{E}[\mu]\,\sum_s \hat\pi_s\, r_s^k \;=\; q_b\, \hat{\mathbb{E}}[r^k] \;=\; \boxed{\;\dfrac{1}{R_f}\,\hat{\mathbb{E}}[r^k]\;}. \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Reading the risk-neutral measure.}}

$\bullet$ \textbf{Discounted-expectation form:} asset price $=$ expected payoff (under $\hat\pi$) discounted at the risk-free rate. \emph{As if} agents were risk-neutral and used probabilities $\hat\pi$.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Distortion:} $\hat\pi_s > \pi_s$ in bad states (where $\mu_s/\mathbb{E}[\mu] > 1$) and $\hat\pi_s < \pi_s$ in good states. The risk-neutral measure \textbf{over-weights bad states}, baking in risk aversion through the distortion.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Usefulness:} you can price any asset without observing $\mu$ or $\pi$ separately --- just need $\hat\pi$ (recoverable from observed asset prices) and $R_f$. \textbf{Foundation of derivative pricing} (Black--Scholes etc.).

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Synthesis.}} Three equivalent representations of the pricing equation:
\[ q_k \;=\; \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\mu\, r^k]}_{\text{SDF form (real probs $\pi$)}} \;=\; \underbrace{q_b\, \mathbb{E}[\tilde R_k]\cdot\text{(risk correction)}}_{\text{CAPM form}} \;=\; \underbrace{\dfrac{1}{R_f}\,\hat{\mathbb{E}}[r^k]}_{\text{risk-neutral form ($\hat\pi$)}}. \]
\emph{All carry the same information; different forms are convenient for different applications.}

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Cross-refs:}} AD $+$ Radner framework, SDF, no-arbitrage, Lucas tree, complete markets.

nodes.title: Value of information --- setting and Bayesian updating
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Setting.}}

A decision maker (DM) --- think of a \emph{judge} --- faces uncertainty over a binary state $\omega \in \Omega = \{I, G\}$ ($I$ = innocent, $G$ = guilty). His belief is summarized by the scalar
\[
\mu \;=\; \Pr(\omega = G) \;\in\; [0,1].
\]

$\bullet$ $\mu = 1$: certain guilt. $\bullet$ $\mu = 0$: certain innocence. $\bullet$ $\mu = 1/2$: maximal uncertainty.

The judge picks an action $a \in \mathscr{A} = \{A, C\}$ (acquit or convict). Payoffs match action to state: $u = 1$ if he ``gets it right'' and $0$ otherwise.

\textbf{Payoff table $u(a,\omega)$:}

\begin{tabular}{p{2cm}|p{2cm}|p{2cm}}
$u(a,\omega)$ & $I$ & $G$ \\
\hline
$A$ & $1$ & $0$ \\
\hline
$C$ & $0$ & $1$ \\
\end{tabular}

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Expected utility of each action (as a function of belief).}}

\emph{Convict:} \;$U(C,\mu) \;=\; (1-\mu)\,\underbrace{u(C,I)}_{=\,0} \;+\; \mu\,\underbrace{u(C,G)}_{=\,1} \;=\; \mu.$

\emph{Acquit:} \;$U(A,\mu) \;=\; (1-\mu)\,\underbrace{u(A,I)}_{=\,1} \;+\; \mu\,\underbrace{u(A,G)}_{=\,0} \;=\; 1-\mu.$

So $U(C,\cdot)$ is linear with slope $+1$ (rewards belief in guilt), and $U(A,\cdot)$ is linear with slope $-1$ (rewards belief in innocence). Plotted together, they form an \textbf{X-shape} crossing at $\mu = 1/2$.

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Optimal action and value function.}}

The judge picks whichever action has higher expected payoff:
\[
a^*(\mu) \;=\; \begin{cases} A & \text{if } \mu \le \hat\mu = \tfrac{1}{2}, \\ C & \text{if } \mu \ge \hat\mu = \tfrac{1}{2}, \end{cases}
\qquad\text{with cutoff } \hat\mu = \tfrac{1}{2}.
\]

The associated maximised expected payoff --- the \textbf{value function} --- is
\[
\boxed{\;U(\mu) \;=\; \max\bigl\{\,U(C,\mu),\; U(A,\mu)\,\bigr\} \;=\; \max\{\mu,\; 1-\mu\}\;}
\]

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Plot: X-shape with convex upper envelope.}}

{{img:0|w=720}}

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Reading: why is $U(\mu)$ convex (and what does it mean)?}}

$U(\mu)$ is the \emph{upper envelope of two linear functions} of $\mu$ $\Rightarrow$ automatically \textbf{convex}. Graphically: V-shape, minimum at the cutoff $\hat\mu = 1/2$, maxima at the corners $\mu = 0$ and $\mu = 1$.

\textcolor{purple}{\emph{Important contrast with vNM utility.}} In standard vNM expected utility, $u$ is concave \emph{in wealth} (risk aversion). Here the value function $U$ is convex \emph{in belief}. Different objects, different reasons:

$\bullet$ \emph{vNM concavity in wealth}: averaging is bad --- a sure middle wealth beats a fair gamble between extremes (risk aversion).

$\bullet$ \emph{Bayesian convexity in belief}: averaging is good --- certainty at the corners ($\mu = 0$ or $\mu = 1$) means the DM \emph{knows the state} and picks the right action with payoff $1$. At $\mu = 1/2$ he is maximally confused and gets only $1/2$. \textbf{More information $\Rightarrow$ beliefs closer to corners $\Rightarrow$ better decisions $\Rightarrow$ higher expected payoff.} This convexity is exactly what will make the value of information non-negative in the next snippet.

\bigskip\bigskip
\hrule
\bigskip

nodes.title: Reading the prior vs posterior plot
nodes.content:
PLOT MISSING
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Reading the plot.}}

$\bullet$ The black $45^\circ$ line is the \emph{no-information benchmark}: posterior $=$ prior.

$\bullet$ The \textcolor{red}{red curve} $\mu_g(\mu_0)$ lies entirely \emph{above} the diagonal: every $g$-signal raises belief in guilt.

$\bullet$ The \textcolor{green!50!black}{green curve} $\mu_i(\mu_0)$ lies entirely \emph{below} the diagonal: every $i$-signal lowers it.

$\bullet$ The \textbf{spread $\mu_g - \mu_i$ is widest at $\mu_0 = 1/2$} (most to learn when most uncertain) and \textbf{narrowest near $\mu_0 = 0$ or $\mu_0 = 1$} (little to learn when already nearly certain).

$\bullet$ \emph{Dashed extreme:} $\alpha = 1$ collapses the curves to the flat lines $\mu_g \equiv 1$ and $\mu_i \equiv 0$ --- after a perfectly informative signal the posterior is at a corner, regardless of where the prior started.

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Anatomy of the information treatment.}}

Two random variables in play:

$\bullet$ \textbf{(1) The signal.} $s \in \{i, g\}$ is Bernoulli with $\Pr(g) = \alpha\mu_0 + (1-\alpha)(1-\mu_0)$ and $\Pr(i) = 1 - \Pr(g)$. So $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}\{s=g\}] = \Pr(g)$.

$\bullet$ \textbf{(2) The state.} $\omega$ is Bernoulli with mean $\mu_0$ and \emph{prior uncertainty} (= variance) $\mu_0(1-\mu_0)$, maxed at $\mu_0 = 1/2$.

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{(3) Decomposing the upward jump $\mu_g - \mu_0$ --- the \emph{treatment effect of information}, read directly off the plot.}}

Algebra (sub $\mu_g = \alpha\mu_0/\Pr(g)$ and simplify):
\[
\boxed{\;\mu_g - \mu_0 \;=\; \underbrace{(2\alpha-1)}_{\substack{\text{signal} \\ \text{strength}}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{\mu_0(1-\mu_0)}_{\substack{\text{prior} \\ \text{uncertainty}}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{\frac{1}{\Pr(g)}}_{\substack{\text{surprise} \\ \text{(rarity of }g\text{)}}}\;}
\]

The three factors pull on $\mu_0$ \emph{in different directions}:

$\bullet$ \emph{Prior uncertainty} $\mu_0(1-\mu_0)$ wants $\mu_0 = 1/2$.

$\bullet$ \emph{Surprise} $1/\Pr(g)$ wants $\mu_0$ small: for $\alpha > 1/2$, $\Pr(g)$ is increasing in $\mu_0$, so $g$ is most surprising when $\mu_0 \to 0$ (the prior says ``unlikely to be guilty,'' so a $g$-signal is shocking $\Rightarrow$ huge belief jump).

\textbf{The compromise.} For $\alpha = 0.7$ the maximum of $\mu_g - \mu_0$ sits at $\mu_0 \approx 0.4$ --- you can read it off the plot as the widest vertical gap between the red curve and the diagonal, biased \emph{left of $1/2$} by the surprise term.

By exact symmetry, the downward gap satisfies
\[
\mu_0 - \mu_i \;=\; (2\alpha-1)\,\mu_0(1-\mu_0)\,\frac{1}{\Pr(i)},
\]
and is maxed at $\mu_0 \approx 0.6$ --- the mirror image, biased \emph{right of $1/2$} since $i$ is most surprising when $\mu_0$ is large.

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Connection to standard Bayes.}} In general $P(A\mid B)$ notation, Bayes' rule reads
\[
P(A \mid B) \;=\; P(A) \cdot \frac{\overbrace{P(B \mid A)}^{\text{signal strength (likelihood)}}}{\underbrace{P(B)}_{\substack{\text{marginal} \\ =\,\text{surprise (rarity of }B\text{)}}}}.
\]
The numerator $P(B\mid A)$ is the \emph{likelihood} of the evidence under hypothesis $A$ $\Rightarrow$ \emph{signal strength} (how diagnostic $B$ is for $A$). The denominator $P(B)$ is the \emph{marginal probability of the evidence} $\Rightarrow$ \emph{surprise} (rare evidence updates more).

In our judge example: $A = G$, $B = g$, $P(A) = \mu_0$, $P(B\mid A) = \alpha$, $P(B) = \Pr(g)$ $\Rightarrow$ recovers $\mu_g = \mu_0 \cdot \alpha/\Pr(g)$.

\textbf{Now subtract the prior to get the update (= treatment effect).} Using $P(B) = P(B\mid A)P(A) + P(B\mid A^c)P(A^c)$ to simplify $P(B\mid A) - P(B)$:
\[
\boxed{\;P(A \mid B) - P(A) \;=\; \underbrace{\bigl[\,P(B\mid A) - P(B \mid A^c)\bigr]}_{\text{signal strength}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{P(A)\,P(A^c)}_{\substack{\text{prior} \\ \text{uncertainty}}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{\frac{1}{P(B)}}_{\text{surprise}}\;}
\]
This is the \emph{general} three-factor decomposition: signal strength $\times$ prior uncertainty $\times$ surprise. Plug back $P(B\mid A) - P(B\mid A^c) = \alpha - (1-\alpha) = 2\alpha-1$ and $P(A)P(A^c) = \mu_0(1-\mu_0)$ and you recover $\mu_g - \mu_0 = (2\alpha-1)\mu_0(1-\mu_0)/\Pr(g)$ exactly.

\textbf{Reading.} Prior uncertainty $P(A)P(A^c)$ now appears \emph{explicitly} --- it was hidden inside $\mu_0$ on the right-hand side of Bayes' rule, and only surfaces once we look at the \emph{change} $P(A\mid B) - P(A)$. And the two arg-maxes of the $\mu_0$-dependent factors disagree (surprise wants $\mu_0 \to 0$, prior uncertainty wants $\mu_0 = 1/2$), so the optimal update sits \textbf{strictly between} them.

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{(4) Maximum spread $\mu_g - \mu_i$.}}

Adding the two updates:
\[
\boxed{\;\mu_g - \mu_i \;=\; (2\alpha-1)\,\mu_0(1-\mu_0)\,\Bigl(\tfrac{1}{\Pr(g)} + \tfrac{1}{\Pr(i)}\Bigr) \;=\; (2\alpha-1)\,\mu_0(1-\mu_0)\frac{1}{\Pr(g)\,\Pr(i)}\;}
\]
The gap is max at 0.5 bacause the product is max

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{(5) Why the slope of $\mu_g$ is steepest at $\mu_0 = 0$ --- but the treatment effect of information is not.}}

Differentiate $\mu_g(\mu_0) = \alpha\mu_0/\Pr(g)$:
\[
\frac{d\mu_g}{d\mu_0} \;=\; \frac{\alpha(1-\alpha)}{\Pr(g)^2}.
\]
At $\mu_0 = 0$: $\Pr(g) = 1-\alpha \Rightarrow d\mu_g/d\mu_0 = \alpha/(1-\alpha)$. For $\alpha = 0.7$ that's $\approx 2.33$ --- the red curve is steepest at the left edge.

\emph{But the treatment effect of information $\mu_g - \mu_0$ is still zero at $\mu_0 = 0$}, because the prior uncertainty $\mu_0(1-\mu_0)$ collapses. The steep slope at the origin is driven \textbf{entirely by the surprise term} $1/\Pr(g)$, with no prior uncertainty to amplify --- nothing yet to transfer.

\textbf{Reading the slope vs the 45-line.} Marginally, $d(\mu_g - \mu_0)/d\mu_0 = d\mu_g/d\mu_0 - 1$. So the treatment effect of information is:

$\bullet$ \emph{Increasing} while $d\mu_g/d\mu_0 > 1$ (red curve climbs faster than the diagonal).

$\bullet$ \emph{Maxed} at the unique $\mu_0^*$ where $d\mu_g/d\mu_0 = 1$ (red curve tangent to the diagonal in slope).

$\bullet$ \emph{Decreasing} thereafter, because the curve concaves below the $45^\circ$ line.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{(6) About rarity: a rare event is more iformative}}
