nodes.title: Bayesian Updating
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Bayesian updating.}}

\emph{Idea.} We now enrich the setting with an \textbf{information structure}: a description of how new data shifts the judge's belief, and hence his decision. Concretely, some new evidence arrives (an \emph{experiment}: a forensic test, a witness, a database query) producing for each suspect a \textbf{signal} $s \in \{i, g\}$ ($i$ = evidence pointing to innocence, $g$ = evidence pointing to guilt).

\textbf{\textcolor{purple}{Sand-grain intuition.}} Picture $100$ suspects, prior $\mu_0 = 0.3$. Without information the judge acquits \emph{all of them} ($\mu_0 < 1/2$, all $100$ grains sit in the acquit bin). The experiment shakes the pile: each grain receives either signal $i$ or signal $g$. Grains receiving $i$ get an even \emph{lower} posterior $\mu_i$ and stay firmly in the acquit bin. Grains receiving $g$ get a \emph{higher} posterior $\mu_g$ --- and if the signal is strong enough to push $\mu_g \ge 1/2$, they jump into the convict bin. \emph{Information sorts the pile.}

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The information structure $\pi(s\mid\omega)$.}}

The experiment is parameterised by a single number $\alpha \in [1/2,\, 1]$ (the \emph{informativeness}):

\begin{tabular}{p{3cm}|p{3cm}|p{3cm}}
$\Pr(s\mid\omega)$ & $\omega = I$ & $\omega = G$ \\
\hline
$s = i$ & $\alpha$ & $1-\alpha$ \\
\hline
$s = g$ & $1-\alpha$ & $\alpha$ \\
\end{tabular}

\emph{Each column sums to $1$: $\pi(\cdot\mid\omega)$ is a probability distribution over signals given the state.} The diagonal entries are the correct calls (innocent $\to$ $i$, guilty $\to$ $g$); the off-diagonals are the ``mistakes''.

$\bullet$ $\alpha = 1/2$: $\pi(s\mid I) = \pi(s\mid G)$ in both rows. The signal is independent of the state $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{no information}.

$\bullet$ $\alpha = 1$: $\pi(i\mid I) = \pi(g\mid G) = 1$. The signal reveals the state $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{perfect information}.

$\bullet$ $\alpha < 1/2$: the signal labels are \emph{flipped} --- $i$ is now correlated with $G$ and $g$ with $I$. WLOG we restrict to $\alpha \ge 1/2$ (otherwise just relabel $i \leftrightarrow g$).

\bigskip

1. FIND POSTERIOR PROBABIOITY
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Bayes' rule: from prior $\mu_0$ to posteriors $\mu_g, \mu_i$.}}

After observing $s = g$, the judge's posterior is
\[
\mu_g \;:=\; \Pr(G \mid g) \;=\; \frac{\Pr(g \mid G)\,\Pr(G)}{\Pr(g \mid G)\,\Pr(G) \;+\; \Pr(g \mid I)\,\Pr(I)} \;=\; \frac{\alpha\,\mu_0}{\alpha\,\mu_0 \;+\; (1-\alpha)(1-\mu_0)}.
\]

Symmetrically, after observing $s = i$,
\[
\mu_i \;:=\; \Pr(G \mid i) \;=\; \frac{\Pr(i \mid G)\,\Pr(G)}{\Pr(i \mid G)\,\Pr(G) \;+\; \Pr(i \mid I)\,\Pr(I)} \;=\; \frac{(1-\alpha)\,\mu_0}{(1-\alpha)\,\mu_0 \;+\; \alpha\,(1-\mu_0)}.
\]

Since $\alpha \ge 1/2$ we always have $\mu_g \ge \mu_0 \ge \mu_i$: signal $g$ \emph{pushes belief up} (toward guilt), signal $i$ \emph{pushes belief down} (toward innocence).

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Special case --- maximally uncertain prior $\mu_0 = 1/2$:}}
\[
\mu_g \;=\; \frac{\alpha \cdot \tfrac{1}{2}}{\alpha \cdot \tfrac{1}{2} + (1-\alpha) \cdot \tfrac{1}{2}} \;=\; \alpha,
\qquad
\mu_i \;=\; \frac{(1-\alpha) \cdot \tfrac{1}{2}}{(1-\alpha) \cdot \tfrac{1}{2} + \alpha \cdot \tfrac{1}{2}} \;=\; 1 - \alpha.
\]

So at $\mu_0 = 1/2$ the experiment moves the belief symmetrically: up by $\alpha - 1/2$ or down by $\alpha - 1/2$.

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Plot: posteriors as functions of the prior.}}

{{img:0|w=720}}

\bigskip\bigskip
\hrule
\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{2. New utilities at the posteriors.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The threshold $\mu_0 = 1-\alpha$: when information stops being worthless.}}

\textbf{The whole point.} \emph{The value of information lives entirely in the fact that it can change your decision} VOI is 0. 

\emph{Where does the threshold come from?} The decision flips on signal $g$ iff $\mu_g \ge 1/2$. Solving $\mu_g = 1/2$:
\[
\frac{\alpha\mu_0}{\alpha\mu_0 + (1-\alpha)(1-\mu_0)} \;=\; \frac{1}{2} \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\; \mu_0 \;=\; 1-\alpha.
\]
Symmetrically, $\mu_i = 1/2 \iff \mu_0 = \alpha$. 

This means on the two tails value of information is 0!


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Switch vs no-switch --- everything in one table.}}

\emph{Reading guide.} Column 1 carries the \textbf{full theory} (formulas, identities, derivations). Columns 2 and 3 evaluate the theory in the two regimes: SWITCH ($\mu_0 \in [1-\alpha,\alpha]$, example $\mu_0 = 1/2$) and NO-SWITCH at the threshold $\mu_0 = 1-\alpha$ (= 0.3 for $\alpha = 0.7$), so that $\mu_g = 1/2$ \emph{exactly} --- the knife-edge case.  Both columns use $\alpha = 0.7$.

\begin{tabular}{p{12cm}|p{13cm}|p{13cm}}
\textbf{Step / Quantity --- theory}
& \textbf{\textcolor{red}{SWITCH ($\mu_0 = 1/2$)}}
& \textbf{\textcolor{red}{NO-SWITCH threshold ($\mu_0 = 1-\alpha = 0.3$)}} \\ \hline

\textbf{(0) Prior utilities and value function (no-information baseline).} By enumeration over states at the prior $\mu_0$:
\[
U(A,\mu_0) = (1-\mu_0)\cdot u(A,I) + \mu_0 \cdot u(A,G) = 1 - \mu_0,
\]
\[
U(C,\mu_0) = (1-\mu_0)\cdot u(C,I) + \mu_0 \cdot u(C,G) = \mu_0.
\]
\emph{Value function at the prior:}
\[
U(\mu_0) = \max\{U(A,\mu_0),\,U(C,\mu_0)\} = \max\{1-\mu_0,\,\mu_0\},
\]
with $a^*(\mu_0) = A$ if $\mu_0 \le 1/2$, else $C$.
\newline \textcolor{blue}{\textbf{At $\mu_0 = 1/2$ (theory):}} $U(A,\mu_0) = U(C,\mu_0) = 1/2 \Rightarrow$ judge indifferent, $U(\mu_0) = 1/2$.
& $U(A,\mu_0) = 1 - \mu_0 = 1/2$, \;$U(C,\mu_0) = \mu_0 = 1/2$. \newline \textbf{Value function:} \;$U(\mu_0) = \max\{1-\mu_0,\,\mu_0\} = \max\{1/2,\,1/2\} = 1/2$. \newline \emph{Sitting exactly on the kink $\mu = 1/2$ where the two arms meet $\Rightarrow$ indifferent (tie-break $\to A$).}
& $U(A,\mu_0) = 1 - \mu_0 = 0.7$, \;$U(C,\mu_0) = \mu_0 = 0.3$. \newline \textbf{Value function:} \;$U(\mu_0) = \max\{1-\mu_0,\,\mu_0\} = 1-\mu_0 = 0.7$ \;(\emph{left arm} since $\mu_0 = 1-\alpha < 1/2$ for $\alpha > 1/2$). \newline $\Rightarrow$ \emph{strictly prefers $a^* = A$ (acquit).}
\\ \hline

\textbf{(a) Posteriors $\mu_s$ and signal probabilities $\Pr(s)$.}
\newline $\mu_g = \dfrac{\alpha\mu_0}{\alpha\mu_0 + (1-\alpha)(1-\mu_0)},\quad \mu_i = \dfrac{(1-\alpha)\mu_0}{(1-\alpha)\mu_0 + \alpha(1-\mu_0)}.$
\newline $\Pr(g) = \alpha\mu_0 + (1-\alpha)(1-\mu_0),\quad \Pr(i) = 1 - \Pr(g).$
\newline \textcolor{blue}{\textbf{At $\mu_0 = 1/2$ (theory):}} \;$\mu_g = \alpha$, \;$\mu_i = 1-\alpha$, \;$\Pr(g) = \Pr(i) = 1/2$.
& $\Pr(g) = \tfrac{1}{2},\;\Pr(i) = \tfrac{1}{2}$. \newline $\mu_g = \alpha = 0.7;\;\mu_i = 1-\alpha = 0.3$. \emph{Straddle $1/2$.}
& \emph{Symbolic at $\mu_0 = 1-\alpha$:} \newline $\mu_g = \dfrac{\alpha(1-\alpha)}{\alpha(1-\alpha)+(1-\alpha)\alpha} = \boxed{1/2}$ \;(\textbf{exactly on the kink}). \newline $\mu_i = \dfrac{(1-\alpha)^2}{(1-\alpha)^2 + \alpha^2}$. \newline $\Pr(g) = 2\alpha(1-\alpha),\;\Pr(i) = \alpha^2 + (1-\alpha)^2$. \newline \emph{Numerical ($\alpha = 0.7$):} $\mu_g = 0.5,\;\mu_i \approx 0.155;\;\Pr(g) = 0.42,\;\Pr(i) = 0.58$.
\\ \hline

\textbf{(b) Expected utilities at each posterior $\mu_s$, by enumeration over states $\omega \in \{I, G\}$.}
\[
U(A,\mu_s) = \underbrace{(1-\mu_s)}_{=\,\Pr(I\mid s)} \cdot \underbrace{u(A,I)}_{=\,1} + \underbrace{\mu_s}_{=\,\Pr(G\mid s)} \cdot \underbrace{u(A,G)}_{=\,0} = 1-\mu_s.
\]
\[
U(C,\mu_s) = (1-\mu_s)\cdot \underbrace{u(C,I)}_{=\,0} + \mu_s \cdot \underbrace{u(C,G)}_{=\,1} = \mu_s.
\]
\emph{Same formulas for $s \in \{i,g\}$ and for the baseline $\mu_0$.}
\newline \textcolor{blue}{\textbf{At $\mu_0 = 1/2$ (theory):}} sub the posteriors $\mu_i = 1-\alpha$, $\mu_g = \alpha$:
\newline $U(A,\mu_i) = \alpha,\;U(C,\mu_i) = 1-\alpha.$ \;\;$U(A,\mu_g) = 1-\alpha,\;U(C,\mu_g) = \alpha.$
\newline Baseline: $U(A,\mu_0) = U(C,\mu_0) = 1/2$ (judge indifferent without info).
& \emph{At $\mu_i = 1-\alpha$:} \newline $U(A,\mu_i) = 1 - \mu_i = 1 - (1-\alpha) = \alpha = 0.7$, \newline $U(C,\mu_i) = \mu_i = 1-\alpha = 0.3$. \newline \emph{At $\mu_g = \alpha$:} \newline $U(A,\mu_g) = 1 - \mu_g = 1-\alpha = 0.3$, \newline $U(C,\mu_g) = \mu_g = \alpha = 0.7$. \newline \emph{Baseline at $\mu_0 = 1/2$:} \newline $U(A,\mu_0) = 1 - \mu_0 = 1/2$, $\;U(C,\mu_0) = \mu_0 = 1/2$. \;\emph{(Indifferent.)}
& \emph{At $\mu_i \approx 0.155$:} \newline $U(A,\mu_i) = 1 - \mu_i \approx 0.845$, \newline $U(C,\mu_i) = \mu_i \approx 0.155$. \newline \emph{At $\mu_g = 1/2$ (\textbf{on the kink}):} \newline $U(A,\mu_g) = 1-\mu_g = 1/2$, \newline $U(C,\mu_g) = \mu_g = 1/2$. \newline \emph{Baseline at $\mu_0 = 0.3$:} \newline $U(A,\mu_0) = 1 - \mu_0 = 0.7$, $\;U(C,\mu_0) = \mu_0 = 0.3$. 
\\ \hline

\textbf{(c) Optimal action and payoff at $\mu_s$.}
\[
a^*(\mu_s) = \arg\max_{a\in\{A,C\}} U(a,\mu_s) = \begin{cases} A & \mu_s < 1/2 \\ C & \mu_s \ge 1/2 \end{cases}
\]
Payoff at the optimum $=$ value function $U(\mu_s) = \max\{1-\mu_s,\,\mu_s\}$.
\newline \textcolor{blue}{\textbf{At $\mu_0 = 1/2$ (theory):}} since $\alpha \ge 1/2$:
\newline At $\mu_i = 1-\alpha \le 1/2$: $a^* = A$, payoff $= 1-\mu_i = \alpha$.
\newline At $\mu_g = \alpha \ge 1/2$: $a^* = C$, payoff $= \mu_g = \alpha$. \textbf{Action flips $A \to C$ on $g$.}
& \emph{At $\mu_i = 0.3 < 1/2$:} $a^* = A$, payoff $= 1-\mu_i = 0.7$. \newline \textcolor{red}{\emph{At $\mu_g = 0.7 \ge 1/2$:} $a^* = C$, payoff $= \mu_g = 0.7$. \textbf{ACTION SWITCHED.}}
& \emph{At $\mu_i \approx 0.155 < 1/2$:} $a^* = A$, payoff $= 1-\mu_i \approx 0.845$. \newline \textcolor{red}{\emph{At $\mu_g = 1/2$ \textbf{exactly}:} judge \textbf{indifferent}; conventionally $a^* = A$, payoff $= 1/2$. \textbf{KNIFE EDGE --- action doesn't strictly flip.}} \newline The fact that information has no value does not mean that utility of the judge is smaller!! he actually isbetter of here (payoff $0.7$) than at $\mu_0 = 1/2$ baseline. Any $\mu_0$ just above $1-\alpha$ would push $\mu_g$ above $1/2$, triggering a real action flip $\Rightarrow$ VOI tips into positive territory. 
\\ \hline

\textbf{(d) Value function $U(\mu_s)$ piecewise on the two arms.}
\[
U(\mu_s) = \begin{cases} 1-\mu_s & \mu_s \le 1/2 \quad\text{(LEFT arm: acquit)} \\ \mu_s & \mu_s \ge 1/2 \quad\text{(RIGHT arm: convict)} \end{cases}
\]
\emph{Convex upper envelope; kink at $\mu_s = 1/2$.}
\newline \textcolor{blue}{\textbf{At $\mu_0 = 1/2$ (theory):}}
\newline $U(\mu_i) = 1 - (1-\alpha) = \alpha$ \;(left arm). \;\;$U(\mu_g) = \alpha$ \;(right arm). \;Both equal $\alpha$. \;Baseline $U(\mu_0 = 1/2) = 1/2$.
& $U(\mu_s) = \begin{cases} 1-\mu_i = 0.7 & s=i \;(\text{LEFT arm}) \\ \mu_g = 0.7 & s=g \;(\text{\textcolor{red}{RIGHT arm}, jumped}) \end{cases}$ \newline Baseline $U(\mu_0 = 1/2) = 0.5$.
& $U(\mu_s) = \begin{cases} 1-\mu_i \approx 0.955 & s=i \;(\text{LEFT arm}) \\ 1-\mu_g \approx 0.794 & s=g \;(\text{\textcolor{red}{ON THE KINK}: $\mu_g = 1/2$}) \end{cases}$ \newline Baseline $U(\mu_0 = 0.3) = 0.7$ (left arm). \emph{Two points on the left arm, one exactly at the kink.}
\\ \hline

\textbf{(e) Expected payoff with information.}
\[
U_{\text{info}}(\mu_0) = \mathbb{E}_{s\mid\mu_0}\!\left[U(\mu_s)\right] = \Pr(g)\,U(\mu_g) + \Pr(i)\,U(\mu_i).
\]

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Alternative derivation: $U_{\text{info}}$ as the probability of being right.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 1 --- Decision rule.}} In the switch regime ($\mu_g \ge 1/2 \ge \mu_i$): signal $g \Rightarrow$ convict (payoff $= 1$ iff guilty); signal $i \Rightarrow$ acquit (payoff $= 1$ iff innocent).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 2 --- Expected utility $=$ probability of being right.}} Sum payoff $\times$ joint probability over the four $(s, \omega)$ pairs:
\[
U_{\text{info}} \;=\; \Pr(g, G)\!\cdot 1 + \Pr(g, I)\!\cdot 0 + \Pr(i, I)\!\cdot 1 + \Pr(i, G)\!\cdot 0 \;=\; \underbrace{\Pr(g, G)}_{\substack{\text{correct} \\ \text{conviction}}} + \underbrace{\Pr(i, I)}_{\substack{\text{correct} \\ \text{acquittal}}}.
\]
\textbf{$U_{\text{info}}$ is literally the probability the judge gets the case right.}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 3 --- Joint $=$ conditional $\times$ prior.}}
\[
\Pr(g, G) \;=\; \underbrace{\Pr(g\mid G)}_{\substack{\text{TP rate} \\ \text{(true-positive)}}}\cdot \underbrace{\Pr(G)}_{=\,\mu_0}, \qquad \Pr(i, I) \;=\; \underbrace{\Pr(i\mid I)}_{\substack{\text{TN rate} \\ \text{(true-negative)}}}\cdot \underbrace{\Pr(I)}_{=\,1-\mu_0}.
\]
So
\[
\boxed{\;U_{\text{info}}(\mu_0) \;=\; (\text{TP rate})\cdot\mu_0 \;+\; (\text{TN rate})\cdot(1-\mu_0).\;}
\]
\emph{The expected utility is a weighted average of the experiment's two accuracies, weighted by the population fractions of guilty and innocent.} For the symmetric experiment (TP rate $=$ TN rate $= \alpha$): $U_{\text{info}} = \alpha\mu_0 + \alpha(1-\mu_0) = \alpha$ \;(flat in $\mu_0$).

\bigskip

\emph{Useful Bayes identity (used below):}
\;$\Pr(g)\mu_g = \Pr(g\mid G)\Pr(G) = \alpha\mu_0,$
\;$\Pr(i)(1-\mu_i) = \alpha(1-\mu_0).$
\emph{Martingale:} $\;\Pr(g)\mu_g + \Pr(i)\mu_i = \mu_0.$

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Claim.}} \;$U_{\text{info}}(\mu_0) = \mathbb{E}[U(\mu_s)] \;\ge\; U(\mu_0)$ \;(value of information is non-negative).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Proof 1 (general --- Jensen + martingale).}} $U(\mu) = \max\{1-\mu,\mu\}$ is \emph{convex} (upper envelope of two linear arms, see Setting). The posterior $\mu_s$ is a random variable; by martingale, $\mathbb{E}[\mu_s] = \mu_0$. Applying Jensen's inequality to the convex $U$:
\[
\mathbb{E}\bigl[U(\mu_s)\bigr] \;\overset{\text{Jensen}}{\ge}\; U\bigl(\mathbb{E}[\mu_s]\bigr) \;\overset{\text{martingale}}{=}\; U(\mu_0). \quad\blacksquare
\]
Equality iff $U$ is affine on the support $\{\mu_i, \mu_g\}$ (i.e.\ both posteriors on the same arm).


\bigskip

\textcolor{blue}{\textbf{At $\mu_0 = 1/2$ (theory):}} $\;U_{\text{info}}(1/2) = \tfrac{1}{2}\alpha + \tfrac{1}{2}\alpha = \alpha.$ \;Baseline $U(\mu_0 = 1/2) = 1/2$. \;Strict lift $1/2 \to \alpha$.
& THIS IS JUST THE EXPECTED VALUE OF THE ABOVE. $U_{\text{info}} = \Pr(g)\mu_g + \Pr(i)(1-\mu_i)$ \newline $\stackrel{\text{Bayes}}{=} \alpha\mu_0 + \alpha(1-\mu_0) = \boxed{\alpha} = 0.7$. \newline Baseline $U(\mu_0) = \max\{\mu_0, 1-\mu_0\} = 0.5$. \;\textbf{Strict lift $0.5 \to 0.7$.}
& THIS IS JUST THE EXPECTED VALUE OF THE ABOVE. \emph{Note $U(\mu_g) = 1/2 = 1-\mu_g$ since $\mu_g = 1/2$ on the kink --- same left-arm formula applies:} \newline $U_{\text{info}} = \Pr(g)(1-\mu_g) + \Pr(i)(1-\mu_i)$ \newline $= 1 - \underbrace{[\Pr(g)\mu_g + \Pr(i)\mu_i]}_{=\,\mu_0\text{ by martingale}} = \boxed{1-\mu_0} = 0.7$. \newline Baseline $U(\mu_0) = 1-\mu_0 = 0.7$. \;\textbf{Identical. No lift.}
\\ \hline

\textbf{(f) Value of information.}
recall that at the prior you are acqiutting them all. 
\[
\boxed{\;\text{VOI}(\mu_0) \;:=\; U_{\text{info}}(\mu_0) - U(\mu_0) \;=\; \Pr(g)U(\mu_g) + \Pr(i)U(\mu_i) - \max\{\mu_0,\,1-\mu_0\} \;\ge\; 0.\;}
\]
\newline \textcolor{blue}{\textbf{At $\mu_0 = 1/2$ (theory):}} $\;\text{VOI}(1/2) = \alpha - 1/2.$ \;(\emph{Tent peak: the maximum VOI achievable for any prior, given experiment quality $\alpha$.})
& $\text{VOI} = \alpha - \max\{\mu_0,1-\mu_0\}$. \newline Numerical: $0.7 - 0.5 = \mathbf{0.2} = \alpha - 1/2$. \;\emph{Max VOI (sits at the peak of the tent at $\mu_0 = 1/2$).}
& $\text{VOI} = (1-\mu_0) - (1-\mu_0) = \mathbf{0}$. \newline \emph{Knife edge: $\mu_g$ touches $1/2$ but doesn't cross. The chord coincides with the left arm of $U$. One nudge of $\mu_0$ rightward and the chord would crack the kink $\Rightarrow$ VOI strictly positive.}
\\ \hline

\textbf{(g) Geometric reading on $U(\mu)$ (Jensen).}
\newline Mark $\mu_i$ and $\mu_g$ on $U$, draw a \textcolor{red}{red chord} between them. By martingale, the chord evaluated at $\mu_0$ equals $\mathbb{E}[U(\mu_s)]$. VOI is the \textbf{vertical gap} from $U(\mu_0)$ up to the chord.
\newline \textcolor{blue}{\textbf{At $\mu_0 = 1/2$ (theory):}} chord endpoints are $(1-\alpha,\alpha)$ and $(\alpha,\alpha)$ --- a \emph{horizontal} segment at height $\alpha$. VOI $=$ height of chord at $\mu_0$ minus $U(1/2) = \alpha - 1/2$.
& Note how with the same expected value of posterior as prior (martingale) we have higher payoff since we took better (more informed) decisions on the same {{img:2|w=520}} \newline Posteriors straddle the kink at $1/2$ $\Rightarrow$ chord crosses over the V-shape and lies \textbf{above} $U$ at $\mu_0$. Gap $= 0.2 = \text{VOI}$.
& It is obvious by martingale $\mathbb{E}[\mu_s] = \mu_0$, so the expected payoff sits at the orange point on the chord. {{img:1|w=520}} \newline At the threshold $\mu_0 = 1-\alpha$, $\mu_g$ lands \emph{exactly on the kink} ($1/2$); $\mu_i$ on the left arm. The chord between them coincides with the left arm of $U$. So the chord value at $\mu_0 = 0.3$ equals $U(\mu_0) = 0.7 \Rightarrow$ \textbf{VOI $= 0$, knife-edge.}
\\ \hline

\textbf{\textcolor{purple}{(h) Punchline.}}
\newline $U$ convex + beliefs martingale $\Rightarrow$ $\mathbb{E}[U(\mu_s)] \ge U(\mu_0)$. Strict iff the chord crosses the kink, iff the action flips for some signal. \textbf{Value of information $\equiv$ value of the decision switch.}
& Each signal pulls the judge onto the arm where the matching action is correct. Experiment buys \textbf{decision flexibility}.
& Beliefs spread but stay on the same arm $\Rightarrow$ same action either way $\Rightarrow$ Jensen kills nothing. \emph{Information without a decision change is information without value.}
\\

\hline

\textbf{(h) How VOI varies across $\mu_0$}
&

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{3. VOI: closed-form summary.}}

Combining the table's case analysis across all $\mu_0$, the full piecewise VOI is:
\[
\text{VOI}(\mu_0) \;=\; \begin{cases}
0 & \mu_0 \in [0,\, 1-\alpha] \quad\text{(no switch: prior too low, even $g$ can't cross $1/2$)} \\[2pt]
\alpha - (1-\mu_0) & \mu_0 \in [1-\alpha,\, 1/2] \quad\text{(switch on signal $g$)} \\[2pt]
\alpha - \mu_0 & \mu_0 \in [1/2,\, \alpha] \quad\text{(switch on signal $i$)} \\[2pt]
0 & \mu_0 \in [\alpha,\, 1] \quad\text{(no switch: prior too high, even $i$ can't cross $1/2$)}
\end{cases}
\]

nodes.title: Value of information --- biased Bayesian signal ($\pm\varepsilon$ tilt)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Setting --- the biased information structure.}}

We relax the symmetric experiment by adding a state-independent tilt $\varepsilon$ toward signal $g$. Each column still sums to $1$; admissibility $|\varepsilon| < \min(\alpha, 1-\alpha)$.

\begin{tabular}{p{4cm}|p{8cm}|p{8cm}}
$\Pr(s\mid\omega)$ & $\omega = I$ & $\omega = G$ \\
\hline
$s = i$ & $\alpha - \varepsilon$ & $1-\alpha - \varepsilon$ \\
\hline
$s = g$ & $1-\alpha + \varepsilon$ & $\alpha + \varepsilon$ \\
\end{tabular}

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The two effects of bias (everything below is driven by these).}}

$\bullet$ \textbf{\textcolor{red}{(1) Marginal shift.}} $\Pr(g)$ rises by $\varepsilon$, $\Pr(i)$ falls by $\varepsilon$ \;(independent of $\mu_0$ and $\alpha$). The over-produced signal becomes more common.

$\bullet$ \textbf{\textcolor{red}{(2) Informativeness redistribution.}} Likelihood ratios shift: $\Lambda_g = \Pr(g\mid G)/\Pr(g\mid I)$ moves \emph{closer to $1$}, $\Lambda_i$ moves \emph{further below $1$}. \;\textbf{Signal $g$ becomes \emph{less} informative; signal $i$ becomes \emph{more} informative.} \;\emph{Why:} adding $\varepsilon$ to both states is the same absolute push, but proportionally hits the smaller term $1-\alpha$ harder $\Rightarrow$ false-positive rate of $g$ grows more in proportion than its true-positive rate.

\bigskip\bigskip
\hrule
\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Comparison table --- unbiased vs biased (at $\mu_0 = 1/2,\;\alpha = 0.7$; biased uses $\varepsilon = 0.1$).}}

\begin{tabular}{p{14cm}|p{12cm}|p{12cm}}
\textbf{Quantity --- theory}
& \textbf{\textcolor{red}{UNBIASED ($\varepsilon = 0$)}}
& \textbf{\textcolor{red}{BIASED ($\varepsilon = 0.1$)}} \\ \hline

\textbf{(a+b) The two primitives bias changes.} \;Everything else in the table is a derived consequence of these two. \newline \textcolor{red}{\textbf{Eff.\ (1) --- Marginals (rarity / weight).}} $\Pr(g) = \alpha\mu_0 + (1-\alpha)(1-\mu_0) + \varepsilon$, $\Pr(i) = 1 - \Pr(g)$. \;\emph{At $\mu_0 = 1/2$:} $\Pr(g) = 1/2 + \varepsilon$, $\Pr(i) = 1/2 - \varepsilon$. \newline \textcolor{red}{\textbf{Eff.\ (2) --- Likelihood ratios (informativeness).}} $\Lambda_g = \dfrac{\alpha+\varepsilon}{1-\alpha+\varepsilon}$, $\Lambda_i = \dfrac{1-\alpha-\varepsilon}{\alpha-\varepsilon}$. \;Pure property of the experiment, independent of $\mu_0$.
&
\emph{(1) Marginals:} $\Pr(g) = 0.5,\;\Pr(i) = 0.5$. \newline \emph{(2) Likelihoods:} $\Lambda_g = \dfrac{0.7}{0.3} \approx 2.33$, $\Lambda_i = \dfrac{0.3}{0.7} \approx 0.43$. \newline \emph{Symmetric: each signal equally common, each equally diagnostic in log-odds.}
&
\textbf{Now we evaluate at $\mu_0 = 0.4$} (a value strictly between the biased threshold $\mu_0^\star = 1/3$ and the canonical center $1/2$): the regime where bias \emph{has bite}. \newline \emph{(1) Marginals:} $\Pr(g) = 0.56$ \;\textcolor{red}{[$\uparrow$ vs.\ unbiased at $\mu_0 = 0.4$ which gives $\Pr(g) = 0.46$]}, $\Pr(i) = 0.44$. \newline \textcolor{red}{\textbf{$\Pr(g)$ IS the conviction rate}}: \textbf{56\% jailed} (up from $46\%$ unbiased). \newline \emph{(2) Likelihoods:} $\Lambda_g = \dfrac{0.8}{0.4} = 2.0$, $\Lambda_i = \dfrac{0.2}{0.6} \approx 0.33$ \;\emph{($\mu_0$-independent, same as before).}

\smallskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Margin scenarios.}}
\newline $\bullet$ \emph{Margin A --- biased threshold $\mu_0 = 1/3$:} $\Pr(g) \approx 0.533$, but $\mu_g = 1/2$ exactly (knife edge, judge indifferent). Conviction rate $53.3\%$, but each is a tie-break call.
\newline $\bullet$ \emph{Margin B --- canonical center $\mu_0 = 1/2$:} $\Pr(g) = 0.6$, $\mu_g = 0.667$. Conviction rate $60\%$. At this point bias effects (1) and (2) cancel \emph{exactly} (see rows below).

\bigskip

\textcolor{red}{\textbf{Toy walk-through (why eff.\ (2) is asymmetric).}} \;Use a sharper baseline $\alpha = 0.8$ so the proportions are easier to see. Bias $\varepsilon = 0.1$ shifts each conditional probability by $\pm 0.1$.

\smallskip

\textcolor{red}{\textbf{Signal $i$ (acquittal trigger).}} Before bias: $\Pr(i \mid I) = 0.8$ (correct acquittal of innocent), $\Pr(i\mid G) = 0.2$ (mistakenly acquitting a guilty). After $-\varepsilon$ on both:
\newline $\bullet$ $\Pr(i\mid I)$: $0.8 \to 0.7$. \;Same absolute drop ($-0.1$), but on a big base $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{$-12.5\%$ relative}: \emph{mild loss} in correct acquittals.
\newline $\bullet$ $\Pr(i\mid G)$: $0.2 \to 0.1$. \;Same absolute drop ($-0.1$), but on a small base $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{$-50\%$ relative}: \emph{huge drop} in missed-guilty (false acquittals).
\newline $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{Signal $i$ becomes a sharper innocence-test:} correct calls down a bit, wrong calls down a lot.

\smallskip

\textcolor{red}{\textbf{Signal $g$ (conviction trigger).}} Before bias: $\Pr(g\mid G) = 0.8$ (correct conviction), $\Pr(g\mid I) = 0.2$ (false conviction). After $+\varepsilon$ on both:
\newline $\bullet$ $\Pr(g\mid G)$: $0.8 \to 0.9$. \;$+0.1$ on a big base $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{$+12.5\%$ relative}: \emph{mild gain} in correct convictions.
\newline $\bullet$ $\Pr(g\mid I)$: $0.2 \to 0.3$. \;$+0.1$ on a small base $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{$+50\%$ relative}: \emph{huge surge} in false convictions.
\newline $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{Signal $g$ becomes a WORSE guilt-test:} correct calls up a bit, wrong calls up a lot.

\smallskip

\textcolor{red}{\textbf{Mechanism in one line.}} Same absolute push $\pm 0.1$, but proportionally it dominates the smaller term $\Rightarrow$ the error rate (small) moves more than the correct rate (big) $\Rightarrow$ informativeness redistributes: $g$ gets noisier, $i$ gets sharper.
\\ \hline

\textbf{(c) Posteriors $\mu_s$ (Bayes).} \;At $\mu_0 = 1/2$: $\mu_g = \dfrac{\alpha+\varepsilon}{1+2\varepsilon}$, $\mu_i = \dfrac{1-\alpha-\varepsilon}{1-2\varepsilon}$.
&
$\mu_g = \alpha = 0.7$, \;$\mu_i = 1-\alpha = 0.3$. \newline \emph{Update size:} $|\mu_g - \mu_0| = 0.2 = |\mu_i - \mu_0|$.
&
\emph{Primary $\mu_0 = 0.4$:} \;$\mu_g = \dfrac{0.8 \cdot 0.4}{0.56} = \dfrac{4}{7} \approx 0.571$ \;\textcolor{red}{[smaller than unbiased $\mu_g(0.4) \approx 0.609$, eff.\ (2): $g$ less informative]}; $\mu_i = \dfrac{0.2 \cdot 0.4}{0.44} = \dfrac{2}{11} \approx 0.182$ \;\textcolor{red}{[smaller than unbiased $\mu_i(0.4) \approx 0.222$, eff.\ (2): $i$ sharper for innocence]}. \newline \emph{Update sizes:} $|\mu_g - \mu_0| \approx 0.171$, $|\mu_i - \mu_0| \approx 0.218$. \newline \textcolor{red}{\textbf{Crucial:} $\mu_g \approx 0.571 > 1/2$. The Bayesian adjustment discounts the biased $g$ correctly, but \textbf{not enough to flip the action} --- judge still convicts on every $g$.}

\smallskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Margin scenarios.}}
\newline $\bullet$ \emph{Margin A --- $\mu_0 = 1/3$ (biased threshold):} $\mu_g = \dfrac{0.8 \cdot (1/3)}{0.533} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ \emph{exactly}. Knife edge: judge indifferent on every $g$; tie-breaks to convict. $\mu_i \approx 0.143$.
\newline $\bullet$ \emph{Margin B --- $\mu_0 = 1/2$ (canonical):} $\mu_g = 0.667$, $\mu_i = 0.25$. Judge strictly convicts on $g$.

\smallskip

{{img:0|w=540}} \newline \emph{Solid: unbiased posteriors. Dashed: biased ($\varepsilon = 0.1$). Both curves shift; threshold moves $0.3 \to 0.333$ (purple arrow).} \newline Note here bayes law is leading the judge to reweight. Judge can observe proabbitlities are biased and adjust posteriors. The problem is the hard cutoff: even if e adjusts, as long as he is to the right of the cutoff, he has to (rationally) convict. Is like a doctor that knows a test is biased for positive, but still if the situation is about the threshodl he has to diagnose the disease. 
\\ \hline

\textbf{(d) Marginal signal probabilities $\Pr(g), \Pr(i)$ via law of total probability.}
\newline $\Pr(g) = \Pr(g\mid G)\mu_0 + \Pr(g\mid I)(1-\mu_0) = (\alpha+\varepsilon)\mu_0 + (1-\alpha+\varepsilon)(1-\mu_0)$.
\newline $\Pr(i) = \Pr(i\mid G)\mu_0 + \Pr(i\mid I)(1-\mu_0) = (1-\alpha-\varepsilon)\mu_0 + (\alpha-\varepsilon)(1-\mu_0)$.
\newline Simplify at $\mu_0 = 1/2$: $\Pr(g) = \tfrac{1}{2}+\varepsilon$, $\Pr(i) = \tfrac{1}{2}-\varepsilon$. \newline (Martingale $\Pr(g)\mu_g + \Pr(i)\mu_i = \mu_0$ holds automatically; verified below.)
&
$\Pr(g) = 0.7 \cdot 0.5 + 0.3 \cdot 0.5 = 0.5$. \newline $\Pr(i) = 0.3 \cdot 0.5 + 0.7 \cdot 0.5 = 0.5$. \newline \emph{Each signal equally common.} \newline Martingale check: $0.5\cdot 0.7 + 0.5\cdot 0.3 = 0.5 = \mu_0$. \checkmark
&
\emph{Primary $\mu_0 = 0.4$:} \newline $\Pr(g) = \underbrace{0.8 \cdot 0.4}_{\text{from }G} + \underbrace{0.4 \cdot 0.6}_{\text{from }I} = 0.32 + 0.24 = 0.56$ \;\textcolor{red}{[$\uparrow \varepsilon = 0.1$ vs unbiased $0.46$, eff.\ (1)]}. \newline $\Pr(i) = \underbrace{0.2 \cdot 0.4}_{\text{from }G} + \underbrace{0.6 \cdot 0.6}_{\text{from }I} = 0.08 + 0.36 = 0.44$ \;\textcolor{red}{[$\downarrow \varepsilon$, eff.\ (1)]}. \newline Martingale check: $0.56 \cdot 0.571 + 0.44 \cdot 0.182 \approx 0.32 + 0.08 = 0.40 = \mu_0$. \checkmark

\smallskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Margin scenarios.}}
\newline $\bullet$ \emph{Margin A ($\mu_0 = 1/3$):} $\Pr(g) = 0.8 \cdot (1/3) + 0.4 \cdot (2/3) \approx 0.533$, $\Pr(i) \approx 0.467$. Martingale: $0.533 \cdot 0.5 + 0.467 \cdot 0.143 \approx 0.333 = \mu_0$. \checkmark
\newline $\bullet$ \emph{Margin B ($\mu_0 = 1/2$):} $\Pr(g) = 0.6$, $\Pr(i) = 0.4$. Martingale: $0.6\cdot 0.667 + 0.4\cdot 0.25 = 0.5 = \mu_0$. \checkmark

\textcolor{red}{\emph{Bias shifts the marginal $\Pr(g)$ up by exactly $\varepsilon$ regardless of $\mu_0$ --- mechanical content of eff.\ (1). Martingale unaffected.}}
\\ \hline

\textbf{(e) Threshold $\mu_0^\star$ where $\mu_g = 1/2$ (action just flips).} \;$\mu_0^\star = \dfrac{1-\alpha+\varepsilon}{1+2\varepsilon}$.
&
$\mu_0^\star = 1-\alpha = 0.3$.
&
$\mu_0^\star = \dfrac{0.4}{1.2} \approx 0.333$ \;\textcolor{red}{[$\uparrow$: eff.\ (2) dilutes $g$ $\Rightarrow$ higher prior needed for flip; eff.\ (1) cannot rescue]}. \newline \emph{Threshold is $\mu_0$-independent.} Position of each scenario relative to it: \newline $\bullet$ Primary $\mu_0 = 0.4$: \emph{above} $\Rightarrow$ inside switch regime, judge strictly convicts on $g$. \newline $\bullet$ Margin A $\mu_0 = 1/3$: \emph{exactly at} $\mu_0^\star$ $\Rightarrow$ knife edge, judge indifferent. \newline $\bullet$ Margin B $\mu_0 = 1/2$: \emph{well above} $\Rightarrow$ deep in switch regime.
\\ \hline

\textbf{(h)}
&
&
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{THE DARK EDGE CASE at $\mu_0 = 1/2$.}} The Bayesian adjustment in $\mu_g$ corrects per-case logic but \emph{never} prevents conviction as long as $\mu_g \ge 1/2$. So the sender's only constraint is to keep $\mu_g \ge 1/2$. \newline \textbf{Mild bias} ($\varepsilon = 0.1$, this column): conviction rate $50\% \to 60\%$. Innocent-share among convicted $= 1-\mu_g = 33\%$ (up from $30\%$). Already a step toward the dark limit. \newline \textbf{Pushed to the limit:} as the experiment becomes nearly uninformative ($\alpha \to 1/2$) biased toward $g$, we can have $\Pr(g\mid I) \approx \Pr(g\mid G) \approx 0.99$. Then: \newline $\bullet$ $\Pr(g) \approx 0.99 \Rightarrow$ \textbf{99\% of cases get signal $g$}. \newline $\bullet$ $\mu_g \approx \mu_0 = 1/2$ (judge learned nothing; indifferent; tie-breaks to $C$). \newline $\bullet$ \textbf{99\% of the population goes to jail}; half of the convicted are innocent ($1-\mu_g = 1/2$). \newline \textcolor{red}{\textbf{Judge rationality is NOT a defense.}} On every individual case the judge is solving his decision problem optimally --- his per-case expected payoff $U_{\text{info}}^{\text{biased}}(1/2) = \alpha$ is unchanged (see VOI section below). He cannot ``acquit more'' without violating his own utility. The collapse happens at the \emph{population} level, invisible inside any single case. \newline \emph{Fix lives outside the judge:} regulate $\alpha$ (force diagnostic content), or change the tie-break rule (acquit on indifference).
\\
\end{tabular}


\bigskip\bigskip
\hrule
\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Deriving the judge's expected utility (and the VOI) --- step by step.}}

The question to answer cleanly: \emph{how exactly does bias change the judge's expected utility, and why does that translate into "bias hurts left of $1/2$, helps right of $1/2$"?} The derivation has 6 steps.

\bigskip


recall 
\[
\boxed{\;U_{\text{info}}(\mu_0) \;=\; (\text{TP rate})\cdot\mu_0 \;+\; (\text{TN rate})\cdot(1-\mu_0).\;}
\]

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 4 --- Plug in the TP/TN rates.}}

\textbf{Unbiased:} TP rate $= \Pr(g\mid G) = \alpha$, TN rate $= \Pr(i\mid I) = \alpha$ \;(diagonal of the experiment table).
\[
U_{\text{info}}^{\text{unb}}(\mu_0) \;=\; \alpha\cdot\mu_0 + \alpha\cdot(1-\mu_0) \;=\; \alpha. \quad \textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Flat in $\mu_0$.}}
\]
Why flat: both accuracies are equal $\Rightarrow$ the weighted average doesn't depend on the weights $\Rightarrow$ population composition is irrelevant.

\textbf{Biased:} TP rate $= \Pr(g\mid G) = \alpha+\varepsilon$ \;\textcolor{red}{($\uparrow$ by $\varepsilon$)}, TN rate $= \Pr(i\mid I) = \alpha-\varepsilon$ \;\textcolor{red}{($\downarrow$ by $\varepsilon$)}.
\[
U_{\text{info}}^{\text{biased}}(\mu_0) \;=\; (\alpha+\varepsilon)\mu_0 + (\alpha-\varepsilon)(1-\mu_0).
\]
Expand:
\[
= \alpha\mu_0 + \varepsilon\mu_0 + \alpha(1-\mu_0) - \varepsilon(1-\mu_0) \;=\; \alpha\bigl[\mu_0 + (1-\mu_0)\bigr] + \varepsilon\bigl[\mu_0 - (1-\mu_0)\bigr].
\]
\[
\boxed{\;U_{\text{info}}^{\text{biased}}(\mu_0) \;=\; \alpha + \varepsilon(2\mu_0 - 1). \;}
\]
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Tilts with $\mu_0$.}} The bias trades a $+\varepsilon$ in TP rate against a $-\varepsilon$ in TN rate. The trade is favourable when the prior weights TP more (i.e.\ $\mu_0 > 1/2$).

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 5 --- The bias effect: $\Delta U_{\text{info}}(\mu_0) = \varepsilon(2\mu_0 - 1)$.}}

\[
\Delta U_{\text{info}} \;=\; U_{\text{info}}^{\text{biased}} - U_{\text{info}}^{\text{unb}} \;=\; \underbrace{(+\varepsilon)\cdot\mu_0}_{\substack{\text{TP rate}\,\uparrow \\ \text{weighted by guilty}}} \;+\; \underbrace{(-\varepsilon)\cdot(1-\mu_0)}_{\substack{\text{TN rate}\,\downarrow \\ \text{weighted by innocent}}} \;=\; \varepsilon(2\mu_0 - 1).
\]

$\bullet$ $\mu_0 = 1/2$: $+\varepsilon\cdot(1/2)$ exactly cancels $-\varepsilon\cdot(1/2)$. \textbf{Bias invisible.}

$\bullet$ $\mu_0 > 1/2$: more guilty than innocent $\Rightarrow$ TP gain dominates $\Rightarrow$ bias \textbf{helps}.

$\bullet$ $\mu_0 < 1/2$: more innocent than guilty $\Rightarrow$ TN loss dominates $\Rightarrow$ bias \textbf{hurts}.

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 6 --- VOI subtracts the no-info baseline.}}

$\mathrm{VOI}(\mu_0) = U_{\text{info}}(\mu_0) - U(\mu_0)$, where $U(\mu_0) = \max\{\mu_0,\, 1-\mu_0\}$ is what the judge could get without any signal (pick the better default).

\[
\boxed{\;\mathrm{VOI}^{\text{biased}}(\mu_0) \;=\; \alpha + \varepsilon(2\mu_0 - 1) - \max\{\mu_0,\,1-\mu_0\}, \quad \text{on the joint switch regime } [\mu_0^{*L,b},\, \mu_0^{*U,b}].\;}
\]
Outside the switch regime, one of the signals fails to flip the action, so $U_{\text{info}}$ collapses back to the no-info value and VOI $= 0$.

\bigskip\bigskip
\hrule
\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Plot: Jensen chord view + VOI tent, side by side for both cases.}}

{{img:1|w=1400}}

KEYYYYYY: we are considering the judge perspective only, not society welfare. Now, the information is not creatign value for the judge at $ \mu_0 = 0.3$ because he updated downards the effect on $\mu_g$. Instead, it is creating value at  $ \mu_0 = 0.75$ because thanks to the precise innocence information. The biased experiment expands the set of priors for which info has decisional value. That's the right-side broadening of the biased tent's base ($0.7 \to 0.75$).

\bigskip\bigskip
\hrule
\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Final plot --- conviction probability $P_C(\mu_0)$.}}

Two panels: no bias on the left, bias ($\varepsilon = 0.1$) on the right. Black dashed: no-info baseline. Red: with-info.

{{img:2|w=1400}}

nodes.title: Information design --- prosecutor manipulates the judge
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Setting --- two players.}}

We now add a second player to the judge's decision problem: a \textbf{prosecutor} (sender) who designs the experiment.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Judge (DM, receiver).} Payoff $u(a, \omega)$: $1$ if correct action ($A$ if $I$, $C$ if $G$), $0$ otherwise.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Prosecutor.} Payoff $v(a) = \mathbf{1}\{a = C\}$: $1$ if the guy goes to jail, $0$ otherwise. \emph{Doesn't care about the state.}

$\bullet$ \textbf{Common prior} $\mu_0 = \Pr(\omega = G)$, both players know it.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Information design.} Prosecutor picks an experiment $\pi : \Omega \to \Delta(S)$ --- the conditional signal distribution $\Pr(s\mid\omega)$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Crucial assumption.}} \textbf{The judge observes the experiment $\pi$ chosen by the prosecutor} before updating. So the judge is fully rational, computes Bayes' rule with the correct $\pi$, and acts optimally. \emph{This is exactly what makes the manipulation story interesting: rational decision-making, transparent design, and yet a bad aggregate outcome.}


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Plots.}}

Three cases: 1) no information, 2) perfect information
{{img:0|w=1400}}

The rightmost plot shows the concavification of the prosecutor payoff. is the smallest concabe funciton you can drow above the basic black U function. 

Recall, again, at $\mu_0 = 0.51$, is the judge sending all to jail

\bigskip\bigskip
\hrule
\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Prosecutor's optimization problem.}}

The prosecutor chooses an experiment $\pi$, which by Bayes plausibility is equivalent to choosing two posteriors $(\mu_i, \mu_g)$ and their signal probabilities $(\Pr(i), \Pr(g))$. His expected utility is $\mathbb{E}[V(\mu_s)] = \Pr(g)V(\mu_g) + \Pr(i)V(\mu_i)$, where $V(\mu) = \mathbf{1}\{\mu \ge 1/2\}$ is the indicator that the judge convicts.

\textbf{The maximization in standard form:}
\[
\max_{\mu_i,\,\mu_g,\,\Pr(g),\,\Pr(i)} \;\mathbb{E}[V(\mu_s)] \;=\; \Pr(g)\,V(\mu_g) + \Pr(i)\,V(\mu_i)
\]
\textbf{subject to:}
\[
\Pr(g)\mu_g + \Pr(i)\mu_i = \mu_0 \;\;\text{(martingale)}, \qquad \Pr(g) + \Pr(i) = 1, \qquad \mu_g \ge 1/2, \qquad \mu_i,\mu_g \in [0,1], \;\;\Pr(\cdot) \ge 0.
\]

\textbf{Why this reduces to maximizing $\Pr(g)$.} The constraint $\mu_g \ge 1/2$ forces $V(\mu_g) = 1$. The martingale + $\mu_0 < 1/2$ force $\mu_i < 1/2$, hence $V(\mu_i) = 0$. So the objective collapses:
\[
\mathbb{E}[V(\mu_s)] \;=\; \Pr(g) \cdot 1 + \Pr(i) \cdot 0 \;=\; \Pr(g).
\]
The prosecutor's expected utility \textbf{equals} the conviction rate. \emph{General pattern: when the payoff is the indicator of an event, expected utility $=$ probability of the event.}

\[
\boxed{\;\max_{\mu_i,\,\mu_g,\,\Pr(g),\,\Pr(i)} \;\Pr(g) \quad \text{s.t. same constraints.}\;}
\]

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Solution.}}

Substitute $\Pr(i) = 1 - \Pr(g)$ into the martingale and solve for $\Pr(g)$:
\[
\Pr(g)\mu_g + (1-\Pr(g))\mu_i = \mu_0 \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \Pr(g) = \frac{\mu_0 - \mu_i}{\mu_g - \mu_i}.
\]
This is the only choice variable in disguise --- we just need to optimize over $\mu_i$ and $\mu_g$. Take the partial derivatives:

\textbf{(i) w.r.t.\ $\mu_g$:}
\[
\frac{\partial \Pr(g)}{\partial \mu_g} = -\frac{\mu_0 - \mu_i}{(\mu_g - \mu_i)^2} \;<\; 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{\;\mu_g = 1/2\;} \;(\text{push to the lower bound of }\mu_g \ge 1/2).
\]

\textbf{(ii) w.r.t.\ $\mu_i$:}
\[
\frac{\partial \Pr(g)}{\partial \mu_i} = \frac{\mu_0 - \mu_g}{(\mu_g - \mu_i)^2} \;<\; 0 \;\;(\text{since } \mu_g = 1/2 > \mu_0) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{\;\mu_i = 0\;} \;(\text{push to the lower bound } \mu_i \ge 0).
\]

\textbf{Plug back:}
\[
\boxed{\;\Pr(g)^\star \;=\; \frac{\mu_0 - 0}{1/2 - 0} \;=\; 2\mu_0, \qquad \Pr(i)^\star \;=\; 1 - 2\mu_0.\;}
\]

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Reading.}} Both posteriors land at \emph{corner solutions}: $\mu_g = 1/2$ (binding the judge's tie-breaking constraint) and $\mu_i = 0$ (the extreme acquittal posterior --- prosecutor ``concentrates the innocence'' on the rare $i$-signal so the common $g$-signal carries minimum residual doubt). Conviction rate $= 2\mu_0$ --- \textbf{double the perfect-information rate}, while leaving the judge's per-case expected payoff unchanged.

\bigskip\bigskip
\hrule
\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{From posteriors $(\mu_i, \mu_g)$ to the experiment $\pi(s\mid\omega)$.}}

\textbf{Key implication of $\mu_i = 0$.} By Bayes,
\[
\mu_i \;=\; \Pr(G\mid i) \;=\; \frac{\Pr(i\mid G)\,\mu_0}{\Pr(i)} \;=\; 0 \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \Pr(i\mid G) \;=\; 0.
\]
\emph{Signal $i$ is never sent in state $G$.} The acquittal signal is reserved for the innocent. Equivalently, $\Pr(g\mid G) = 1$ (every guilty defendant gets the conviction signal). Basically you want max true positives!! the martingale as a given probabilty do distribute and you want to do it in the most effectieve wya. 

\textbf{Key implication of $\mu_g = 1/2$.} From the Bayes formula for $\mu_g$:
\[
\frac{1}{2} \;=\; \mu_g \;=\; \frac{\Pr(g\mid G)\,\mu_0}{\Pr(g\mid G)\,\mu_0 + \Pr(g\mid I)(1-\mu_0)} \;=\; \frac{\mu_0}{\mu_0 + \Pr(g\mid I)(1-\mu_0)}.
\]
Solving for $\Pr(g\mid I)$:
\[
\Pr(g\mid I) \;=\; \beta \;=\; \frac{\mu_0}{1 - \mu_0}.
\]
\emph{Innocent defendants get the conviction signal with probability $\mu_0/(1-\mu_0)$ --- the false-positive rate calibrated to dilute $\mu_g$ exactly to the tie-break point.}

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The KG-optimal manipulated experiment $\pi(s\mid\omega)$} (at $\mu_0 = 0.3$).}

\begin{tabular}{p{3cm}|p{3cm}|p{3cm}}
$\pi(s\mid\omega)$ & $\omega = I$ & $\omega = G$ \\ \hline
$s = i$ & $1 - \beta$ & $0$ \\ \hline
$s = g$ & $\beta$ & $1$ \\
\end{tabular}

with $\beta = \dfrac{\mu_0}{1-\mu_0} = \dfrac{3}{7}$ at $\mu_0 = 0.3$. Each column sums to $1$.

Basically only innocents can generate innocent signals! 
For I: Min false negatives (you are guilty, and test says you are innocent = i arrives to a guilty guy), max false positives ( you are innocent, and test says you are guilty = g arrives to an innocent. recall the prior mu0 is on every agent, so in this situation the innocent is cooked )


Again you can compute p(conviction) and you fidn out that the maximum number possible of people are going to jail. 


note how VOI for the judge is 0. he is switching at 0.5 but this switch is creating no value to him.

nodes.title: Martingale property
nodes.content:
gskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Martingale property of Bayesian beliefs.}}

\emph{Statement.} The expected posterior equals the prior:
\[
\boxed{\;\mathbb{E}[\mu_s] \;=\; \Pr(g)\,\mu_g \;+\; \Pr(i)\,\mu_i \;=\; \mu_0.\;}
\]

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Reading: information is a mean-preserving spread of beliefs.}}
Say $\mu_0$ = 0.7.

1. $\mathbb{E}[\mu_s] \;=\; \mu_0.\ $ The expecyed balue of the information signal is 0.7. The point is that the martingla is just an internal coheence properlty: 1) prior was a "true" understandign of $\omega$, and so  2) if omega has not changed, it must be $\mathbb{E}[\mu_s] = \Pr(g)\,\mu_g \;+\; \Pr(i)\,\mu_i  \;=\; \mu_0.\ $

2. A violation $\mathbb{E}[\mu_s] > \mu_0$ means inconsistency between your stated prior and your stated likelihoods. Two sources: 
- (i) your prior $\mu_0$ doesn't match your true belief — you'd update up on average because you already think it's higher; 
- (ii) the experiment is mis-specified — the lab/coin/test isn't actually generating signals from $\pi(s\mid\omega)$ as you claim (rigged) <- this is what purely **rigged** is, but not what we mean in this ocurse (explained before)

$\rightarrow$ Both collapse to: "stated model ≠ honest model." 


3. The above implies information has to be a priori unpredictable to have value. Indeed, if you know what will happen (probabioty = certianty) this means pg = 1 : $\mathbb{E}[\mu_s] = 1 \mu_g \;=\; \mu_0.\ $  and $\mu_g \;=\; \mu_0$

4. To have martingale holding and information beign valable, you need  $p(g), p(i) \in (0,1)$, this will lead to  $\mu_i < \mu_0 < \mu_g$. Recalling we need $p(i) + p(g) = 1$. As one signal becomes rare ($\Pr(g) \to 0$, say), the corresponding posterior $\mu_g$ jumps far from theprior (huge surprise), while the other ($\mu_i$) barely moves — exactly the $1/\Pr(g)$ surprise factor from earlier.                                                                       
 

Remark: unpredictability is necessary but not sufficient for the spread. If $\alpha = 1/2$, then $\Pr(g), \Pr(i) \in (0,1)$ — the signal is genuinely random — but it's independent of $\omega$, so $\mu_g = \mu_i = \mu_0$. Randomness alone is noise!             


Martignale fixes a rigged experiment: 

Example:

\[
\Pr(g \mid G) = 0.99,
\]

The experiment almost always produces \(g\).

\[
\Pr(g \mid I) = 0.90.
\]

Many people would call this ``rigged.''

**But Bayesianly, there is no problem**. If you know these probabilities, then your prior and Bayes' rule already account for them.

The martingale property still holds:

\[
\mathbb{E}[\mu_s] = \mu_0.
\]

Problem is if judge misperceives the probabilities!!!!!!

nodes.title: 3 states 3 signals
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Setting.}} Three states $\Omega = \{\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3\}$, three actions $\mathscr{A} = \{a_1, a_2, a_3\}$, three signals $S = \{s_1, s_2, s_3\}$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Comparing 2-state and 3-state cases side by side.}}

\begin{tabular}{p{9cm}|p{14cm}|p{14cm}}
\textbf{Quantity --- theory} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{2 states / 2 actions (judge)}} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{3 states / 3 actions}} \\ \hline

\textbf{Belief} $\mu$ over states.
& $\mu = \Pr(\omega = G) \in [0,1]$ \;(scalar, 1-D)
& $\mu = (\mu_1, \mu_2, \mu_3)$ on 2-simplex \;($\mu_i \ge 0$, $\sum\mu_i = 1$)
\\ \hline

\textbf{Payoff matrix} $u(a, \omega)$ (diagonal = correct).
& $u(A,I) = u(C,G) = 1$, off-diagonal $= 0$.
& $u(a_i, \omega_j) = \mathbf{1}\{i = j\}$ (diagonal identity).
\\ \hline

\textbf{$U(a, \mu)$ --- expected payoff of action $a$ at belief $\mu$.}
\[
U(a, \mu) = \sum_\omega \mu(\omega)\,u(a, \omega)
\]
\emph{Linear in $\mu$.} One line per action.
&
$U(A, \mu) = (1-\mu)\cdot 1 + \mu \cdot 0 = 1-\mu$ \newline
$U(C, \mu) = (1-\mu)\cdot 0 + \mu \cdot 1 = \mu$ \newline
\emph{2 lines, slopes $\mp 1$, cross at $\mu = 1/2$.}
&
\emph{Show the computation for $a_1$ (others identical):} \newline
$U(a_1, \mu) = \mu_1\,\underbrace{u(a_1,\omega_1)}_{=\,1} + \mu_2\,\underbrace{u(a_1,\omega_2)}_{=\,0} + \mu_3\,\underbrace{u(a_1,\omega_3)}_{=\,0} = \mu_1$. \newline
By symmetry: $U(a_2, \mu) = \mu_2$, $U(a_3, \mu) = \mu_3$. \newline
\emph{Each action action $a_i$ a payoff $\mu_i$}
\\ \hline

\textbf{Value function} $U(\mu) = \max_a U(a, \mu)$. \;Why? Rational DM picks the best action available at belief $\mu$. So i take the best action given my belief :
\[
a^*(\mu) = \arg\max_a U(a, \mu)
\]
$U(\mu)$ = payoff of whichever action is optimal, not of any fixed action.
&
$U(\mu) = \max\{1-\mu,\; \mu\}$ \newline
\emph{V-shape, kink at $\mu = 1/2$.} \newline
$a^*(\mu) = A$ if $\mu < 1/2$, else $C$.
&
$U(\mu) = \max\{\mu_1,\; \mu_2,\; \mu_3\}$ \newline
\emph{Tent with 3 facets on the 2-simplex.} \newline
$a^*(\mu) = a_i$ where $\mu_i$ is the largest coordinate.
\\ \hline

\textbf{Geometric reading.} Plot $U(a, \mu)$ for each action; at each $\mu$ the DM picks the highest line; $U(\mu)$ traces the \textbf{upper envelope}. Below the envelope $=$ sub-optimal. Upper envelope of linear functions $\Rightarrow$ \emph{piecewise linear, convex}, with kinks where the optimal action switches.
&
Two crossing lines $\to$ V-shape upper envelope. 1 kink at $\mu = 1/2$.
&
Three crossing planes on the simplex $\to$ tent upper envelope. 3 indifference lines meeting at the centroid $(1/3, 1/3, 1/3)$ where $U = 1/3$ (most uncertain).
\\ \hline

\textbf{Corner values.}
& $U(\mu = 0) = 1$ (sure innocence, acquit), $U(\mu = 1) = 1$ (sure guilt, convict), $U(\mu = 1/2) = 1/2$ (most uncertain).
& $U(\mu = e_i) = 1$ for each vertex (sure state), $U(\mu = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3)) = 1/3$ (most uncertain).
\\
\end{tabular}

\textbf{\textcolor{purple}{Pattern.}} Same logic in both cases: \emph{each action gives a linear payoff in beliefs; the value function picks the highest one}. Number of states/actions changes the geometry (V-shape $\to$ tent), but the convex piecewise-linear structure is identical. The plot below makes this concrete with 3 lines.

\bigskip\bigskip
\hrule
\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Two extreme information structures $\pi(s\mid\omega)$.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(A) Perfectly informative.}} Identity matrix: each signal reveals the state.

\begin{tabular}{p{2cm}|p{2cm}|p{2cm}|p{2cm}}
$\pi(s\mid\omega)$ & $\omega_1$ & $\omega_2$ & $\omega_3$ \\
\hline
$s_1$ & $1$ & $0$ & $0$ \\
\hline
$s_2$ & $0$ & $1$ & $0$ \\
\hline
$s_3$ & $0$ & $0$ & $1$ \\
\end{tabular}

Posterior = degenerate on the true state. Action always matches. $U_{\text{info}} = 1$.

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(B) Perfectly uninformative.}} Columns all equal: signal independent of state.

\begin{tabular}{p{2cm}|p{2cm}|p{2cm}|p{2cm}}
$\pi(s\mid\omega)$ & $\omega_1$ & $\omega_2$ & $\omega_3$ \\
\hline
$s_1$ & $q_1$ & $q_1$ & $q_1$ \\
\hline
$s_2$ & $q_2$ & $q_2$ & $q_2$ \\
\hline
$s_3$ & $q_3$ & $q_3$ & $q_3$ \\
\end{tabular}

with $q_1+q_2+q_3 = 1$. Posterior = prior, regardless of signal. $U_{\text{info}} = U(\mu_0)$ --- no lift.

\bigskip\bigskip
\hrule
\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Value function as upper envelope of linear utilities.}}

For each action $a$, $U(a, \mu)$ is a \emph{straight line} in $\mu$. The value function $U(\mu) = \max_a U(a, \mu)$ is the \textbf{upper envelope (red)} --- pick whichever line is highest at the current $\mu$.

{{img:0|w=900}}

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Reading.}} Three dashed lines = three actions: $U(a_1) = 1-\mu$ (best at low $\mu$), $U(a_2) = 0.6$ (best in the middle), $U(a_3) = \mu$ (best at high $\mu$). The red curve is the upper envelope; the kinks at $\mu = 0.4$ and $\mu = 0.6$ are the \emph{indifference points} where the optimal action switches. \emph{Convex, piecewise linear, three facets} --- same logic as the V-shape for 2 actions, extended to any number of actions.

nodes.title: Preamble: why a single-price monopoly is inefficient (road to adverse selection)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Preamble: why a single-price monopoly is inefficient, and the road to adverse selection.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{1. Welfare benchmark: $MSB = MC$.}}

Imagine \emph{one} consumer with declining marginal valuation: she pays \$9 for unit 1, \$8 for unit 2, \$7 for unit 3, \ldots At unit $q$ she is willing to pay $P(q) = 10 - q$. This curve \emph{is} her demand curve and equivalently her \textbf{marginal social benefit} MSB. With $n$ identical consumers the aggregate demand is the horizontal sum, still satisfying $D = MSB$ at every $Q$.

{{img:0|w=560}}

\emph{Welfare-maximising rule.} Produce while $MSB > MC$, stop when $MSB = MC$. Every unit on this range adds positive social surplus $= MSB - MC$. The whole triangle between $D$ and $MC$ up to $Q^\ast$ is realised welfare.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{2. The monopolist's problem: $MR < MSB$.}}

The firm maximises $\pi(Q) = P(Q) \cdot Q - C(Q)$. FOC:
\[ \boxed{\;MR(Q) = MC(Q)\;}. \]
The catch: $MR(Q) < P(Q) = MSB(Q)$ whenever the demand curve slopes down --- to sell one more unit, the firm must lower the price on \emph{every} previous unit.

\begin{tabular}{p{9.5cm}|p{9.5cm}|p{9.5cm}|p{9.5cm}}
\textbf{P} & \textbf{Q  (from $P = 10 - Q$)} & \textbf{MSB  (value of the unit)} & \textbf{MR  ($\Delta$TR)} \\
\hline
9 & 1 & 9 & 9 \\
\hline
8 & 2 & 8 & 7 \\
\hline
7 & 3 & 7 & 5 \\
\hline
6 & 4 & 6 & 3 \\
\hline
5 & 5 & 5 & 1 \\
\hline
4 & 6 & 4 & $-1$ \\
\end{tabular}

\emph{Reading the table.} At $Q = 3$, the 4th unit is worth \$6 to a buyer, but selling it only adds \$3 to the firm's revenue, because the firm must shave \$1 off the price of the 3 units already being sold. The firm cares about \emph{its} margin, not the buyer's.

\textcolor{purple}{\emph{Jacket intuition.}} You sell 10 premium jackets at \$10{,}000 each. To sell 100, you'd have to drop the price to \$1{,}000 each. The 90 extra jackets earn \$1{,}000 each, but the original 10 lose \$9{,}000 each --- catastrophic, even though there are buyers happy to pay \$1{,}100 for a jacket whose marginal cost is only \$900.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{3. The deadweight loss: helpful trades not executed.}}

{{img:1|w=560}}

At the monopoly quantity $Q^M$ where $MR = MC$, units satisfying $MSB > MC$ are \emph{not produced}. There exist buyers willing to pay \$1{,}100 for a jacket that costs \$900 to make --- a socially valuable trade --- yet the firm refuses, because executing it requires dropping the price for the buyers who would have paid \$10{,}000.

\textbf{The entire inefficiency is generated by ``one price for everyone''.} A single price cannot simultaneously extract \$10{,}000 from the rich buyer and \$1{,}100 from the price-sensitive one. To preserve the margin on the rich, the firm sacrifices the low-end trade.

\emph{In terms of marginals (no externality involved --- this is a firm-side wedge).} $MR < P = MSB$ at every $Q > 0$, because each price cut applies to \emph{all} inframarginal units. The firm stops at $MR = MC$; the social planner would stop at $MSB = MC$. Since $MSB > MR$ everywhere, the firm halts before the social optimum: $Q^M < Q^\ast$ --- \textbf{quantity is under-produced}.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{4. The road to screening: airline cabins.}}

Forget jackets. Switch to airline cabins, with two passenger types: \textbf{business flyers} (high WTP, expense account) and \textbf{leisure flyers} (low WTP, paying out of pocket).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 1 --- one cabin, one fare.}} 
$\bullet$ \emph{High fare:} only business buys --- fat margin per ticket, but leisure is shut out (DWL).
$\bullet$ \emph{Low fare:} leisure also flies, but you lose margin on every business traveler.
Single pricing is inefficient \emph{either way}: the wedge between the two WTPs cannot be exploited with one number.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 2 --- the dream: perfect price discrimination.}} Charge each their max --- high fare to business, low fare to leisure. Both fly, $MSB = MC$ at the marginal unit, no DWL, the firm extracts everything. But you cannot \emph{see} who is flying on an expense account.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 3a --- give up: one fare for all.}} Back to single-price monopoly. Inefficient. \emph{Can we do better than that, without observing the type?}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 3b --- engineer a menu: business class + economy.}} Two cabins, two fares, \textbf{self-selection}. ``Looks solved'': business flyers pick business, leisure flyers pick economy.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 4 --- it doesn't work naively: business flyers defect.}} A business flyer can fly economy just fine. If economy is cheap and not too bad, they \textbf{buy down}: take the economy ticket, pocket the big surplus instead of paying the high business fare. The menu falls apart.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The key idea behind every screening problem:}} the business flyer's WTP is \emph{higher than the leisure flyer's at every quality level}. Whatever bundle the firm designs for leisure, the business flyer wants it too --- unless something stops them. (Single-crossing / Spence--Mirrlees.)

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 5 --- restore incentive compatibility (IC).}} Two instruments to prevent defection:

$\bullet$ \textbf{Cut the business fare} just enough to leave business better off than mimicking economy. The amount by which the fare is cut below full WTP is the \emph{\textbf{information rent}}.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Degrade the economy product} (narrow seat, no flexibility, no lounge) until business flyers don't want it. Cheaper than paying rent, but socially \emph{inefficient} --- leisure flyers get a worse trip than they would in first best.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 6 --- the Mussa--Rosen trade-off.}} Degrading economy is wasteful (real social loss on leisure's missing quality) but saves rent paid to business. The firm equates the marginal trade-off:
\[ \boxed{\;\;\text{marginal rent saved on business} \;\;=\;\; \text{marginal surplus lost on leisure}\;\;} \]
The second-best contract picks the optimal mix of \emph{rent + downward distortion}. \textbf{Both are real, both are paid simultaneously}; the firm just minimises their combined cost.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{5. Aside: is the rich's WTP really higher at \emph{every} quality?}}

The textbook screening logic assumes WTP$_H(q) > $ WTP$_L(q)$ for every $q$ (linear, single-crossing). Real life is messier.

\emph{Hotel example.} If you're used to 5-star hotels, a 3-star feels \emph{bad} --- barely an upgrade from staying home, almost a disutility. For someone whose default is staying home, a 3-star vacation is \emph{great}. Similarly, a poor consumer may think a \$10k jacket is crazy: they value it at \$1k, same as the \$1k jacket; the rest is wasted money.

Both WTPs are S-shaped (sigmoid); the poor's plateau hits earlier and lower:

{{img:2|w=560}}

The two curves \textbf{cross}: at low quality, poor's WTP $>$ rich's WTP; at high quality, rich's WTP $\gg$ poor's WTP.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why this matters.}} In this realistic case the IC problem becomes \emph{easier}, not harder. The rich is \textbf{already disincentivised} from the low-quality bundle, because they get \emph{little utility} from it. Screening works \textbf{more cleanly}: less degradation needed, less rent paid.

\textcolor{purple}{\emph{Reading: the linear-WTP / single-crossing case is the \textbf{worst} scenario for the firm --- the rich is maximally tempted by every cheaper bundle. Any non-linearity (saturation, taste differences, sigmoidal preferences) makes screening strictly easier. Our analysis is the binding case.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Key takeaway.}} The screening contract is the firm's \emph{best response} when perfect PD is impossible. It is \emph{strictly better} than ``one price for everyone'' (the naive monopoly outcome) and \emph{strictly worse} than first-best (which would require observable types). This second-best, with its IC + IR constraints, is the workhorse of the adverse-selection chapter --- the rest of the analysis just works out the optimal menu.

nodes.title: First Best vs Second Best screening: Mussa--Rosen complete table (book ch.\ 6)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{First-best vs second-best screening: complete side-by-side (Mussa--Rosen).}}

\emph{Setting.} Monopolist airline facing two passenger types:

$\bullet$ \textbf{Frugal / leisure type} $\theta_1$ (low marginal value of quality).

$\bullet$ \textbf{Sophisticated / business type} $\theta_2 > \theta_1$ (high marginal value).

Each type's utility from a bundle (quality $q$, fare $t$) is \textbf{quasi-linear}:
\[ U_i(q, t) \;=\; \theta_i\, q \;-\; t. \]
Outside option normalised to $0$. Cost $C(q)$ is convex with $C(0) = C'(0) = 0$ and $\lim_{q\to\infty} C'(q) = \infty$. Probability of frugal is $\pi$.

\emph{Read.} $\theta_i q$ = value of a flight of quality $q$ to type $i$; $t$ = fare paid. Higher $\theta_2$ means \emph{steeper indifference curve} in $(q,t)$-space (sophisticated will pay more for the same quality bump) --- this is the \textbf{Single Crossing Property} / Spence--Mirrlees.

\begin{tabular}{p{5cm}|p{16cm}|p{17cm}}
\textbf{Step} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{First Best (firm OBSERVES type)}} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Second Best (firm CANNOT observe type)}} \\
\hline
\textbf{Problem} &
\[ \max_{q_i, t_i}\; t_i - C(q_i) \quad \text{s.t.}\;\; \theta_i q_i - t_i \ge 0\; (\text{IR}_i),\;\; i=1,2. \]
One IR per type; the firm tailors a separate offer to each.
&
\[ \max_{q_1, t_1, q_2, t_2}\; \pi\bigl(t_1 - C(q_1)\bigr) + (1-\pi)\bigl(t_2 - C(q_2)\bigr) \]
s.t.\ $\textbf{IR}_1, \textbf{IR}_2$ AND $\textbf{IC}_1: \theta_1 q_1 - t_1 \ge \theta_1 q_2 - t_2$, $\textbf{IC}_2: \theta_2 q_2 - t_2 \ge \theta_2 q_1 - t_1$.
\\
\hline
\textbf{FOC for quality} &
\textbf{Both types efficient:} $C'(q_i^{FB}) = \theta_i$ for $i = 1, 2$. \;The marginal cost of quality equals the marginal value to the type buying it.
&
\textbf{Frugal degraded, soph.\ untouched:}
\[ C'(q_2^{SB}) = \theta_2 \;\;\text{(\textbf{no distortion at the top})} \]
\[ C'(q_1^{SB}) = \theta_1 - \tfrac{1-\pi}{\pi}(\theta_2 - \theta_1) \;\;\text{(\textbf{downward distortion at the bottom})} \]
$q_1^{SB} < q_1^{FB}$, $q_2^{SB} = q_2^{FB}$.
\\
\hline
\textbf{Fares} &
\textbf{Full extraction:} $t_i^{FB} = \theta_i q_i^{FB}$.\;Each type pays their full WTP; both IRs bind.
&
\textbf{Frugal: zero surplus, IR$_1$ binds.} $t_1^{SB} = \theta_1 q_1^{SB}$. \newline
\textbf{Business: rent left on the table, IC$_2$ binds.} $t_2^{SB} = \theta_2 q_2^{SB} - \underbrace{(\theta_2 - \theta_1) q_1^{SB}}_{\text{information rent}}$. \newline
The bracket is exactly what business would gain by mimicking leisure --- the firm has to leave it.
\\
\hline
\textbf{Buyer surplus} &
$0$ for both types.
&
$U_1^{SB} = 0$ (frugal, IR binds). $U_2^{SB} = (\theta_2 - \theta_1) q_1^{SB} > 0$ (business earns the rent).
\\
\hline
\textbf{Why this allocation?} &
Types observable $\Rightarrow$ no defection possible. Set $q$ at the tangency $C'(q) = \theta_i$ and charge full WTP. The point in $(q,t)$-space is the tangency between the firm's iso-profit curve and the type's indifference curve through the origin.
&
The first-best is \emph{not} IC: at $B$ (frugal's FB bundle), business gets utility $\theta_2 q_1 - t_1 = (\theta_2 - \theta_1) q_1 > 0$ --- they would lie and grab B. \newline
Two options to restore IC:
$\bullet$ Cut $t_2$ to give business the same surplus they'd get at B (still $q_2 = q_2^{FB}$). \emph{Costs rent, no efficiency loss.}
$\bullet$ Reduce $q_1$ (degrade economy) so that B is less attractive for business. \emph{Saves rent, but distorts leisure away from efficiency.}
Optimum: \textbf{both at once} until $\pi(\theta_1 - C'(q_1)) = (1-\pi)(\theta_2 - \theta_1)$.
\\
\hline
\textbf{Plot} & 
{{img:1|w=620}}
&
{{img:2|w=620}}
\\
\hline
\textbf{Reading the plot} & 
$A = $ sophisticated bundle, $B = $ frugal bundle. Indifference curves pass through origin (IR binds = zero buyer surplus). Iso-profit curves $t = \bar\Pi + C(q)$ are convex. \textbf{Tangency} between IC and iso-profit $\Rightarrow$ $C'(q_i^*) = \theta_i$ (slope of IC equals slope of iso-profit). \textbf{Production efficiency, full extraction.}
& 
$A \to A'$: same quality $q_2$, but the fare drops by the rent $(\theta_2 - \theta_1) q_1^{SB}$ so business is willing to stay. \newline
$B \to B'$: reduce $q_1$ and $t_1$ along the frugal's indifference curve (IR$_1$ stays binding, $U_1 = 0$). Lower $q_1$ shrinks the rent $(\theta_2 - \theta_1) q_1$ that business would steal at B --- saving on $A'$. The optimal trade-off equates the marginal saved-rent on business to the marginal lost-profit on frugal.
\\
\hline
\textbf{DWL} &
$0$. Both types served efficiently, surplus fully transferred (not destroyed).
&
$> 0$. Frugal's missing quality $q_1^{FB} - q_1^{SB}$ destroys real surplus. \textbf{The DWL is the price of asymmetric information.}
\\
\hline
\textbf{Comparative statics} & 
$q_i^{FB}$ depends only on $(\theta_i, C(\cdot))$ --- not on type distribution.
& 
$q_1^{SB}$ decreases in $(\theta_2 - \theta_1)$ (bigger type gap $\Rightarrow$ stronger temptation $\Rightarrow$ more degradation needed). \newline
$q_1^{SB}$ decreases in $\frac{1-\pi}{\pi}$ (more sophisticated relative to frugal $\Rightarrow$ rents matter more $\Rightarrow$ more aggressive degradation). \newline
\emph{Reading: the firm is willing to sacrifice profits on each frugal customer in proportion to how many sophisticated customers it can extract more from.}
\\
\hline
\textbf{Mussa--Rosen logic in one line} & 
First best $=$ perfect PD: $C'(q_i) = \theta_i, t_i = \theta_i q_i$, $U_i = 0$.
& 
Second best $=$ \textbf{degrade the bottom + leave rent at the top}: $\boxed{C'(q_1^{SB}) = \theta_1 - \tfrac{1-\pi}{\pi}(\theta_2 - \theta_1),\;\; t_2^{SB} = \theta_2 q_2^{FB} - (\theta_2 - \theta_1) q_1^{SB}}.$
\\
\hline
\textbf{Connection to airline cabins} & 
If airline could check expense reports: business class at \$2{,}000 (full WTP), economy at \$300 (full WTP). Both fly, no rents leak.
& 
Real world: business class \$1{,}700 (after the \$300 rent left to deter defection); economy is \textbf{intentionally degraded} (cramped seat, no upgrades, no lounge access) so business flyers don't even consider it. Leisure gets a strictly worse trip than they would in first best --- that's the DWL.
\\
\end{tabular}

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Take-aways.}}

$\bullet$ \textbf{No distortion at the top, downward distortion at the bottom.} The high type always gets the efficient quality; only the low type's bundle is shrunk.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Two costs of asymmetric information}: (i) the rent left to the high type, (ii) the DWL from shrinking the low type's quality. The firm chooses the mix that minimises their sum.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Mussa--Rosen trade-off:} $\frac{\partial(\text{rent on } H)}{\partial q_L} \;=\; \frac{\partial(\text{lost profit on } L)}{\partial q_L}$. Lower $q_L$ saves rent but kills surplus on leisure.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Single Crossing is the binding case:} this analysis assumes $H$'s WTP exceeds $L$'s at every $q$ (linear). With sigmoidal / saturating preferences (real life), the IC is naturally slacker and screening gets \textbf{strictly easier}. The linear case is the firm's worst-case scenario.

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Cross-refs:}} preamble on monopoly + AS, adverse-selection taxonomy, screening with continuous types, signaling (Spence), used cars (Akerlof).

nodes.title: Asymmetric Information --- intro (adverse selection vs moral hazard)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Setting --- asymmetric information.}}

A market or contracting situation involves \textbf{asymmetric information} when one party knows something relevant to the trade that the other does not. The informed side has private knowledge about a \emph{type} (who they are) or an \emph{action} (what they do); the uninformed side can only condition on what is observable.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Two canonical forms.}}

The asymmetry shows up in two structurally different ways. The distinction is \emph{when} the private information arises relative to the contract:

\begin{tabular}{p{8cm}|p{15cm}|p{15cm}}
 & \textbf{Adverse Selection (AS)} & \textbf{Moral Hazard (MH)} \\
\hline
\textbf{a) what's hidden} & \emph{Hidden type / hidden characteristic.} The informed party knows who they are (risk class, productivity, quality). & \emph{Hidden action / hidden effort.} The informed party chooses an action the principal cannot observe (or verify in court). \\
\hline
\textbf{b) timing} & \textbf{Pre-contract.} Private info exists \emph{before} the contract is signed. & \textbf{Post-contract.} Action is chosen \emph{after} the contract is signed. \\
\hline
\textbf{c) keyword} & Who am I dealing with? & What will they do? \\
\end{tabular}

\bigskip


\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Reading: why this taxonomy matters.}}

The two problems require different instruments:

$\bullet$ \textbf{AS} is about \emph{sorting} types --- the contract must reveal who the agent is. The principal designs a menu and lets the agent's choice signal type (incentive-compatibility on \emph{types}).

$\bullet$ \textbf{MH} is about \emph{motivating} an action --- the agent's identity is fixed, but his effort must be elicited. The contract ties payment to a noisy signal of effort (incentive-compatibility on \emph{actions}).

\textcolor{purple}{\emph{Same mathematical tool, different binding constraint:}} in both cases we solve a constrained optimisation where the IC constraint is what asymmetric information adds on top of the standard participation (IR) constraint. In AS the IC is \emph{across types}; in MH it is \emph{across actions of one agent}.



\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The cost of inducing revelation.}}

Getting types to reveal themselves is not free. The IC constraint forces the principal to leave \emph{information rents} to good types and to \emph{distort the contract of bad types away from first best} so that good types do not want to mimic them.

Resulting inefficiencies:

$\bullet$ \emph{Information rents:} good types are paid more than their reservation utility just to keep them from pooling.

$\bullet$ \emph{Downward distortion at the bottom:} the bad type's allocation (quantity, coverage, quality) is reduced below the efficient level --- this hurts the bad type but slackens the good type's IC, lowering the rent the principal must pay.

$\bullet$ \emph{Exclusion / partial unravelling:} if rents are too costly, the principal drops the worst types from the menu altogether and gains from trade with them vanish.

So the screening menu is \emph{2nd-best}: it is the best one can do given that types are private, but strictly below the symmetric-information first best.

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Three markets with adverse selection.}}

\begin{tabular}{p{10cm}|p{14cm}|p{14cm}}
\textbf{market} & \textbf{the AS problem} & \textbf{market solution} \\
\hline
\textbf{1) Health insurance} & High-risk individuals know their own risk; insurer doesn't. A single pooled premium attracts the sick and repels the healthy $\Rightarrow$ premium rises $\Rightarrow$ healthy drop out (death spiral). & \emph{Differentiated plans} (menu of deductible/coverage pairs): low deductible at high premium for high-risk, high deductible at low premium for low-risk. Types self-select. \\
\hline
\textbf{2) Used cars (Akerlof)} & Seller knows if the car is a peach or a lemon; buyer doesn't. At the average price peaches won't sell $\Rightarrow$ only lemons trade. & \emph{Third-party screening:} certified inspections (CarFax, mechanic reports), dealer warranties, return policies --- the uninformed side buys a verification technology that converts hidden info into hard info. \\
\hline
\textbf{3) Labour market (Spence)} & Worker knows his productivity; employer doesn't. Pooled wage = average productivity drives high types out. & \emph{Signaling through education/tests:} costly signal (degree, certification, exam) acquired by high types because their cost-per-signal is lower. Wage conditions on the signal and separates types. \\
\end{tabular}
